en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Discourse on the Homage and Other Preliminaries from the *Rasavāhinī*.
The feet praised by the Teacher, the refuge for all people,
which bring forth the rays of the jewels from the crowns of Brahmā and others,
and which possess the soft, delicate, and beautiful luster of a lotus.
I pay homage to the one who bears the supreme wheel-mark,
by whom— through long and tireless effort— the Victor has accomplished that path of safety which the practitioner attains.
I perpetually bow down to that peerless Path of Dhamma which shines like a wish-fulfilling tree, a jewel that grants radiance;
[and] to the pure, excellent son of the Sugata, whose faculties are tranquil.
I bow my head in reverence to the Sangha— the worthy recipient of offerings, the pure field of merit,
the refuge for those seeking protection, who have abandoned all suffering,
and who are free from blemish and of great value.
By whatever merit there is here from this praise of the Triple Gem,
having dispelled all misfortune through that merit,
I shall speak this [work] which flows with most sweet flavor.
O good people, listen! That [work] which brings joy—
those various subjects established by the Arahant in former times—
they were illuminated in the Dīpa language and preserved as such by those ancients.
In the Mahāvihāra, a protector of that [tradition], a resident of the Vaṅka Pariveṇa,
known by the name Raṭṭhapāla, a mine of virtue, conduct, and moral discipline,
he translated for the benefit of people from the Pāli language.
All that was previously confused by faults such as repetition and the like, I shall now render free from confusion;
listen to it with concentrated minds.
Since those free from passion spoke it in the past, therefore indeed it has been spoken.
For this is indeed to be honored, always [praised] as "well done" by those who are good.
The Foundation Stories of the Birth in Jambudīpa.
The Dhammasoṇḍaka Chapter.
1. Regarding the story of Dhammasoṇḍaka, this is the sequential narrative.
In that regard, the origins of those stories are twofold: those occurring in Jambudīpa and those in Sīhaḷadīpa.
Among them, there are forty-five in Jambudīpa and sixty-three in Sīhaḷadīpa. Of these, first, the stories originating in Jambudīpa will be made manifest.
Even more than that, the story of Dhammasoṇḍaka is the beginning. How so?
It is said that long ago, in this very Bhaddakappa, a Teacher named Kassapa appeared in the world before our Blessed One.
Not long after the disappearance of that Blessed One’s dispensation, our Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī.
Immediately after his birth, the perception of Dhamma arose in the minds of all beings; therefore, they gave him the name Dhammasoṇḍika.

That prince grew up with a great retinue, attained proficiency in all arts and crafts, and, being honored by his father with the position of viceroy, fulfilled the ten paths of wholesome action, beginning with generosity.
Upon his father’s passing, he was consecrated to the kingship by the ministers.

While that Great King Dhammasoṇḍaka was ruling the kingdom of Bārāṇasī—resembling that of a wheel-turning monarch—in the city of Bārāṇasī, which was like the city of the gods, he thought thus while reclining on his royal couch after the lapse of a month and a half:
"This enjoyment of royal splendor by me alone does not shine, being devoid of the Dhamma; it is like the sun separated from the day."
He reflected on various causes, beginning with "the sky is vast," and thus it is said here:
"By merit consisting of virtue and so forth,
performed in the past without sloth, I have attained this."
Like the king of the gods in the city of Masakkasāra,
he was in his supreme capital, which was rich in royal splendor.
He was captivating in form, a delight to the eyes.
By sound, through the delight of right hearing;
by scent, through the beauty of the nose’s inhalation;
and also by taste, through the flavor of accumulated merit.
Through contact that brings great pleasure to the body,
I have attained the fruits of spiritual success and possess great psychic power; yet, I am not at all negligent.
Knowing that it was not right for me to refuse him, with a mind full of faith,
I thought: "I shall give him even my limbs and my life,
as well as my grain and my wealth."
I shall proclaim the Dhamma that bestows peace, uttered by the Jina,
which brings about the destruction of birth and old age.
Just as water does not shine in the sky without the lord of light (the sun), [so it is with the Dhamma without its teacher].
Just as the night does not shine without the moon, its lord, so too my administration of the kingdom does not shine without Dhamma.
My administration of the kingdom does not shine without Dhamma.
Even if adorned, an elephant does not shine without its tusks;
likewise, my administration of justice does not shine without the Dhamma.
Just as [the ocean] garlanded with waves...
Just as a royal court does not shine without its proper time, so too for me,
the Dhamma does not shine without it.
Just as King Sumaṇḍita shines,
while Kupaṭa does not shine at all,
so too is my administration of the kingdom.
"Without the Dhamma, one does not shine.
I shall listen only to the Dhamma; my mind delights in the Dhamma.
For there is nothing higher than the Dhamma; the Dhamma is the root of the threefold excellence."

Having thought thus, at dawn he emerged from the inner chamber and sat upon a well-prepared royal throne adorned with a raised white parasol, surrounded by a host of ministers, shining like the king of the gods. Seated there, the king spoke thus to his ministers:
"Whosoever among you, sirs, knows any portion of the Dhamma spoken by the Buddha, let him speak it; I wish to hear the Dhamma."
"Your Majesty, we do not know any of them," they replied. Upon hearing this, King Anattamaṇo thought to himself:

"What if I were to place a thousand pieces of gold upon the back of an elephant and have a drum beaten throughout the city, so that perhaps someone, out of greed for wealth, might teach even a single four-line verse of Dhamma? That would be for my long-term welfare."
Thinking, "It will lead to my happiness," he then did accordingly; yet, not finding a teacher of the Dhamma, he gave two thousand, then three, four, five, and even up to ten million pieces of gold.
Then he gave villages, market towns, and provinces; then the positions of treasurer, general, and viceroy;
and furthermore, he gave away the white parasol, casting off his royal attire and himself—

Having proclaimed himself a slave while preaching the Dhamma, and even after having a drum beaten with the cry "I am a slave," King Dhammasoṇḍaka—finding no one to preach the Dhamma—was moved by spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Thinking, "What is the use of sovereignty to me if it means separation from the Dhamma? he handed over the kingdom to his ministers.
Seeking the True Dhamma, the Great King Dhammasoṇḍaka entered the Great Forest, passing through villages, market towns, and royal capitals in succession; thus it was here.
Having caused the pure drum to be sounded,
King Dhammasoṇḍa [proclaimed] the Teacher’s proclamation of the True Dhamma.
Having failed to obtain even ten million pieces of gold,
I abandoned my sovereignty over the country and became a slave to this man.
Thus spoke that protector of the earth:
"Oh, what a greed for worldly things!
Having handed over his delightful kingdom to his ministers,"
"The king entered the forest, seeking the supreme Dhamma.
At the moment he entered the Great Forest, however, by the power of the Great Being's merit, Sakka’s throne manifested a sign of heat.
Then the King of the Devas thought: "Unwillingly, my stone seat of pale-white wool has become hot; what indeed could be the cause?"

While surveying the world, Sakka, the King of Devas, searched throughout the entire Jambudīpa and saw that the Great King Dhammasoṇḍaka, having failed to find anyone who would uphold the True Dhamma, had entered the forest.
The Great King Dhammasoṇḍaka had entered the wilderness, renouncing his kingdom, wealth, kinsmen, and even his life for the sake of the True Dhamma; indeed, he was no ordinary being.

Thinking, "In this very kappa he will become a Buddha; and if this Bodhisatta-to-be enters the great forest today and, failing to find the True Dhamma, should fall into great suffering—that would not be right.
Today I must go there, anoint him with the nectar of the Deathless Dhamma, and establish him in the kingdom," he relinquished his physical form.
Having fashioned a terrifying and massive form in the guise of a *rakkhasa*, he showed himself not far away, facing the Great Being.
Thus it was here: "The tiger, leopard, lion, buffalo, boar, elephant, and panther;
the herd of deer, the thorny rocks, and the trees."
The Lord of Men, desiring the Dhamma, entered the grove and wandered here and there;
by the power of that Purindada, [the rain fell].
The stone seat became warm at will;
by that very means, while surveying the world,
he beheld the Wise One wandering in the forest.
Having today properly satisfied him with the essence of the Dhamma,
they choose their departure; having considered his appearance,
which was as formidable as a mountain peak.
With a great mouth from which terrifying fangs protrude,
with wide eyes resembling blazing fires,
with a sunken middle and a flat-tipped nose;
With a thick mane of hair like a donkey’s bristle,
a dark belly, and a roar as terrifying as thunder;
with long, sharp, blood-stained claws upon his hands and feet.
With a large, clean, and long sword in one hand,
and the other arm marked by a mace-weapon,
he was terrifying with his bared fangs and a forehead furrowed with wrinkles.
Having well-concealed within the forest interior one who was fond of drinking human flesh, terrifying,
and of a harsh yakṣa-like appearance—
"He presented himself before the lord of men.
Then the Great Being saw the rakkhasa standing not far from him;
upon seeing him, he felt no fear, nor trepidation, nor even the slightest alarm. What did he think about this? "Could it be that such a rakkhasa..."
He thought, "I should know the Dhamma; what if I were to listen to the Dhamma in his presence? That will lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time.
Having reflected thus, he thought, "It is fitting that I approach him today and ask," and so, having gone there, he spoke while conversing with the Rakkhasa.
In this forest, adorned with groves of trees and teeming with many blossoming creepers,
you have taken up residence, O one of great majesty.
I ask you, O Lord, speak to me to dispel my doubt.
Seeking the Dhamma, I have come to the forest,
having abandoned my kingdom as well as the assembly of my kinsmen.
"If you know, dear friend,
tell me even a single verse taught by the Sugata.
Then the yakkha said:
I understand only a single portion of the Dhamma proclaimed by the Conqueror,
which is the most excellent of all flavors;
yet here I shall teach you the path of the Dhamma.
"What indeed will you do for me, O giver of the land?
Then the Great Being said:
"If I were to remain established in kingship, O sir..."
I perform worship with formless offerings;
now, having entered alone into the midst of the forest,
what can I do with this body, setting it aside?
If you desire my flesh and blood,
I shall provide for you with that today;
there is nothing else worthy of your worship.
"Desire the Dhamma praised by the Sugata," [said the Buddha].
Then the yakkha said:
"Having eaten meat and being well-satisfied..."
"Having quenched my thirst by drinking blood,
I am now able to preach the Dhamma to you;
I cannot speak, being overcome by hunger."
Then the Great Being said:
"O Yakkha, having first eaten me yourself,
whom will you teach the Dhamma afterwards?"
"Regarding my Dhamma and your acquisition of flesh, you yourself must know how it should come to be.
When this was said, Sakka, the lord of the devas, replied, "Excellent, Great King! I alone know what is appropriate," and he stood not far from him.
"O Great King, having fashioned a great mountain three gavutas in height and the color of collyrium, ascend it; standing upon the summit of this mountain, let yourself fall into my mouth.
As you fall, I shall teach you the Dhamma. If this happens, there will be for you the attainment of the Dhamma, and for me, the attainment of flesh.
Having heard that, the Great Being [reflected] as he wandered through the beginningless cycle of existence...
Thinking, "I have no limit to the number of births in which I have been food for lions, tigers, leopards, fish, turtles, birds, and so forth;
today it is fitting that I sacrifice my life for the sake of the Dhamma and the Truth of the Fully Enlightened One," he spoke thus:
"Wandering through the cycles of saṃsāra..."
Many people experience suffering;
for indeed, O sir, this has not been for one's own benefit or for another's, but was empty and in vain.
"You are a thief of what is not given," "you are an adulterer," "you are a killer of living beings," "you have spoken falsehoods";
"you are a drinker of intoxicants"— thus you have committed these offenses.
They take it up and give it away many times in suffering.
For this, O sir, whether for oneself or for another, has not been for one's welfare; it has been in vain.
Some, having fallen from trees or down precipices,
or through the difficulty of binding or the swallowing of foul poison;
by diseases with various kinds of piercing pains—
Beings suffer from sensations born of temperature;
for this, O sir, has brought no benefit to oneself or to another— it was empty and in vain.
For one who has died within the womb of a tigress, there is no measure of time;
indeed, O sir, whether it be for oneself or for another, [this is the case].
"It was not for my benefit; it was empty.
This gift of intoxicants given by me today will not lead to sovereignty over the gods or any such state."
But having attained omniscience,
for the sake of leading beings across the cycle of existence—
O friend, you have been a great benefactor to me many times.
Therefore, I shall do as you say;
teach me the Dhamma without fear,
for now your heart's desire is being fulfilled.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being climbed the mountain and, standing there, said:
"Today, together with my sovereignty, I give my life and the flesh of my body for the sake of the True Dhamma.
Filled with joy, he said, "Teach me the Dhamma," and as the great-toothed one stood there with his huge mouth wide open, he approached him head-on. Then Sakka...
Somanassa, the lord of the gods, filled with wonder and joy, cast off his own form and manifested a celestial body adorned with divine ornaments.
Shining like the rising sun in the sky, he firmly caught the Great Being with both hands as he was falling from the heavens,
led him to the world of the gods, seated him upon the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, and [honored him] with divine...
Having honored [the Buddha] with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and having heard the Dhamma himself, he became inspired.
Displaying his inspiration, he [recited] the verses taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa which illustrate impermanence and other truths:
"Impermanent indeed are all conditioned things; their nature is to arise and pass away."
"Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is bliss.

By teaching this Dhamma verse, he brought the king's aspiration to its fulfillment. Having shown him the great glory and majesty in the world of the gods, and having brought him back and established him once more in his own kingdom, he exhorted him, saying, "O Great King, be heedful," and then departed for the world of the gods.
Thus, O friend, the virtuous do not even recall their immeasurable glory or their life,
but practice only the praised Dhamma;
for their wealth is more fleeting and their lifespan is short.
"Here, what negligence regarding the wholesome could there possibly be for those such as yourselves?
This is the first story, that of Dhammasoṇḍaka.
2. In the story of the deer-hunter, this is the sequential narrative:
It is said that in the thirty-first aeon from now, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Sikhī, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and attained supreme full enlightenment,

was at one time cultivating seclusion while uplifting the world with its devas from the wilderness of *saṃsāra*, raining down the rain of the jewel of the Dhamma, beating the drum of the Dhamma, and raising the banner of the Dhamma.
He entered a forest grove; having entered, he sat down upon a delightful, cool stone slab—

adorned with groves of various trees such as the *capana*, *supupphita*, *nāga*, and *punnāga*, crowded with various flowering creepers such as the *sumana* and *mālattika*, and frequented by many kinds of two-footed and four-footed creatures—
having spread out his outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) folded fourfold, [illuminating] the directions with his six-colored rays.
Fulfilling [the needs of the assembly], gods, Brahmas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others then gathered there;
honoring, praising, and venerating the Blessed One with divine perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they stood by.
At that great assembly, the Blessed One, emitting a sweet voice with the Brahma-voice, taught the Dhamma connected with the Four Noble Truths—a rain of the Deathless.

It was as if he were making it rain. At that time, a deer-hunter who had entered the forest, having killed deer and pigs and was eating their meat, arrived at that place and saw the Blessed One teaching the Dhamma. Upon seeing him, he stood to one side;

having heard the Dhamma and gained confidence in his heart, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the heavenly world, and subsequently among humans in the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure.
Experiencing successive sovereignties, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during this appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he went forth in the Blessed One’s dispensation.

One day, while listening to the Blessed One preaching a discourse on the Dhamma connected with the realization of the Four Noble Truths, he attained Arahantship through the four analytical knowledges (*catu-paṭisambhidā*). Then, one day...
Having entered into the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he uttered words of joy by declaring his own past deeds:
"In the thirty-first aeon from this one,
a Leader appeared in the world."
Having crossed over the thirty-two marks,
he was the Fully Awakened One known as Sikhī.
Blazing like a lamp-tree, he was like the sun risen in the sky.
The Fully Awakened One, the King of Mountains,
the Lord of Men, possessed of majesty— having filled the vessel of the Dhamma,
that Protector establishes all his offspring from the wilderness of saṃsāra onto the ground of peace.
Raising high the banner of the Dhamma, beating the drum of the Dhamma,
and liberating beings from suffering— the Victor was master there, truly a master.
At one time, the Protector—
The Conqueror, the Illuminator of the World,
the Fully Awakened One who desires solitude,
has gone to the delightful forest.
It was crowded with various trees such as the *puṇṇāga*, *nāga*, and *pūga*;
its branches were entwined by creepers and it was filled with fragrant flowers.
It was frequented by swarms of bees, intoxicated with the joy of the blossoms.
Crowded with herds of various deer, where flocks of peacocks dance,
it possesses excellent cool pools and reservoirs of water with beautiful landing-places;
it is filled with hundreds of cascades by means of showers of rain-like torrents.
Having gone to the great forest,
to the cool surface of the sand,
you sat down upon a stone slab.
Bestowing gifts, he wandered about. The gods,
having gathered there, honored the Supreme among Bipeds with divine perfumes, garlands, dances, and musical instruments.
Then the God of Gods, O Lord, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha,
proclaimed the Four Truths, uttering sweet words.
At that time, I was a hunter, a slayer of deer and swine.
"I live by the flesh of deer; with that I nourish my children. While thus supporting my wife and children, I once went out on a hunt, equipped with my quiver and my bow.
I saw the stainless Buddha,
honored by the assembly of devas;
like the moon amidst a host of stars, or like Mount Meru rising from the midst of the ocean.
I stood there at one side and heard the supreme Dhamma from the Radiant One, who was seated and proclaiming the Four Noble Truths.
Having gained confidence in my mind, I experienced great joy.
In the thirty-first aeon from now,
whatever merit has been accumulated by me—
by that meritorious deed, I...
I was born in a divine womb.
Having experienced successive states of excellence within the realm of the six sense-pleasures,
surrounded by hosts of gods, I dwelt in a palace made of jewels.
I have become a partaker of that which is supreme among humans;
there is no deficiency in my wealth—this is the fruit of hearing the True Dharma.
In this auspicious aeon...
In the most excellent city of Sāvatthī,
I was born into a wealthy, affluent,
and prosperous Śāla family of high standing.
Surrounded by a great retinue, having attained growth and maturity,
I set out on my journey and reached the excellent Jetavana.
There I saw the Sugata seated together with his disciples.
I heard the sweet Dhamma that proclaims the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard the sweet Dhamma and having gone forth in the Teaching,
I have reached the supreme Nibbāna— cool, free from aging and death.
For a single moment I heard the well-taught Dhamma;
because of that, I have not been born in the four lower realms, nor is there any fear for me from anywhere.
Raising my hand, I shall speak: act according to my word!
"Having made me your mother, listen well to the Dhamma.
Having spoken thus, he directed beings toward listening to the Dhamma.
Thus, having listened well to the Dhamma for a very short time, [he attained realization].
Having heard of the power of those who have attained liberation from existence,
O friends, you who desire the happiness of both worldly existence and its cessation,
abandon idleness, listen to the Dhamma— so difficult to hear, so difficult to obtain!
The second story: The Story of the Deer-Hunter.
3. In the story of the three people, this is the sequential narrative:
It is said that in former times there was a great heat in Jambudīpa; at that time, due to the scorching sun, even the ponds [were dried up] along with their rays of light.

Having drunk the water dry from lotus ponds, rivers, mountain caves, cascades, and so forth, when the water was completely exhausted, fish, turtles, and other creatures for the most part met their destruction.
Then, in the great wilderness regions, the trees, grasses, creepers, and so on became exceedingly withered.
Even the beasts and birds, scorched by the heat and parched with thirst, mistook a mirage for water.
Running here and there, they fell into great suffering.

At that time, a young quail, thirsty and searching for water here and there in the great forest, smelled the scent of water from a sixty-fathom deep pit beneath a rotten tree and, out of greed, descended into it to drink.
Due to drinking too much, he became so heavy that he fell right there and was unable to rise.
Then another pair, a snake and a human, also fell right there; for snakes, having obtained seclusion, cast off their bodies.
Therefore, this one, not having obtained seclusion, was unable to rise up. And the human also [could not rise] due to a lack of support.
Being unable to rise and terrified by the fear of death, they remained right there without harming one another. Then one...
A man living in Benares entered the forest and, while searching for water, reached that place;
seeing those three, his heart trembled. He tied a basket with a creeper, placed it in a carrying-net, lowered it down, and pulled up all three of them.
Then, out of joy at the thought, "They have given us our lives," he spoke thus to them.
"Master, we have obtained our livelihood by depending on you; from now on, you are our companion and we are yours.
We wish to come to your dwelling place," they said. Then, among them, the young parrot said:
"Master, there is a great banyan tree at the southern gate of Bārāṇasī; I dwell there, and for such a task as yours..."
Having said, "When you need me, come into my presence and make a sound," he departed after establishing a firm bond of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
The snake also said, "I have a great anthill not far from that very *nigrodha* tree; I dwell there.
When you need me, come there and make a long, loud sound," and likewise departed. The man [remained] in Bārāṇasī.
"I live in such-and-such a house on such-and-such a street; when you are there, come to me," he said, and then departed.

Later, when that helpful man had some business of his own to attend to, he went according to the appointment, thinking, "I shall go to my companions," and standing at the foot of the banyan tree, he made a sound with his beak. Hearing it, [the parrot]...
The young bird, arriving with speed, greeted him and said, "Friend, you have been gone for a long time; tell me the reason for your coming.
He replied, "Friend, being unable to live any longer, I have entrusted my wife and children to my kinsmen and have come into your presence.
The young bird said, "Excellent, friend! You have done well in coming into my presence."
"She gave me my life; it is fitting that I too should provide a means for your life.
Rest here for a short while until I return," he said, and departed in search of a means to save her life.
At that time, it is said, the King of Bārāṇasī had come out from the city, entered a well-prepared garden, and after sporting with his retinue, it was now midday.
Having seen the auspicious lotus pond, which was in full bloom and strewn with five kinds of lotuses, he desired to bathe;
so, having removed all his ornaments and entrusted them to the royal guards, he descended into the water to bathe.
At that time, a young parrot that had arrived at that place, perched among the branches, seeing the negligence of the royal guards, bit the king’s pearl necklace and flew up into the sky.
Having arrived in haste and given it to his companion, he said, "Use this with care," and handed it over.
Then, taking it, he thought, "Where shall I put this? and considering, "I have a friend living within the city;
I will place it with him," he went to the appointed place, saw him, and exchanged greetings.
Having made this known, he said, "After revealing the service rendered by Suvapota, place this pearl necklace safely," and gave it to him.
At that moment, the king, having bathed and anointed himself while putting on his ornaments, did not see the pearl necklace.
Then the king’s men, searching among the attendants both inside and outside, and not seeing the pearl necklace, beat the drum in the city.
They made a proclamation: "Whoever sees the pearl necklace, to him the king will grant great honor.
Hearing this, that betrayer of friends thought: "I am suffering; what if I were to show the pearl necklace to the king and live in comfort?
What use is this to me? Thus, failing to recognize the benefit he had rendered, that great betrayer of friends acted accordingly.
A man approached the king’s officers and told them that he had placed a pearl necklace near him, saying, "Sirs, a certain man placed a pearl necklace near me.
Thus it is with association with an unwholesome person; for it is so:
just as the *nimba* tree, though nurtured, yields sweet milk when tapped.
That sweet benefit you have done for me, though performed with no expectation of reward, does not go to waste. Just as a young tree,
even when watered upon its head, does not fail to yield sweet fruit, so too that kindness you have shown me,
being done without expectation, does not go to waste.
Just as a snake reared constantly on milk and water turns that very milk into poison,
so does a base person turn a kindness back upon its giver.
Just as fire produced by oneself will certainly not provide coolness.
In the same way, an evil deed committed toward an inferior person consumes one's own body like fire.
Therefore, having investigated with the faculty of wisdom through various gestures and expressions, beings should practice loving-kindness; for an enemy finds no happiness.
Then, at the word of Mittadubbhin, the king’s men took the pearl necklace and the man, and presented them together with the goods to the king.
When the king saw the thief together with the goods, he became enraged and commanded, "Take this man away and impale him alive at the southern gate!
The king’s men departed, carrying out his command; and as the man was being led away by them, [the story continues].
Having emerged from the southern gate and remembering his companion, thinking,
"Perhaps there might be some safety from him," he saw the anthill by following the previously agreed-upon signal and called out, "Friend Dīgha!
Seeing him emerging from the anthill and approaching in that manner, [Dīgha] was moved with emotion and, overcome by suffering, reflected on his friend's present state.
Thinking, "It is necessary for me to become a support by means of my disguise," he comforted him;
then, casting off his own form and approaching the king's men in another guise, he spoke firmly, saying, "Do not kill this man for a moment!
After a short while, he went to the place where the King’s chief queen resided, bit the queen in the form of a snake, and by her—

At the time he was fainting from the poison, he said, "I know the antidote to poison," and having reached the state of being condemned to death in the guise of a human, he went at that very moment to his companion.

He told him, "When you have been cooked by the king, go at the time of the meal and strike the queen’s body with a handful of water, saying, 'Make it free of poison,' and then depart. Thereupon, the king, searching for a physician for the poison, [sent for him].
Having heard that news, he commanded, "Bring him here as one who has reached the point of execution," and then said, "Make her free from the poison.
He made her free from the poison in the manner described by the Nāga king; she became happy and free from disease.
When the king saw her, he was delighted and paid great honor to him with gifts of fields, land, vehicles, draft animals, and so forth. Then he approached the king.
He revealed everything that he had done himself. Therefore it was said:
"Once, O Great King, having gone to the forest for some business, I saw a young golden bird fallen in a great enclosure."
Furthermore, out of compassion,
I lifted up both Rāga and Manussa when they had fallen into suffering, overcome by hunger.
Then those three said to me:
"You have given us our life; you are our benefactor.

His son was named Uposatha. To Uposatha was born a son named Mandhātā.
Endowed with the seven treasures and the four supernormal powers, he ruled as a universal monarch (*cakkavattin*).
When he contracted his left hand and snapped his right hand, a rain of the seven treasures fell from the sky to the depth of his knees, like divine clouds.
It rained. Such a marvel occurred. For eighty-four thousand years he played the games of a prince;
for eighty-four thousand years he exercised the office of viceroy; for eighty-four thousand years he ruled as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), and his lifespan was incalculable.
One day, being unable to satisfy his craving for sensual pleasures, he showed signs of weariness, and the ministers—
"Your Majesty, what is this longing? they asked. He replied, "When I look upon my meritorious deeds, this kingdom is not sufficient for me;
what place, indeed, is delightful? "The world of the gods, Great King," they said.
He then sprinkled water over the Wheel-Treasure and, together with his retinue, went to the Cātumahārājika heaven, where the four Great Kings [received him].

With divine *māla* flowers in their hands and surrounded by hosts of deities, they went out to meet him, took him, and went to the realm of the Four Great Kings (*Cātumahārājika*), where they handed over the kingdom to him.
While he was ruling the kingdom surrounded by his retinue, a long period of time passed.
Being unable to satisfy his craving even there, he became disenchanted and showed signs of distress. Then, the four...
The great kings asked, "Great King, why are you distressed? Of what place is this world of the gods more delightful?
"Your Majesty, we are like attendants to others; the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is a hundred times more delightful than this.
Then Mandhātā, having caused the wheel-treasure to ascend, surrounded by his own retinue—
He set out toward the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Then Sakka, the king of the gods, with a divine *māla* flower in his hand and surrounded by a host of deities, went out to meet him;
taking him by the hand, he said, "Come this way, Great King.

Thereupon, as the king was departing surrounded by the host of deities, the Wheel-Treasure, acting as the commander-in-chief, took charge and, together with the assembly, descended to the realm of men.
He entered his own home. Sakka led Mandhātā to the celestial realm of Sakka, divided the gods into two portions, and having split his own sovereignty down the middle, gave it to him.
From that time forth, both kings ruled over their respective realms.
As time passed in this way, Sakka exhausted his lifespan of three *koṭis* and sixty-one hundred thousand years.
Another Sakka was reborn; he too, having exercised divine sovereignty in the same manner, passed away at the end of his lifespan.
In this way, thirty-six Sakkas passed away. However, Mandhātā continued to exercise divine sovereignty by means of human power alone.
As time passed for him in this way, an even greater craving for sensual pleasures arose within him, and he thought: "What use have I for half a kingdom?"
He thought, "Having killed Sakka, I shall rule as a sole monarch. However, it was impossible to kill Sakka; rather, this craving for sensual pleasure is the root of misfortune.
For it is said: "It is better here to endure suffering than for a man to be destroyed by unbridled desire."
Whether here or in the world beyond, one never finds anything pleasant.
From craving arises sorrow;
from craving arises fear.
For one who is completely free from craving, there is no sorrow;
whence could there be fear?
A man who is a slave to craving here [encounters] that which arises from kings, thieves, and so forth.

Through the arising of that greed by which living beings are constantly overcome— [greed for] fields, lands, gold, cattle, horses, slaves, and servants— one encounters suffering such as the cutting off of one's hand and is tormented.
"That greed must be abandoned by the wise with all their might.
Consequently, for him who was struck down by excessive desire, the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) declined and old age assailed his body;
for a human body indeed does not burst open in the world of the gods. Thus, having passed away from the world of the gods, he entered the park of the city of Bandhumatī.
The park-keeper informed the royal court of his arrival. The king came from the palace and had a seat prepared right there in the park.
Then, Mandhātā lay down upon the excellent seat prepared in the park and made his bed for the night without rising.
Thereupon, the ministers asked, "Your Majesty, what shall we say after you? He replied, "After me, you [shall say] this..."
"You should proclaim the Teaching to the great multitude, saying:

'The Great King Mandhātu, having exercised the sovereignty of a Wheel-turning Monarch over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands, having exercised sovereignty among the Cātumahārājika devas, and having exercised sovereignty in the world of the gods for the full lifespan of thirty-six Sakkas, passed away. Having spoken thus, he passed away according to his karma."
To reveal this meaning— that [Mandhātu] had passed away— the Blessed One spoke these verses in the midst of the four great assemblies:
"As far as the sun and moon revolve, illuminating and shining upon all directions—
every one of those living beings who depend upon the earth were slaves to Mandhātu."
No satisfaction in sensual pleasures is found even by a rain of gold coins;
sensual pleasures offer little gratification and are full of suffering—thus the wise man understands.
Even regarding celestial pleasures, he finds no delight in them.
"He delights in the destruction of craving, he is a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having heard this, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other fruits.
Thus, for those whose destiny is fixed and who are supreme in awakening;
Craving that has transcended suffering gives [gifts] by bringing them under one's own power;
what need is there to speak of those whose destiny is uncertain, such as people like me?
Thinking, "Abandon that craving," O friends, devote yourselves to the Triple Gem.
The eighth story: The Story of Mahāmandhātā.
9. In the Story of the Merchant Buddhavamma, this is the sequential narrative:
It is said that in the city of Pāṭaliputta in Jambudīpa, there was a merchant named Buddhavamma who lived by the work of a merchant.
While he was still living, he later traveled about engaged in trade with caravan leaders among villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals.

At that time, the Blessed One, surrounded by a thousand bhikkhus, was wandering on a tour of the countryside, delivering many gods and humans from the wilderness of saṃsāra. Then he saw the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Seeing the Blessed One—who was like a golden Mount Meru rising from the water, resplendent and surrounded by a great community of monks—the body of the man was suffused with supreme joy.
With palms joined in reverence, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and because of his unfamiliarity with the Buddha’s teaching, invited the Blessed One for a meal that evening.
Then the Blessed One [replied], "We abstain from eating at the improper time."
"Thus have the Tathāgatas spoken," he said. Then, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he asked, "Venerable sir, will the Blessed Ones eat at an improper time?
Thereupon, in response to his question, the Blessed One explained that eight kinds of drinks are permitted for the Tathāgatas to consume at an improper time.
They are as follows: mango juice, rose-apple juice, plantain juice, breadfruit juice, *phārusaka* juice, honey juice, and grape juice.
"Regarding 'drinking of lotus roots' (*sālūkapāna*): Having heard that, the merchant prepared a drink of grapes with various flavorful juices and gave it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.

After the Teacher, together with the Saṅgha of monks, had consumed the juice of the drink, he taught the Dhamma to him and departed on his journey through the countryside. He too, with a mind full of faith, turned back along with the merchants."
Engaging in trade in various regions, he reached a wilderness known as Mahāvattanīya;
there, the water in all their carts was completely exhausted. Neither the people nor the oxen had any water left.
Then that merchant, overcome by thirst, searched for water among those various carts.
He was wandering about. Then, some people in a cart saw him and, out of compassion, said, "Come here;
there is a little water in this jar, drink it. He went and drank the water. To him, that taste was like the juice of a grape drink;
even as he was drinking, he thought: "At that time, for me, [it was like] the Perfectly Enlightened One..."

Thinking, "Today the result of the gift of grape-wine will be realized," he went there with a heart filled with wonder and amazement and, moved by joy, opened the lid of the jar himself. The entire jar was completely full of grape-wine.
Then, seeing that water—which was fragrant, flavorful, inexhaustible, and like a divine drink—he [drank].
With his body suffused with supreme joy, he cried out, "Let all drink the water! Hearing this, they all gathered together, and upon seeing the water, they were struck with wonder.
Standing in their midst, the merchant, proclaiming the power of the Buddha, said:
"Behold, sirs, this majesty of the Great Sage!"
Inconceivable is the power of generosity, visible in this very life and immediate in its result.
This water which I gave with a mind full of faith toward the Buddha is ripening right now through the power of the Sage’s vehicle.
Like rice-gruel rich with nutritive essence, like cool and sweet water,
or like the divine drink of the gods— this wonderful, inexhaustible [gift] has arisen.
What wise person indeed would not give to those possessed of virtue?
In this world and the next, the supreme gift is that which bestows happiness.
May they take as much as they desire and drink sweet water;
may they fill their vessels and go away with everything they wish for.
Having spoken thus, he satisfied all the people and the oxen with grape juice alone.
Even as they drank water from here and there, the water remained inexhaustible.
Then the merchant, having engaged in trade together with the caravan leaders, was returning to his own city; seeing the Blessed One, he thought, "I shall go to Veḷuvana."
Having gone and paid homage to the Teacher, and having received permission, he sat down to one side. The Teacher also engaged in pleasant conversation with him.
The lay follower said, "Venerable sir, having seen your miracle and being filled with faith, I came after paying homage, thinking, 'I shall depart.
And such was that miracle," and he related it in detail. Then the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. He—
Having heard the Dhamma and invited the Teacher for the following day, he gave a great almsgiving and returned to his own home.

From that time forth, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in size, surrounded by celestial nymphs and endowed with divine sovereignty. For the purpose of making known his former karma:
In various places, it was filled with divine grape-juices in jeweled vessels.
Having drunk the beverage, the gods danced, played music, and sported.
Thus people do not know the vast essence of the Victor.
One obtains vast wealth from the gift of even a mere drink;
O friends, you who have recognized the multitude of virtues in the three bases,
you shall indeed obtain a distinction through giving to those possessed of virtue.
The ninth story: The Story of the Merchant Buddhavamma.
10. In the story of Rūpadevī, this is the sequential narrative:
It is said that in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, a certain village girl was wandering about in the monastery in that city.
Seeing a certain sick monk, her heart trembling, she approached him, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, what illness afflicts you?

Does it cause pain to your body? When he replied, "Sister, a severe illness afflicts me," she invited him, saying, "In that case, Venerable sir, I shall cure that disease. Having gone home, she informed her parents of this matter.
Having spoken thus, she was granted permission by them; on the following day, she prepared various excellent flavors of medicinal food.
Then, on the next day, that bhikkhu, having put on his robe and going for alms, went to her house and stood there.
Seeing that the Elder had arrived, she became filled with joy, took his bowl, prepared a seat, and gave it to him. Therein—
Having served him food with great care while he was seated, she paid him honor. Then, by the power of her faith, as soon as he had finished eating, that illness was completely pacified.
Consequently, with his disease cured, he did not go to her house on the following day.
Thereupon, she went to the monastery, paid homage to him, and asked, "Why have you not come? He replied, "Sister, my illness..."
"It has subsided; therefore, I have not come," he said. Hearing this, she was filled with joy and exclaimed, "Excellent, venerable sir! and returned home.
Having passed away through that meritorious deed, she was reborn in the world of the gods.
There, a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in extent appeared for her. Enjoying divine sovereignty there, she spent the interval between six Buddhas.
In our Blessed One’s time, he took rebirth in Jambudīpa, in the city of Devaputta, in the womb of the wife of the senior brahmin of an eminent brahmin family.
When she perceived that [the fetus] had reached maturity, she emerged from her mother’s womb.
From the moment of her emergence from the mother’s womb, day by day, [she required] rice measuring eight times eight *nāḷi*s.
She was reborn. Seeing her physical beauty, her parents, filled with faith, gave her the name Rūpadevī.

Later, they united her with a suitable young man. Then, when she began to cook a measure of rice, all the sauces she desired, such as meat and the like, as well as cow-products such as ghee, fresh butter, curds, and milk, and pungent condiments such as ginger and pepper, appeared.
She is born having produced utensils such as plantains, jackfruit, honey, and molasses, which fill her vessels;
whatever hard or soft food she takes in her hand does not become putrid;
and even when she serves the entire city's inhabitants from a single bowl of rice, the spot where even that single ladleful was taken is no longer visible. Thus, her merit is inexhaustible.
She became as renowned throughout the entire city of the sons of devas as the moon and the sun;

then, having invited five hundred bhikkhus, she constantly fed them in her own residence. At that time, among them was a certain Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā);
seeing with his divine eye the power of this woman’s merit, he did not know the kamma she had performed in the past.

Thinking, "What if I were to reveal her [past] lives? one day, after eating at her residence and offering a blessing of thanksgiving, he asked, "Do you know, sister, what deed was performed by you in the past? "I do not know, venerable sir. "I wish to hear it," she said;
thereupon, he revealed her past karma to her.
In the ninety-first aeon from now,
there was a leader named Vipassī,
the sole eye of the world in the world.
The Leader has severed his bonds.
At that time, in that delightful city, you were a village girl;
while wandering about, you saw a disciple of the Conqueror in a monastery.
Having seen him afflicted by disease, emaciated and pale, gasping for breath again and again, your heart trembled;
and having invited that sage, you gave him both medicine and food. Because of that, he was a renunciant.
Free from affliction, free from distress, and free from calamity, you existed in that state. Then,
having passed away from there due to that well-performed deed,
you were born in the world of the devas, where all desires are fulfilled.
There, by the power of their merit, there was a palace made of jewels,
strewn with hundreds of jewel-stūpas and adorned with gabled chambers;
it was filled with many hundreds of rooms and furnished with couches and seats.
Crowded with hundreds of celestial nymphs and filled with dancing, singing, and the like,
it was adorned with rows of pleasure gardens featuring groves of *rambhā*,
*ambaja*, and *jambu* trees, as well as *pūga*, *punnāga*, *pāṭalī*, *nāga*, and other trees.
Adorned with clusters of lotuses and water-lilies, and graced by groves of *kunda* flowers;
filled with swarms of bees intoxicated by honey, and crowded with cranes and female cranes;
[it was frequented] by many sons of the gods as well as by celestial nymphs.
While enjoying such great wealth, a celestial mansion that brings joy to the mind,
and thus possessing great glory in the world of the gods,
you shall spend the duration of your time until the Conqueror Gotama has attained final Nibbāna.
Now you have been reborn here in Jambudīpa in a noble family;
you are an abode of the virtues of merit and wisdom, preeminent in beauty, and sweet-spoken.
This marvelous sovereignty of a goddess that you possess in the world of the gods—
All this human happiness that you have here in this world is the fruit of that gift you gave to a single sick bhikkhu at the time of the Buddha Vipassī.
"Merit must always be performed by one who desires the attainment of happiness;
therefore, O Bhaddā, you should always be diligent in wholesome deeds.
Having thus revealed the karma he had performed in his previous existence, he now said: "Be heedful in meritorious deeds."
He instructed her. Having heard the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma, she was filled with supreme joy;
from that time forth, devoted to giving and other meritorious deeds, she performed acts of virtue, and through that very joy, she became a stream-enterer and a noble female disciple.
Thus, the young maiden found the essence in meritorious deeds.
Having given alms to a bhikkhu while ignorant of his virtues,
you have obtained the happiness of gods and humans in this world;
since you understand the ripening of wholesome deeds, why should you not attain peace?
The tenth story, concerning Rūpadevī.
The first chapter, the Dhammasoṇḍaka Chapter.
The Nandiyarāja Chapter.
11. This is the sequential narrative concerning the story of King Nandiya.
It is said that one hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara arose in the world, delivering the world—including the devas—from the wilderness of saṃsāra.
At that time, it is said, a certain householder [attended] the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching.
Having heard this, with a mind full of faith, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having prepared a great almsgiving and adorned his own residence like the abode of the gods, he arranged a great seat worthy of the Buddha.
Then, having gone to the Blessed One, he requested: "Venerable Sir, it is now time for the Blessed One to come to the meal. Thereupon, the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus—
Having arrived through the great power of the Buddha, he sat upon the excellent seat prepared for the Buddha.
Then the householder, joyful and elated, together with his retinue, served the Blessed One with many kinds of sweet foods, drinks, and other offerings.

At that time, in the teaching of the Blessed One, the great disciple named the Elder Vasabha—who was foremost among those who maintain the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)—was walking for alms according to the practice of sequential begging.

While wandering, he stood at the door of that householder’s residence; then, seeing the elder, the householder requested, "Venerable sir, the Teacher is seated within the house; you too should enter. Without entering, the elder departed.
The householder approached the Blessed One and reported that matter, asking, "Venerable sir, is there anyone in the world with its devas who is superior even to the Blessed One?"
"He is known by his virtue," he said. Then the Teacher, illustrating this with the simile of a son and praising the elder’s virtues, spoke thus:
"The sons of the Sage, possessing few desires, maintain the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so forth, making it stainless, and they have undertaken the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)."
In constant hand-to-hand combat, they are like proud warriors clad in armor;
having become the very foundation of merit, they bestow gifts upon gods and humans.
I wear a beautiful robe, even one from Sivi.
The sons of the Buddha, those great nagas, do not wear such things.
Free from desire and greed, they wear rags from a dust heap,
stitched together with scraps of cloth, like a garment for covering a wound.
"O friend, I always accept the invitation of a lay follower;
yet the Perfectly Awakened One does not approve of a son's begging for food.
Whatever is obtained by going from house to house, whether it be coarse or refined,"
My sons are content with that, being free from craving for flavors.
I lie down well upon a comfortable, pleasant bed, yet they,
fearing the terror of saṃsāra, do not prepare a bed for themselves.
By moving from place to place, they maintain their deportment;
we dwell in palaces crowded with many stories.
Those sons of the Buddha never enter such a dwelling as that.
They delight at the foot of trees, in charnel grounds, and in the open air.
Having cultivated the supreme cause for the destruction of becoming,
I shall dwell in the village, bringing peace to the people.
"My sons delight in remote lodgings, Kakā;
among them, this great elder Vasabha is the most eminent.
A cleanser of evil, the foremost of those who practice the ascetic virtues (dhutaṅga), he is renowned throughout my teaching."
Thus the Blessed One, having raised his hand as if striking the lunar disk, proclaimed the Elder’s virtues;
then, having heard that account of his virtues and desiring that very position for himself, he resolved upon that state, thinking:
"What if I were to become the foremost among those who maintain the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) in the dispensation of some future Perfectly Enlightened One?"
Making his aspiration, he prostrated himself at the feet of the Blessed One. The Teacher, having investigated the matter, gave him this prediction:
"One hundred thousand kappas from now, a Teacher named Gotama will appear. At that time, you shall become the foremost among those who uphold the dhutaṅgas, and the fame of your name shall spread.
From then on, filled with joy, he performed meritorious deeds. Thereafter...
Having passed away from there, while enjoying sovereignty among gods and humans, he became a brahmin named Ekasāṭaka during the time of the Sammasambuddha Vipassī and gave a great alms-offering.
Passing away from there, after the Parinibbāna of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, he was reborn in the city of Bārāṇasī as the merchant-chief of Bārāṇasī;
having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he passed away from there and wandered through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
During a human lifespan of ten thousand years, he was reborn as a householder in Bārāṇasī.
While wandering for exercise through the forest, this householder saw a certain paccekabuddha in a remote wilderness region.
That paccekabuddha was there engaged in making robes, but the wind did not blow against him.
Having gathered it together, he began to set it aside. Seeing this, the householder asked, "Venerable sir, what are you doing?
That Paccekabuddha, out of fewness of desires, said nothing when questioned by him.
Realizing that the cloth was not enough for his robe, the householder placed his own upper garment at the feet of the Paccekabuddha and departed. The Paccekabuddha—
Having taken it, he hung it up with the wind and made a robe from it, which he then put on.
At the end of his life, the householder passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
there, having enjoyed celestial splendor for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from that state and was reborn in a certain city located about three leagues from Bārāṇasī. To him—
The parents gave him the name Nandiya; thus they bestowed that name upon him in all respects.
He had seven brothers, and while the remaining six were occupied with various occupations and supported their parents, Nandiya was indolent and lived at home.
Consequently, the others were angry with him. Then the parents, having addressed Nandiya—
They exhorted him, but he remained silent. Later, on another occasion, when a festival had been proclaimed in the village, he said to his mother:

"Mother, give me a garment; I shall play at the festival. She brought out a washed cloth and gave it to him, but he said, "Mother, this is too coarse," and she brought out another and gave that to him, but he rejected that as well. Then his mother—
He said, "Father, since we were born into such a household as this, there is no merit for us to obtain anything more refined than this;
Mother, I shall go to a place where such things can be obtained. His mother said, "Son, I desire that you obtain the kingdom in the city of Bārāṇasī this very day.
"Very well, Mother," he replied, and having paid homage to his mother and circumambulated her, he departed. [His] mother—
It occurred to him: "Where will he go? He will come back and sit here in the house, just as he did before.
However, impelled by the force of his merit, he departed from the village, went to Bārāṇasī, and stayed in the house of Senagutta.
Then one day, while sitting and conversing with his workmen, he said:
While nodding off, he saw a dream: [a snake] emerged from his mouth, spread across the whole of Jambudīpa, and then re-entered his belly. Upon waking, he was terrified and let out a great cry.
Then Mahāsenagutta questioned him. He said, "Nandiya saw a dream. When asked by him what kind of dream it was, he told it; then Senagutta—
He asked his own female wanderer, who was a frequent visitor to his family, "What is the result of that?
The wanderer replied, "Sir, if a woman sees it, she receives anointment within seven days; if a man sees it, he likewise becomes a king.
Having heard these words from her, Senagutta thought, "I shall make this my relative," and [acted] accordingly.
Having summoned her seven daughters, she questioned them one by one. "Dwell in the presence of Nandiya," she said;
but all the others refused, saying, "We do not know this man who has just arrived—whether he is of noble birth or of low birth.
Then she questioned the youngest. She replied, "Whomever my parents shall give me to, I will not break their word."
He accepted it; then Senagutta, having summoned Nandiya and given him his own daughter, bestowed upon him great wealth.

Then, on the seventh day, Nandiya, wandering here and there, went with the thought, "I shall see the king’s auspicious garden," and lay down covering his head with a coarse cloth, for the King of Bārāṇasī had passed away.
The seventh day arrived. Having performed the funeral rites for the king, the ministers and the chaplain sat in the royal courtyard and deliberated:
"The king has only one daughter and no son. A kingdom cannot endure without a ruler.
We shall dispatch the chariot of Phussa. Having yoked four horses with the color of white lotus petals, they prepared the fivefold regalia of royalty, headed by the white parasol.
Having set the prince down on the chariot itself, they released the chariot and had the musicians take up their positions behind it.
The chariot departed through the eastern gate and headed toward the park. Because of his familiarity with the place, he proceeded toward the park.
"Turn back! some said. The chaplain said, "Do not stop him. The chariot circumambulated the prince.

Having prepared himself for the ascent, he stood ready. The chaplain, having removed the corner of his upper robe and standing while gazing at the soles of the prince's feet, said, "Let this island suffice;
he is capable of ruling over the four great continents surrounded by the two thousand islands.
Having thus spoken, he caused the musical instruments to be played three times in order to test the prince’s fortitude. Then the prince opened his mouth.
Having looked [at them], he asked, "For what reason have you come? They said, "Your Majesty, the kingdom has come to you.
The king asked, "How so? "The master has passed away," they replied. He asked, "How many days have passed? "Today is the seventh day. He asked, "Is there no son or daughter?
"There is a daughter, Your Majesty. He asked, "But no son exists? "In that case, I shall take the kingdom," he said, and they...
At that very moment, having had an initiation pavilion constructed, they adorned the princess with all her ornaments, led her to the park, and performed the consecration for the prince.
Then, when his consecration was completed, they brought him a garment worth a hundred thousand [pieces].
He asked, "What is this, father? "It is the lower garment, Your Majesty. "Is it not too thick, father? [He replied,] "For men..."
"There is nothing finer than these garments for use, O King; such is what your king wears.
"Yes, Your Majesty," they replied. "I do not think your king is a man of merit," he said, and added, "Come now, bring the golden pitcher;
we shall obtain garments. They brought the golden pitcher. He rose, washed his hands, and [washed] his face.
Having rinsed his hands, he took water in his hand and sprinkled it toward the eastern direction;

immediately, having split the solid earth, sixteen *kappa*-trees sprang up. Again, taking water in his hand, he sprinkled it toward the south, the west, and the north—thus he sprinkled all four directions—and in every direction, sixteen by sixteen, sixty-four *kappa*-trees appeared.

They arose; he, having dressed himself in one divine garment and wrapped another around him, caused a drum to be beaten throughout the realm of King Nandiya, saying, "Let not the women who spin thread spin any more!
Then, raising his royal parasol, adorned and prepared, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, he entered the city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed great prosperity.
"Aho! Such was the ripening of the favor bestowed upon the Paccekabuddha at that time. Regarding this, the ancients have said:
"Just as from a seed the size of a mustard grain, a Nigrodha tree arises with a hundred branches, resembling a great dark-blue cloud."
"In the same way, from even a minute meritorious deed, a vast fruit arises;
therefore, a wise person should not despise even a small amount of merit.
As time passed in this manner, one day the queen, seeing the king’s prosperity, thought with an expression of compassion, "Oh, what an ascetic!"
She presented herself. When asked, "What is this, O Queen?", she replied, "O King, your prosperity is exceedingly great. This is due to the wholesome deeds performed during past times.
Now, perform wholesome deeds for the sake of the future. [The King asked: "To whom shall we give? There are no virtuous ones. [She said:
"O King, Jambudvīpa is not empty of Arahants; you should prepare the gift, and I shall find the Arahants."
He said: On the following day, the king prepared a magnificent almsgiving.
The queen, thinking, "If there are any Arahants in this direction, let them come here and accept our alms," threw flowers upward while facing the northern Himalayas and lay down on her chest.
Then those flowers went through the air and reached those dwelling in the Himalayan regions.
The five hundred sons of Padumavatī fell at the feet of the Elder Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha. Indeed, it was thus:
"Aha! Behold now, sirs, the wonder of meritorious karma!"
Even insentient flowers are engaged in the work of messengers. Therefore,
one who possesses wisdom and desires to act in this world should always perform meritorious deeds with all their might, bringing everything under their own control.
Then the Paccekabuddha Mahāpaduma, having understood this, addressed his remaining brothers: "Sirs, King Nandiya has invited you.
Accept his invitation. Having accepted, they traveled through the air and descended at the northern gate.
People reported to the king, "Five hundred Paccekabuddhas have arrived."
The king, together with the queen, went and paid homage; taking the bowls, he escorted the Paccekabuddhas up to the palace.

Having given them alms there, at the conclusion of the meal, the king prostrated himself at the feet of the senior elder of the Saṅgha and the queen at the feet of the junior member of the Saṅgha, saying:
"May the noble ones not be troubled for lack of requisites; may we not diminish in merit."
"Grant us permission to dwell here," she said, and having obtained this promise, she had dwelling places and other facilities established in the park.

She attended upon the Paccekabuddhas for as long as they lived; when they had attained Parinibbāna, she had a grand festival held, performed the funeral rites with sandalwood, aloes, and other substances, collected their relics, and erected a stupa. Even for such as these...
"Death will come even to those of great power and majesty; how much more so for one such as me? Thinking thus, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having established his eldest son in the kingdom, he himself went forth into homelessness. When the king had gone forth, the queen thought, "What shall I do now? and she too went forth.
Both of them, dwelling in the pleasure grove, developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*), and lived in the bliss of those absorptions.

Having spent their lives in this way, at the end of their lifespan they were reborn in the Brahma-world. During the time of our Blessed One, they were reborn into brahmin families and went forth into the Buddha’s dispensation.
At that time, King Nandiya became the elder Mahākassapa, the foremost of those who uphold the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga);
like the moon and like the sun, he became renowned throughout the world, and after the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, [he upheld] the Buddha’s dispensation.
He shone exceedingly. His wife was named Bhaddakapiḷānī.
Having given even a mere whiff of wind from his forest retreat to a Paccekabuddha in the past...
Having made the kingdom and the island of Kuru beautiful, you,
of great majesty, were the lord of the earth;
indeed, you were truly virtuous beings.
Give gifts that are not small;
they shall be your support in other worlds,
as essential as a wish-fulfilling gem or a celestial tree.
The first account: the story of King Nandiya.
12. In the account of a certain man, this is the sequential narrative:
After our Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, there lived in a certain village near Pāṭaliputta a certain man of poor means.
He lived there, and one day, while traveling to a certain village, he put on two garments and reached a vast wilderness.
Seeing him going along in that manner, a certain bandit followed him, thinking, "I shall seize his clothes.
Seeing the bandit approaching from afar, he thought: "Should I flee from him, or should I fight with him?"
"Or if I am unable [to give it], this man will surely come and take my cloth even against my will.
It is not possible for me to carry it away fruitlessly; I shall give it to him as an act of generosity"—thus he made his resolution.
Then the thief came and touched the cloth. Thereupon, that man, having composed his mind, [thought]: "This gift of my cloth..."
Having given a cloth with the thought, "May this be a condition for the happiness of enjoying existence," he abandoned the main road because he was poorly dressed and traveled by another footpath;

there he was bitten by a venomous snake, died, and was reborn in a golden celestial mansion (*vimāna*) twelve *yojanas* in extent in the Himalayan region, surrounded by many thousands of nymphs (*accharā*). Furthermore, surrounding his mansion for three *yojanas*...
Kalpavṛkṣas appeared in that place; seeing this great divine prosperity, he spoke, expressing his joy:
"By the mere act of dedicating a gift, one gives away one's own possessions and receives in return abundant wealth, divine sovereignty, and excellence."
Twelve yojanas in height, difficult to look upon, dazzling to the eyes,
adorned with pinnacles and turrets, beautiful and made entirely of gold— this palace,
crowded with many banners of various colors, was produced by my merit.
Likewise, it was adorned with pure canopies.
Along the perimeter of the palace, celestial garments hung down;
stirred by the wind, they shone like white plaster being splashed.
On the ground surrounding my palace for three yojanas,
there grew celestial trees that granted whatever was desired. There, with dances,
songs, recitations, and musical instruments, [they provided entertainment].
"I do not rejoice in my abode with thousands of celestial nymphs.
One who gives clothing improperly sees no fruit;
but who can describe the fruit for one who gives properly in a worthy field?"
Having performed such wholesome deeds as these,
a person attains divine splendor described by the Sage. Knowing this,
O sirs, give excellent gifts to those of virtuous character.
"Through faith and a pure mind, he partakes in distinction.
This is the second story concerning a certain man.
13. In the story of the youth Visamaloma, this is the sequential narrative.
In the past, it is said, in this Jambudīpa, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Kassapa— having fulfilled the perfections, attained omniscience,
and become the remover of the world’s suffering and the bringer of happiness— dwelt filling the world with the supreme great city of Nibbāna.
At that time, a certain man, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, became filled with faith toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Giving gifts, guarding his virtue, and performing the Uposatha rites, he performed various meritorious deeds and was reborn in the world of the gods like one awakening from sleep.
Surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs in divine dwellings made of every kind of jewel, he remained there for the full span of his lifespan.
Passing away from there, he was born in the city of Pāṭaliputta in Jambudīpa after our Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
He was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Dhammāsoka, the Great Wheel-Turning Monarch.
When they were performing his naming ceremony, because the hair on his head had grown unevenly at birth, they recognized him as "Visamaloma Kumāra" (the Boy with Uneven Hair).
In due course, he attained maturity and became endowed with strength; he was possessed of great power, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.

He dwelt there, endowed with a retinue of glory. Then, at a later time, the great king of men, Dhammāsoka, surrounded by eighty-four thousand kings and with an infinite army and transport, went to the Himālaya mountains for sport.
Having sported there as long as he desired, while returning, he reached the Ganges river named Candabhāgā. That river was one *yojana* wide and three-quarters of a *yojana* deep.
At that time, she was filled with great foam due to the floods that had recently come, crossing many regions, moving from both banks with great speed, and proceeding everywhere with great velocity.
Then the king, seeing the Ganges, said: "What man indeed will be capable of crossing such a great river as this? Having heard that, Prince Visamaloma—
Having arrived and paid his respects, he said, "O King, having crossed the Ganges, I am able both to go and to return. The king accepted this, saying, "Very well.
Then the prince, having dressed himself firmly and tied up Makaradantī’s hair, stood on the bank of the Ganges;
leaping eighteen cubits upward, he fell at a distance of about the length of a bull and began to swim across. Thereupon—

Having cut through the fierce current and crossing over, he struck with his hand the fierce crocodiles that had come to seize him at the time of going and returning, pulverizing them and killing two hundred of them.
Having brought them across and emerged from the water, he paid homage to the king and stood before him.
Seeing this feat, the king was seized by fear, thinking, "This man will surely kill me and seize even my kingdom."
He was capable of seizing it. Thinking, "It is right to kill him," he arrived at the city, summoned the prince, and said to his ministers:
"Men, place this one in prison! They did so accordingly;
then, while he was dwelling in prison, four months passed by. After the lapse of those four months, the king [ordered] a space sixty cubits in length...
Having had sixty bundles of bamboo brought, having had the knots cleared out, and having had them filled with an iron core, he had them placed in the royal courtyard.
Then, having had Prince Visamalomakumāra brought from the prison, he gave this command to all the ministers:
"Sirs, let this prince cut these bundles of bamboo into four-inch pieces using this sword. No.
"He is able to cut it down. Kill him," they said. Upon hearing this, the youth thought:
"I have lived in prison for a long time, oppressed by hunger and distressed for food; what if I were to eat some food and then cut it?
They replied, "There is no food for you now. He said, "In that case, I shall drink water from the lotus pond."
Saying "Very well," they led him to the lotus pond. The prince descended into the lotus pond, bathed, and having submerged himself, ate as much mud as he desired and drank water.
Then, rising up and taking his sword, while the great crowds of people were looking on from every side, he leaped into the air to a height of eighty cubits and [seized] all the bundles of reeds.
Cutting it into pieces about four finger-breadths thick, he descended and reached a thick iron stake at the base;
hearing the sound "kiṇi," he cast aside his sword-leaf and stood there weeping. Then, when the king’s men asked, "Why are you weeping?
he replied, "Among all these men, not even one is my dear friend. If there were such a person among them..."
"If one were to speak of the existence of iron as the core within a bundle of bamboo, I, knowing it for certain, would cut these bundles of bamboo joint by joint," he said.
Then the king, observing the deed performed by the youth, was impressed and granted him the position of viceroy along with great wealth;
thus, the attainment of power and success does not depend on birth, lineage, family status, or similar factors.
It is power. It is not the power of misconduct such as killing living beings. Of whom is this power?
It is the ripening of wholesome kamma, such as the giving of alms, performed for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa. Therefore it was said:
"In the time of Kassapa, the Lord of Sages, there was a certain man..."
Having approached the Perfectly Enlightened One and heard the well-taught Dhamma,
he became one who had gained faith in the virtuous bhikkhus; then,
with a joyful mind, he gave abundant sweet food and drink.
She gave robes, alms-bowls, and likewise waist-bands;
she gave milk-spoons and many wooden staffs.
She gave the gift of a fine bed, as well as couches, stools, and so forth.
She gave woolen blankets and such to ward off the cold;
she gave medicinal offerings for the sake of the monks' health.
Having thus performed various kinds of merit, she went to the third heaven.
There, having been reborn in a celestial mansion, he possessed great supernormal power;
surrounded by celestial nymphs and preceded by a divine army,
he was entertained with celestial dances and songs, and with the melodies of celestial musical instruments.
Rejoicing with manifold celestial attainments,
he remained there for the duration of his lifespan; then, in the delightful Jambudīpa,
in the city of Pāṭaliputta, [he appeared] before King Dhammāsoka.
Having been reborn as a son, he was of great majesty and great strength;
he possessed great fame and great wealth, being the foremost among the Buddha’s disciples.
Therefore, one should perform wholesome deeds, for through such merit comes success in future existence.
"Furthermore, virtue must be guarded, and meditation must be cultivated. Then,
having obtained the position of viceroy and enjoying his prosperity, the prince performed acts of honor toward the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus—
beginning with the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa— by providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
"Having practiced virtue, having observed the Uposatha rites, and having performed the duties of the fast day, he has gone according to his karma at the end of his life.
Having performed such good conduct with a joyful mind throughout various existences,
[he attained] the state of one who possesses manifold wealth.
"You too, O Sucarita, having performed good deeds in accordance with your wealth,
make the state of Nibbāna your own.
This is the third story concerning Prince Visamaloma.
14. In the story of Kañcanadevī, this is the sequential narrative:
It is said that in Jambudīpa there was a certain city named Devaputtanagara, which was beautiful to behold.
At that time, people for the most part performed the offering known as *pattamaho*; they would take the bowl used by the Blessed One and—
Having performed many kinds of worship, they hold a festival; this is called "having attained greatness.
At that time, in the city of Devaputta, the king had a chariot made entirely of all kinds of jewels adorned with every ornament.
He yoked four horses the color of white water-lily petals, and [he prepared] eighty-cubit long bamboo poles finished with the seven precious gems by well-trained masters of craft.
Having adorned the stone bowl used by the Teacher with nets of pearls and other ornaments, having fixed a bamboo handle to it, and having placed the bamboo pole upon a chariot,
they decorated the city like the city of the gods; they raised flags, banners, and the like,
and set up arches, golden pots, full jars, rows of lamps, and so forth, [entering] the city with many modes of worship.
Having performed a circumambulation and placed the bowl-relic in a beautifully adorned jeweled pavilion in the center of the city, he caused a great Dhamma-assembly to be held on the seventh day.

At that time, many people, deities, yakkhas, rakkhasas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others from that region entered that gathering for the most part in human guise; such was the marvelous nature of that ritual of worship.
At that time, a certain Nāga king, seeing a maiden of supreme beauty—a woman never before encountered by him—seated within the circle of the Dhamma assembly, became infatuated with her.

He entreated her in many ways, but when he did not obtain her, he grew angry and released a breath from his nostrils, thinking, "I shall kill her. By the power of her faith, no harm whatsoever came to her.

He was not able to do so. Then the nāga, having coiled his body from her feet up to her entire body and spread out a hood over her head, stood there frightening her. Because she had no other intention and was listening to the Dhamma, she did not experience even the slightest bit of suffering.
When the night had turned to dawn, people saw her and asked, "What is this? inquiring about the cause.
She too, having spoken to them, performed an act of truth (saccakiriya) as follows:
"I was a celibate practitioner (brahmacārī) when I was born here among humans;
by this truth, may the nāga release me immediately."
"Since I did not grant an opportunity to the Naga who was afflicted by lust,
by that truth may the Naga release me immediately.
I am struck by the poisonous wind of the enraged serpent."
If I am not angry, by that truth may he release me quickly.
While listening to the true Dhamma with heavy reverence and devotion, I heard it;
by that truth, may the Naga release me quickly.
"Without losing even a single syllable or word from the beginning, I have heard it;
by this truth, may the Naga be released quickly!
At the conclusion of this act of truth, the Naga King, being exceedingly pleased with her, uncoiled his body and expanded his hood into a hundred folds.
Having seated him within the interior of his hood, he performed a ritual offering called *udakapūjā* together with many young nāgas.
Seeing this, many city-dwellers were struck with wonder and amazement, and they made offerings worth eighteen crores of wealth. For it is said:
"In this world, there is nothing equal to faith; it is well-disposed and grants all desires."
