Behold the power of faith: by honoring [the Triple Gem] in this way, a person attains even in this very world some small measure of existence and enjoyment.
Therefore, one endowed with faith should cultivate reverence for the Triple Gem.
Thus, having obtained great wealth, she lived her entire life as a celibate virgin;
at the end of her lifespan, having passed away, she took rebirth in that very city in the womb of the king’s chief queen, and after ten months had elapsed, she emerged from her mother’s womb.
On the day of her birth, a rain of jewels fell throughout the entire city of the sons of the gods.
It rained. Therefore, they gave her the name Kañcanadevī. She was beautiful on all sides; she was as lovely as a celestial nymph.
From her mouth issued the fragrance of a blue lotus, and from her body issued the fragrance of sandalwood.
From her entire body, emitting rays like the rising sun, there was no need for lamps within her four-cubit chamber. The whole chamber...
Her body possessed a radiance that was unique in the world, and her physical perfection became renowned throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
Consequently, the kings dwelling throughout Jambudīpa sent gifts to her father, the king, for her sake.

However, she, being unstained by the five sensual pleasures, obtained her father’s permission, went to the Bhikkhunūpassaya, and having gone forth, applied herself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).

Having heard this with great reverence, like a young maiden, she protected her stainless virtue and, having increased her practice, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Thus, indeed, while protecting her pure conduct, she heard the Dhamma.
"Having attained manifold prosperity, you have now come to ruin;
O sirs, do not ever be negligent in the application of wholesome deeds.
This is the fourth story concerning Kāñcanadevī.
15. In the Story of the Tiger, this is the sequential narrative:
In the city of Bārāṇasī, situated in the Lesser Kingdom (Cūlaraṭṭha) in Jambudīpa, there was a great highway that pierced through a mound of earth.
In the middle of it lived a tiger who was supporting his own blind father in a mountain cave.
He lived there. At the forest entrance of that very mountain, a young parrot named Tuṇḍila lived in a tree.
The two of them became dear friends to one another. At that time, a man living in a border village, having quarreled with his wife, was traveling toward Bārāṇasī and arrived at that forest entrance.
Then, seeing him distressed and deprived of his former state, the young parrot, with a trembling heart, called out to him and said, "Sir, where are you going?
When he replied, "I am going to another forest grove," Tuṇḍila said, "Sir, a tiger dwells in the middle of this forest grove.
He is harsh and cruel; having killed whoever comes before him, he devours them. Do not go there!"
"I am going," he said. But that unfortunate man, disregarding the words of the one who desired his welfare, replied, "I shall indeed go.
Then Tuṇḍila said, "In that case, my friend, if you go without turning back, this tiger is my companion;
having heard these words from me, he will not seize you. Disregarding him, the king of swans, with a mind corrupted [by anger], departed.
Having struck him with a club and killed him, he made fire with a fire-drill and ate the flesh.
Indeed, association with a person of bad character brings only suffering in this world and the next. For instance:
"This was done by me; it is mine," thus [thinking], a man [approaches] Vessānara...
The serpent embraces him, yet it burns his body.
Though nurtured with love by the giving of honey,
milk, and other gifts, the serpent, when provoked, bites his very frame.
Thus, even when one of low birth, evil, and ungrateful,
meets with a person of noble character and virtue,
that encounter is rendered fruitless by the former being a person of no merit— this being known by the latter.
"One should not associate with such a person even for a moment; that association brings no good.
Then that wicked man, having eaten the meat, proceeded on his way and reached the middle of a forest thicket.
Thereupon, a tiger saw him and, letting out a great roar, sprang up to seize him. Seeing the tiger, he was overcome with fear and [cried out to] Tuṇḍila...
Having heard the words, he said, "Sir, I have come from the presence of your companion Tuṇḍila.
Upon hearing this, the tiger was delighted and called out, "Come, friend!

He led him to his own dwelling, satisfied him with food fit for consumption, seated him in the presence of his father, and then departed again for the forest thicket. Then his father [addressed] his son...
While conversing with him as he departed, the tiger learned from his words that Tuṇḍila had been killed and eaten.
Then, when his son returned, he said to him, "Your friend was killed by him. Upon hearing this, the tiger became distressed;
he rushed to Tuṇḍila’s dwelling place and, crying out "Friend Tuṇḍila!", found him nowhere.
Seeing his featherless wings, he returned lamenting and wailing, grieving that "without a doubt, my companion has been killed by him.
Then that wicked man, having gone there while [the other] was away, struck the boy’s father with a stone and killed him;
thinking, "Now I shall kill the tiger," he remained hidden, watching the path by which the tiger would approach. At that moment—
A tiger also came there. When she had gone, the tiger, terrified by his power, went and prostrated himself at his feet with his chest, saying, "Master, give me my life!
But the tiger, seeing the deed he had done, calmed his mind toward him and thought, "It is not right to betray one who has come bearing a message from my companion. Having thus consoled him, he—
"Go, friend," he sent him off happily. For indeed, association with the virtuous brings happiness both in this world and in the world beyond. As it is said:
"One should sit together only with the wise; one should cultivate intimacy only with the wise.
Through such intimacy in all circumstances, it becomes better, never worse."
The company of the virtuous always brings happiness and dispels suffering;
therefore, let people associate only with true friends.
Then, through the power of that benevolent mind, the tiger passed away and was reborn in heaven.
Even such a cruel man, a consumer of human flesh,
a tiger who had attained compassion and wisdom, went to a happy destination.
Therefore, people, always practice compassion toward living beings.
"He gives that to you—both prosperity and wealth amidst worldly existences.
This is the fifth story, concerning the tiger.
16. In the story of the one who gave a wooden plank, this is the sequential narrative.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain man, thinking "I am going to the Northern Country," set out on a long journey.
Becoming exhausted by the intense heat at midday during the summer months, he entered the shade of a tree and sat down on a wooden plank while chewing betel.
Then, another man coming from the Northern Country, likewise exhausted by the heat, arrived and [sat] in the same manner as the first.
Sitting nearby, he asked, "Sir, is there any water? The other replied, "There is no water.
Then, although he said to him, "Sir, give me some betel too; I am thirsty," he did not receive any.
Having purchased a single betel leaf for four kahāpaṇas, he sat right there, chewed it, and quenched his thirst. Because of that kindness...
Out of affection for him, he set out on the road to his own destination.
Later, having reached a port, he boarded a ship and set out for trade; he arrived in the midst of the ocean. Then, on the seventh day, the ship was wrecked.
The people became food for fish and turtles. That very man, remaining unhurt, [clung to] a piece of timber.
Placing a plank against his chest, he crossed the ocean. Then, that other man also, having likewise survived after the ship was wrecked, while crossing the ocean, encountered the former.
As they were crossing the ocean for seven days, they recognized one another.
Among them, the one who had received betel by paying a kahāpaṇa was crossing with a piece of a plank placed against his chest. This was the case for the other as well.
There was none. Then, having taken some coins and remembering the mere favor of the betel he had been given, he gave his own wooden plank to him.
He, lying upon it, crossed over and went on, leaving it behind; another, crossing without support, lost his vigor and was about to sink in the water.
At that moment, the one named Maṇimekhalā, who dwelt in the ocean, [appeared].
Seeing him sinking, the daughter of a deva, recollecting his virtues as those of a true man (*sappurisa*), went with great speed and, by her own power, brought him to the shore of the ocean.
She also brought the other man to the shore through the power of his virtues alone.
Then, the man who had crossed over on the raft, seeing her, was amazed and asked, "How did you come to be ahead? He—
"I do not know. However," he said, "I have reached the shore by means of happiness alone.
Then the goddess, appearing in her visible form, spoke to announce that she herself had brought him there:
"He who here supports his mother or father according to the Dhamma..."
The gods always protect him, whether at sea or on land,
who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha;
the gods always protect him, whether at sea or on land.
The fivefold and the eightfold restraint, and the Pātimokkha—
those who protect these are protected everywhere and at all times by the gods.
He who practices good conduct with body, speech, and mind, indeed...
The gods always protect him, whether at sea or on land:
he who stands firm in the qualities of the noble ones, having done his duty.
The gods always protect him, whether at sea or on land.
Then he said:
"I gave no gift, nor did I observe moral virtue;
by what meritorious deed do deities protect me?"
"I ask you about a doubt; explain it to me, O deity.
The deity said:
"In the bottomless, terrifying ocean that brings about misfortune, on the far shore..."
While crossing with a broken ship, you took a block of wood to heart;
standing firm in the Dhamma of the virtuous and examining yourself,
you gave your own plank to the man with whom you had but a moment’s acquaintance.
"Your friendship and your gift of fruit have found their support in the ocean; know this, O noble sir.
Having spoken thus, she satisfied him with divine food and adorned him with divine garments and ornaments. Then she herself—
By his supernatural power, he established them right there in the city of Sāvatthī.
From that time forth, taking that very object as their focus, they gave gifts, guarded their virtue, and performed the Uposatha rites; at the end of their lives, they became destined for heaven.
Thus, even by a small amount of wholesome merit, in the midst of the ocean—
Indeed, beings obtain refuge from the deities;
you too, not destroying your state as true men,
should never be negligent in the application of what is wholesome.
The sixth story: The Story of Phalakakhaṇḍadatta.
17. In the story of the Accomplice of the Robbers, this is the sequential narrative:
After our Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, there was a certain man suffering in the city of Devadaha in Jambudīpa.
Wandering there, he went to a certain village on the frontier and took up residence in a household there.
The people there supported him by providing him with rice porridge and food;
subsequently, having established a friendly relationship with the people there, he stayed for a few days and then went elsewhere, where later he engaged in banditry.
He made his living by doing so. Then one day, royal officers seized him as he was stealing and presented him to the king.
The king commanded, "Put him in prison. They led him to the prison, bound him with chains, handed him over to the guards, and departed. Twelve years passed while he remained in that prison.
The years passed by. Later on, a former companion of his who lived in a border village came to Devadaha on some business;
while wandering here and there, he saw him bound in the prison. Upon seeing him, his heart trembled;
weeping and lamenting, he asked, "What can I do for you, friend? Then—
"Twelve years have now passed while I have been living in this prison;

for all this time, I have endured great suffering due to poor food and other hardships. Until I return after seeking and eating some food, find a means to release me from here," said he. Then that good man—
But what is the use of beauty devoid of virtue and moral conduct?
What is the use of the wit of a gambler who dwells in falsehood?
Or what is the use of wealth that is free from the practice of giving?
"What is the use of friends who turn their backs at the time of misfortune?
Having said this, he went to the guards and said, "Sirs, as long as he returns after eating his meal, I shall stand as his surety; release him."

Then he said, "Sirs, it is not possible for us to release him; however, until he returns, you shall sit bound by an iron chain, and in this way we shall release him—if you say it cannot be done otherwise.
He replied, "So be it," and having said "Very well," he released the chain from his feet and [placed it] upon his own feet.
Having constructed a prison and entered it himself, he had the other released.
Yet even that unvirtuous man, once freed from bondage, did not go back to that place. Oh, how difficult it is to know the nature of those who are ungrateful! As it has been said:
"Just as in a water-filled pit, one cannot distinguish the uneven from the level;"
Thus, the nature of the unvirtuous is perceived arising within the mind:
they speak one thing with their mouth, think another in their mind, and perform yet another with their body;
such is the natural disposition of the unvirtuous.
Of those, he who understood their true nature was indeed the one born wise;
he alone was the man of great learning, and he alone was the knower of others' minds.
Thus, twelve years passed while he dwelt in the prison. During all that time, he was oppressed by hunger.
Because of that, he had never before asked another for food; indeed, the days on which he did not receive food were more numerous than the days on which he received food that was not left over.
Then, after twelve years had passed, a son was born to the king.
At that time, the king caused all the prisons within his realm to be opened; he even caused the deer and birds to be released from their bonds.
As soon as the gate was opened, the people in the prison went wherever they wished. But he alone did not go with them and remained behind.
When the guards asked him, "Sir, why do you not go?", he replied, "Sirs, because of my well-known reputation, I will not go now.
My limbs are extremely emaciated; I shall go in the darkness."
Having spoken thus, when darkness fell, he went out. Thinking, "Since there are no trustworthy people within the city, where shall I obtain food?
he departed and wandered through the dark of night toward the raw charnel ground, thinking, "I shall obtain food there.
There, seeing a human body that had just been discarded, he cut flesh from a human bone, placed it in a skull, and—
Having built a funeral pyre with three human heads as the hearth, he kindled a fire with embers taken from the cremation mound.
For the purpose of extinguishing the flames in the cemetery, he stirred the meat with a human bone soaked in water, then removed it from the heat.
Covering his private parts with branches he had broken off, and using a discarded cloth as a windbreak, he sat down. At that moment—
Thereupon, the deity dwelling in that *pippalī* tree, having seen his actions, thought, "I shall first question him," and approaching him,
spoke thus: "O sir, in this thick night, crowded with dense darkness, strewn here and there with scattered human bones,
filled with the carcasses of dogs, jackals, and the like, and teeming with hideous *rakkhasas* who feed on human flesh— "
In that terrifying charnel ground, where many funeral pyres were blazing here and there, she asked, "What are you doing, cooking human flesh?
and replied: "In the midst of the cemetery, crowded with corpses in the darkness of night."
"You are cooking human flesh on your head;
tell me, what is your purpose for that?
Then he replied:
Neither for the sake of sacrifice nor for the sake of giving do I cook this meat in the midst of the charnel ground;
there is no other hunger for a man like this one.
"I am cooking this for the destruction of Khudāvināsa.
Then the deity asked him, "May it be so for you; however, why do you make a wind-shield with this rag? What is the purpose of this?
[He replied: "The branch I am wearing is for the restraint of shame (*hirisaṃvara*)."
"Stretching out a pilotikā cloth there,
you are making a wind-shield, my friend;
tell me when asked, for what purpose is this?"
Thus, as he was explaining it to her, he said: "The cool breeze,
mixed with the beautiful and the sublime,
is itself mindless, because of its state of being mindless."
Having touched my body, you who are unwholesome,
ungrateful, and a betrayer of friends—
if you were to bring [harm] to my person, [what could I do]?
"It touches, it touches, it bites, it intoxicates"— having understood that such things are merely wind,
O friend, know that they give rise to suffering.
This ragged garment is bound on only to avoid [the cold].
The deity said:
"What have you done, O man, that you are so wretched?
You have destroyed both your wealth and your grain."
"Mother, father, relatives, fields, and lands have been ruined by him;
tell me, what do you have to say for him?
Then he replied:
Whatever great fear there may be from a king,
such as the seizure of all one's possessions or even execution—
that comes from an ungrateful man who is not a true person.
O friend, that cry is to be avoided.
For whatever fear there is in the world from thieves and enemies,
as well as from water and fire—
Even that entire [merit] belongs to one who is ungrateful;
O sir, such a person is to be avoided from afar.
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, ...
Approaching another’s wife and lying;
drinking intoxicants and quarreling;
slanderous speech and frivolous talk; association with rogues, and in some places, association with gamblers and the like.
All that is harmful, inauspicious, and undesirable,
leading to states of misery and endless suffering— this is what comes from one who is ungrateful and lacks the character of a true person.

"O sir, that noise is to be avoided," he said, and then he related all the suffering he had experienced through association with unwholesome persons. Thereupon the deity said: "O sir, on the very day the Teacher taught the *Maṅgala Sutta*, I too was sitting right here in this tree.
[The verses are: 'Avoiding the foolish and associating with the wise...'"
"And honoring those worthy of honor— this is the supreme blessing. Having said,
"I heard this verse," he became inspired with faith toward him, led him to his own celestial mansion, bathed him,
adorned him with divine garments and ornaments, gave him divine food and drink, and paid him great honor and respect.
By his own power, he had himself consecrated to the kingship in that city.
While ruling there, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and at the end of his life, he departed according to his karma.
Thus, [one should avoid] association with and residence among wicked people.
Truly, by associating today with the virtuous, the pure,
and the noble, and by fulfilling manifold wholesome deeds such as giving,
may you fully attain the splendor of the heavenly realms and the supreme state of liberation.
The seventh story: The Story of the Thief’s Companion.
18. In the story of the Brahmin Marutta, this is the sequential narrative:
In Jambudīpa, on the banks of the river Candabhāgā, there was a village named Homagāma. In that place lived a man named Marutta.
A brahmin was living there. At that time, having gone to Takkasilā for business and returning home, he saw on the road a dog suffering from leprosy in a certain shed.
Out of compassion for it, he rubbed the dog with a cloth made of blue creeper-fiber and gave it water to drink.
The dog’s disease being cured, it returned to its normal state, and the brahmin [reflected upon] the service he had rendered to it.
Observing this, he went along with him. Later, the brahmin’s wife conceived;
when her pregnancy was full term and she was in the process of giving birth, the boy fell crosswise and died right inside the womb.
Then, having cut him into pieces with a knife, they carried him out. When the brahmin saw this, his heart became filled with world-weariness.
Having abandoned the household life and gone forth as an ascetic, he dwelt in the forest.
Then his wife, living with another man, became ill-disposed toward the brahmin, thinking, "He has gone forth, abandoning me.
She consulted with her husband, saying, "O brahmin, kill this [ascetic]. A dog, having overheard their conversation, [approached] together with the brahmin himself.
He was living there. Then one day, her husband, thinking, "I shall kill her," set out taking his bow and quiver;
at that time, the ascetic had gone into the forest for the sake of gathering fruits. He did not return to the hermitage itself.
A man, watching the path by which the ascetic would return, remained hidden in wait among the trees. Observing the man's negligence, the dog gnawed the string of the bow.
He cut it off. The ascetic then restored the branch to its natural state and fixed it back on. In this way, he ate every time it was fixed back on.
Then that wicked man, knowing the ascetic was approaching, went along with his bow, thinking, "I shall kill him.
But his dog bit his foot, knocked him down, gnawed at his face until he was weakened, and let out a loud howl.
For it is in this way that true persons (sappurisa) repay those who have assisted them.
As it is said: "Doing a service in return, that grateful dog, having struck down his enemy, gave life back to the seer."
"Even animals always recognize a small favor done for them.
Thinking thus, may wise beings be grateful.
Then the ascetic, hearing the sound of the dog, went there, saw its distress, and out of compassion began to lick it.

Having nourished him until his wounds were healed and he had regained his strength, [the man] remained right there; having developed the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā), at the end of his life, he was destined for the Brahma-world.
Having heard this, one should acknowledge: "Excellent is the service rendered by the dog."
Having heard what was done for Mettiyā by the seer,
practice compassion and benefit others rightly;
that will always be the cause for your attainment of existence and its enjoyments.
The eighth story: The Story of the Brāhmaṇa Marutta.
19. In the story of the giver of drinking water, this is the sequential narrative:
It is said that in a certain province in Jambudīpa, a certain man traveled from kingdom to kingdom and from province to province.
Wandering along in due order, he reached the bank of the river Candabhāgā, boarded a boat, and was crossing to the other side.
Then another pregnant woman was traveling in that same boat; when the boat reached the middle of the Ganges, her kamma-born winds began to stir.
Thereupon, unable to give birth and becoming exhausted, she cried out, "Give me water! I am thirsty!"
She begged the people for help. They did not give her water, as if they were not even hearing her words.
Then that countryman, feeling compassion for her—[the text reads] *karuṇāyapānīyaṃ*, *karuṇāyantopānīyaṃ*, or in some places *karuṇāyatoyaṃ*—took water and sprinkled it on her face.
At that moment, she found relief and gave birth to the child with ease. Then...
Having reached the shore, they arrived at their respective destinations within a few days.
Later on, that countryman, on account of some business, arrived at the city where that woman lived;
wandering here and there, and finding no place to stay, he went to a hall at the city gate and lay down there. At that very moment...
One day, thieves entered the city, broke into the royal palace, and took away the finest treasures.
As they were departing, they were pursued by the king’s men; they abandoned their loot right there in the hall and fled. Then the king’s men arrived;
not seeing the thieves, they saw that countryman and, thinking "This man is a thief," seized him and bound his arms tightly behind his back.
Having bound him, they presented him to the king again on the following day. When the king asked, "Tell me, why did you commit the act of a thief?
he replied, "I am not a thief, Your Majesty; I am a newcomer. When the king had searched for the real thieves but could not find them, he commanded, "This man himself is the thief!
Put him to death! Then, after the king's men had bound him tightly and led him to the place of execution, that woman—

Seeing him being led away in that manner, she recognized him; with a trembling heart, she went to the king’s presence in a moment, paid homage, and said, "Your Majesty, this man is not a thief, nor is he a stranger; release him, Your Majesty!
The king, not believing her words, said, "If you wish to release him, give him his ransom and have him set free. She replied, "My lord, in my house..."
"I have no wealth. Furthermore, O King, make me a slave together with my seven sons;
release this man. Then the king said, "You say he has only just arrived. Yet, relying on him, you have declared yourself a slave along with your sons.
Is he a kinsman of yours, or perhaps a benefactor? Thus he questioned her.
"What is this man to you? I ask you about your doubt:
Is he your brother, or your father, or your husband, or your brother-in-law?
Is he a blood relative, or perhaps a creditor?"
"Is he perhaps a benefactor? Why then do you give him his life?
To this she replied:
"O King, this man has previously rendered me a service."
"Alone and without protection, I was alone—so it is said in some places—suffering and standing at the brink of death.
Unable to give birth, a pregnant woman experiencing agonizing pain, you attended to me with water; because of that, I was happy then."
Just as the world, parched with thirst, abandons the great ocean— though it is overflowing with a succession of waves and surging tides—
to go and drink from a mere well, even so, O Lord of Men,
while [worthy] persons are present, [people act in such a way].
The virtue remains well-established within the mind of one person alone.
Having slain the elephant, certain people seeking its flesh pursue a single hare running away, still intent on that meat.
Even so, O lord of men, among people who exist,
those possessed of virtue follow the true person who is mindful of what has been done for them.
Therefore, O lord of men, I shall be established in the qualities of a true person.
By means of this, they remember one who has previously performed services for them:
"Both I and my sons have been made happy by him;
even at the cost of our lives, he must be released by me."
Then the king summoned the doorkeeper and, having questioned him, learned that she had only just arrived.
Delighted by her virtuous conduct as a true person (*sappurisa*), he bestowed great honor upon both of them.
Having attained such renown, they performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms from that time forward and became destined for heaven.
Even women whose minds are established in the Dhamma obtain in this way both prosperity and praise; likewise,
one who keeps in mind the Dhamma and virtuous conduct [attains the same].
"Always abide among the teachings as pure and virtuous people.
This is the ninth story concerning the gift of drinking water. 20.
In the story of the friend who sacrificed his life, this is the sequential narrative.
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, two brahmins named Somabrāhmaṇa and Somadattabrāhmaṇa lived in Sāvatthī.
There, Somabrāhmaṇa frequently played at dice with Somadattabrāhmaṇa.
Then one day, having defeated Somabrāhmaṇa, Somadatta took from him his upper robe and his signet ring.
As he was going to his own house, he said to the brahmin Soma, "Come, let us go home.
Then Soma replied, "Friend, being clad in only a single garment, I am not able to enter the middle of the street. For me, staying right here rather than going is better.
When Somadatta said, "If that is so, friend, take this upper robe," he gave it to him. Now...
Although he was told, "Come, my good man," he did not come. When questioned by him again, "My good man, why do you not come?
he replied, "Because my wife, children, and others, not seeing the ring on my hand, quarrel with me.
Then [the other] said, "That being the case, give it to me whenever you have the opportunity. Having given even the ring, he took it and went home.
He arrived. Then they became companions for that much time. Later on, people caught this man committing adultery with another's wife and presented him to the king.
The king, seeing his physical beauty, did not issue a royal decree of punishment;
instead, he admonished him, saying, "Sir, do not do such a thing again," and released him. After the king had admonished him and released him up to three times, [he was caught again].
On the fourth occasion, he commanded: "Go, take him to that execution ground and kill him.
Thus, those devoted to evil deeds cannot be restrained even when admonished in many ways.
For it is said: "Even jackals and dogs, crows and blue flies,"
These beings are attached to this putrid corpse; it is not possible to restrain them.
Likewise, toward the taking of life, adultery, intoxicants, false speech, and theft—beings are not prevented from these seven [transgressions].

Then the king’s men bound him and departed. At that time, the brahmin Soma, seeing Somadatta being led away in such a manner, his heart trembling, went to the presence of the king’s men and said, "Sirs, do not kill him for a moment;
let me first inform the king. Having spoken thus, he went to the king, paid homage, and stood before him, saying, "O King, my life..."
"I shall give [the reward] to the brahmin Somadatta. Release him! If you wish to kill me, then kill me," he said.
The king was silent and satisfied; in some accounts, he remained so. The king's men released Somadatta and led the brahmin Soma to the execution ground and killed him.
"Oh, how grateful and appreciative he was! they exclaimed.
And in this regard there is this verse: "Some humans, remembering their own likeness to the hollows of crow-beaks,
give up their lives as Soma did for Somadatta."
Thus, by that gift of his life, he was reborn in the world of the gods and dwelt there, enjoying divine splendors in a vast golden celestial mansion surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs.

Then the brahmin Somadatta, saying, "He has liberated me from death," gave a gift for his sake and assigned the merit to him; at that very moment, the king's sovereignty became even greater than before.
And there was the manifestation of divine power. Then Somadeva, surveying his own divine sovereignty, saw that he had given the gift of life to his friend.

Having seen this, he abandoned his celestial form and, approaching the brahmin Somadatta in the guise of a young man, exchanged greetings with him, declared that he had been reborn in the world of the gods, and took him [with him].
Having said, "I shall lead you to the world of the gods by my own power and let you enjoy prosperity as you desire," he granted the god celestial glory for seven days.
On the seventh day, having led him back, he established him in his very own home.
For one who has experienced celestial prosperity there, human prosperity appears repulsive. Consequently, as he recalled that celestial prosperity, he became emaciated.

He became weak and turned pale. Then one day, a son of the gods, observing him and seeing him thus fallen into suffering, thought, "It is not possible for a human being to enjoy divine prosperity," and gave him a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) that grants whatever is desired.
By his own power, he also made his wife beautiful, glorious, and radiant in form.

He rendered their appearance beyond that of ordinary humans; later on, those husband and wife, having personally witnessed the splendor of divine attainments, gave gifts and guarded their virtue, and were reborn right there in the presence of the companion son of the gods.
By that helpful one, whose mind was gladdened by his own dullness...
Thinking, "Good people give even their very lives," O friends,
do not become betrayers of those who have helped you;
always be praiseworthy among virtuous people.
The tenth story: The Sacrifice of Life by the Companion.
The second chapter, the Chapter on King Nandiya.
The Chapter on Being Deceived by a Yakṣa.
21. The Story of Being Deceived by a Yakkha: This is the sequential narrative.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, it is said that in the kingdom of the King of Kosala there was a village named Tuṇḍagāma.
There lived a man named Buddhadasa who [declared]: "For as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to the Buddha. The Buddha is my refuge, my protection."
"Having gone for refuge to the Buddha as one's shelter and ultimate resort," thus he dwelt having gone for refuge to the Buddha for as long as life lasted.
At that time, a certain inhabitant of the countryside, wandering here and there, arrived at that village of Tuṇḍa and took up residence in that very man’s house.
Now, a certain *yakkha* had possessed that countryman’s body and was tormenting him; at that moment—

At the time of entering that village, the yakkha Buddhadasa, unable to enter his house due to the power of the lay follower’s virtue, released him and stood outside the village for seven days, watching for his arrival.
Then that countryman, having stayed there for seven days, departed from the village on the seventh day, desiring to go to his own kingdom. Then—
Seeing him thus departed, a *yakkha* seized him and asked, "Where have you been for all this time?
The *yakkha* replied, "Sir, seven days have passed while I was living here for your sake. Then [the man] said, "What need have you of me?
What shall I give to you? Thereupon the *yakkha* said, "Sir, I am oppressed by hunger; [give me] food."
When it was said, "I am here for you," he asked, "That being so, why did you not take me in while I was living in your house?

The yakkha replied, "Sir, there is a certain lay follower (*upāsaka*) in that house who has gone for refuge to the Buddha; unable to enter the house because of the power of his virtue (*sīla*), I stood outside.
When this was said, the man from the countryside, not knowing what "refuge" meant, asked, "What is this 'refuge'? and then he took refuge.
He questioned the yakkha. The yakkha said, "I go for refuge to the Buddha," and thus took refuge.
Hearing this, the countryman thought, "Now I shall deceive him," and said, "In that case, yakkha, I too go for refuge to the Buddha.
As soon as he had spoken these words, the yakkha let out a great shout and began to whirl about.
He fled. Thus, taking refuge in the Perfectly Enlightened One serves to ward off fear and calamity in this world, and brings about heaven and liberation in the next world.
For it is said: "The word 'Buddha' brings fear to non-human beings."
It brings constant joy to all beings who revere the Buddha;
it is the destroyer of all calamities, the peerless divine spell possessing celestial power, great majesty, great efficacy, and great wonder.
Therefore, that fierce yakkha,
seeing him standing for refuge,
became agitated and overcome with fear.
And Lomahaṭṭha was terrified;
seeing her running as she whirled about, he was like one blinded by darkness when the sun has risen,
or like a tuft of śimbalī-wool scattered by a fierce wind.
"Whatever suffering arises from kings, thieves, enemies, yakkhas, or petas,
a person who desires [freedom from it] must go for refuge to the Triple Gem.
Then, that countryman, seeing the great virtue and great benefit in going for refuge, became respectful and full of faith toward the Buddha.

“Until the end of my life, I go for refuge to the Buddha. Having thus gone for refuge, by the very power of that act of taking refuge, at the conclusion of his life, he was reborn in the world of the gods like one awakening from sleep.
Having seen him who had thus gone for refuge, [the Teacher said:]
Even the yakkhas flee out of great fear;
therefore, guard your virtue and take refuge,
abandon evil, and seek a happy rebirth.
The first story: The Deception by a Yakkha. 22.
In the story concerning the one of wrong view, this is the sequential narrative:
While the Blessed One was still living, it is said that there dwelt in the city of Rājagaha a certain man who was a devotee of Brahmā and held wrong views.
There was also one named Sammādiṭṭhika. Both of them had two sons each, who grew up playing together.

Later on, while they were playing with marbles, the son of Sammādiṭṭhika would say, "Homage to the Buddha," and as he threw his marble, he won day after day. The son of Micchādiṭṭhika, however, said, "Homage to Brahmā," and...
He threw [the sugar] and lost. Then, seeing the son of the one with wrong view constantly losing while the boy with right view was always winning, he asked:
"Friend, you are always winning; why do you throw the sugar saying 'Homage to the Buddha'?
He replied: "Friend, I say 'Homage to the Buddha' and then throw it. From that time on, he too began saying, "Homage to the Buddha," and...
He threw [the dice], and then those messengers were for the most part equal in number. Later on, the son of a man with wrong view went to the forest with his father for the sake of timber;
while returning after taking timber by cart, he unyoked the cart near the city gate and released the oxen to eat grass. As the oxen were eating the grass, they were [attacked] by others...

Together with the oxen, they entered the city. Then his father, searching for the oxen, turned back his son, saying, "Look at the cart," and entered the city. When evening had come, the people closed the city gates;
consequently, the prince fell asleep while lying beneath a wooden cart outside the city.

Then, during that night, two *yakkhas*—one of right view and one of wrong view—while searching for food, saw the boy lying beneath the cart. Of them, the one of wrong view said, "I shall eat this. Then the other said, "Do not do so;
he is one who utters the words, 'Homage to the Buddha! "I will certainly eat him," said the first, and by the other—
Although he was being restrained up to three times, he went forward, seized the man’s feet, and dragged him.
At that moment, by virtue of his previous familiarity, the boy cried out, "Homage to the Buddha! Upon hearing this, the yakkha was struck with fear;
his hair stood on end, and releasing his hand, he stepped back and stood still. "Oh, how wonderful! How marvelous is the power of the Buddhas! Having thus brought himself under control..."
Through familiarity, even when one merely says, "Homage to the Buddha," there is no fear, trepidation, or calamity.
How much more so for one who has dedicated oneself and gone for refuge to the Buddha for as long as life lasts! For it is said:
"Just as the cry of a peacock brings terror to serpents..."
Thus the word "Buddha" brings fear to non-human beings.
Just as evil is brought to dissolution by the recitation of a mantra,
so too by the word "Buddha," the Piśācas everywhere flee and abandon [the place].
Just as a clod of earth dissolves from afar upon seeing fire,
so too do the hungry ghosts (petas) flee from afar upon seeing one who has gone for refuge— some even called "petāpentāva.
The two rare words "Buddha" and "Iccha" are truly wonderful.
For the destruction of all calamities, it is a firm wall, a sprout of growth,
a palace of the seven jewels, that very diamond cave,
that very ship, that island, and that very beautiful armor.
That very crown made of jewels, shining upon his head;
the lovely *tilaka* mark of camphor on his forehead;
earrings on his pair of ears; and a beautiful golden garland around his neck.
A single-stringed necklace and a pearl garland, ornaments worn for the sake of beauty;
an armlet for the upper arm, likewise a bracelet on the wrist;
rings for the fingers and finger-rings, and a sword esteemed as auspicious.
With a head shorn like a heated golden platter, like a bow among all weapons;
he alone is the possessor of all ornaments, he alone is the remover of misfortune.
Therefore, indeed, the wise person—
Of the Teacher Lokālokanasatthu;
one should go for refuge to him,
whose name "Guṇa" is to be verified by coming and seeing.
First the word "Homage," and then the cry "To the Buddha!"—
these were uttered by the sleeping prince, the son of a heretic.
Hearing this, those who delight in human corpses likewise cried out.
"Ah, the Buddhas do not harm others; they are great in the essence of their virtues.
Then the yakkha of right view said to the yakkha of wrong view: "Sir, you have acted improperly. You have struck at the virtues of the Buddha;
you must undergo punishment for this. [The other asked: "What must I do about it, friend?"
When this was said, he replied, "Give food to one who is hungry.
Then, saying "Very well," and adding, "Stay here until I return," he brought a meal of savory delicacies served on a golden platter from King Bimbisāra;
having fed the boy with food that had the color of his father's [the king's] flesh, he repeated the words of the Buddha spoken by the prince.
Having written everything, including the effort exerted by himself, upon the slate, they departed with the resolve, "Let this be known as the King's own work.
Then, when night had turned to dawn and it was time for the King’s meal, the King’s men, not seeing the slate there, searched the city;
they saw the cart, the boy, and the slate, and taking them along with the slate, [they returned].
They showed it to the king. When the king saw the letters and other marks on the tablet, he read them;
becoming impressed by his virtues, he bestowed upon him the position of treasurer along with great honor.
Thus, even through a dream, the name of the Victor [was revealed].
Since there is no fear through flattery,
therefore, O seekers of refuge, constantly remember the Lord of Sages and,
recollecting his virtues, go for refuge.
The second story concerning one of wrong view.
23. In the story of the footstool, this is the sequential account:
It is said that in Jambudīpa, on the southern side of the Great Bodhi tree, there was this frontier city. There, a person endowed with faith...

A certain lay follower, devoted to the Triple Gem, was residing there. At that time, a monk whose taints were destroyed took the footstool used by the Blessed One, placed it in a carrying-bag, and as he went from place to place, paid homage to it.

Eventually arriving at that city, well-robed and well-clad, he took his bowl and entered the middle of the street with the graceful deportment of one gone forth, looking ahead only the distance of a plough-yoke.
While pleasing the people, that lay devotee saw the Elder walking in such a manner;
with a mind full of faith, he approached, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, took his bowl, and fed him. He then requested, "I wish for you to come to my house regularly;
out of compassion for me, please stay right here, Venerable Sir," and [he established him] in a delightful grove near the city on the bank of a river.
Having built a leaf-hut and having offered it to the Elder, he dwelt there, attending to him, honoring him, and worshipping him with the four requisites. The Elder also,
having deposited the relic of the Blessed One’s footstool in a convenient spot there and having constructed a stupa of sand,
made his abode while constantly worshipping it with perfumes, incense, lamps, flowers, and other offerings.
At that time, a certain wealthy devotee living next door to that lay follower was constantly worshipping his own deity.
Seeing him, the lay follower spoke of the Buddha’s qualities and said, "Good man, do not exert your energy toward an unworthy field;
abandon this view. Then that sectarian devotee of the lord asked, "What power of qualities does your Teacher possess?"
Having said, "The virtue of our lord alone is great," he spoke while describing his faults as virtues:
"He destroyed Tripura with the fire from the eye on his forehead;
and the great lord destroyed the asuras with his triple-pointed spear."
His matted locks, coiled and turned, danced at the junction of day and night;
he played the drum, the lute, and other instruments, and he sang songs as well.
Of his three wives, one would pull up a single lock of his matted hair.
Looking about from side to side, one should wander alone, clad in an elephant-hide garment;
by that very [garment] is austerity obstructed for one who is so manifest in beauty and possesses sons such as there are none other like them.
Constantly preoccupied with sensual pleasure and the drinking of honeyed wine, he carries a human skull upon his head and eats from that bowl.
For him there is no birth, no fear, and no death; he is eternal.
"Such is my Great God; there is no other with such qualities.
Having heard this, the lay follower said, "Friend, let these be the qualities of your lord for now. But how many are his faults? Then, enumerating all the qualities of the Blessed One, he spoke:
"Just as the ocean is the receptacle of all rivers in the world..."
The Tathāgata is the very foundation for all masses of virtues.
Just as this earth is the foundation for all things, both moving and unmoving,
so too the Tathāgata is the foundation for all virtues.
Thus he is peaceful, discerning, and self-controlled—such is he who is devoted to compassion.
Such are his various kinds of meditative absorption, and such indeed are his virtues.
Even a Buddha is unable to describe his praise in full.
Even if one were to speak for an eon, one could not reach the end of it;
how much less, then, can even the gods,
including Brahmā and the Suras, describe the virtues of Him whose qualities are infinite?
Speaking thus, both of them increased their quarrel, saying, "Our deity is supreme! Our deity is supreme! and went into the presence of the king.
Having heard their words, the king said, "In that case, we shall know the greatness of your deities through a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*).
Show us your psychic power. He then had a drum beaten throughout the city. From here—
"Indeed, after the lapse of seven days, the miracles of these two teachers will take place. Let everyone assemble!

Hearing this, many people from various directions gathered together. Then, those of wrong view, thinking, "Today we shall behold the majesty of our god," performed a great offering, yet they perceived no essence therein. Those of right view likewise...

Thinking, "Today we shall behold the power of the Blessed One," they went to the sand mound, honored it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, circumambulated it, and stood with palms joined in reverence. Then the king also, surrounded by his powerful army, stood to one side.
Those who propounded various doctrines also [assembled], thinking, "Today we shall witness his miracle," and arranged themselves in tier upon tier of platforms.
Having done so, they stood there. In their assembly, those of right view, facing the sand stupa and raising their joined palms in reverence, cried out:
"Lord, our Blessed One, having completed all the duties of a Buddha, has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
The eighty great disciples, including Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna, have also attained final Nibbāna; there is nothing left here."
Saying, "We have no other refuge," they made an act of truth (saccakiriya) and said:
"If we have gone for refuge to the Buddha from the very limit of existence,
by that truth, may the relic display a miracle."
If we have gone for refuge to the Dhamma since the beginningless past,
by that truth may the relic display a miracle.
If we have gone for refuge to the Saṅgha since the beginningless past...
By that truth, may the relic display a miracle!
At the time of the Sage-King’s joy, his sandals were truly marvelous;
by that truth, may the relic display a miracle!
When the Sage was at the time of the Six-Tusked Elephant, his tusks emitted six rays of light;
by that truth, may this relic emit six rays.
At the moment of his birth, the Buddha stood upon the heart of a lotus.
By means of the words beginning with "The foremost, the best," he uttered a speech accompanied by thirty-two signs.
By that truth, may this relic display a miracle.
Having seen four omens, he went forth, making his great departure.
By that truth, may this relic display a miracle.
Having put to flight the army of Māra, he sat and awakened at the Bodhi tree;
by that truth, may this relic display a miracle.
The Conqueror then set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma at Sīpātana;
by that truth, may the relic display a miracle.
[May it show] the Naga king named Nālāgiri, the lord of the Nanda and Upananda serpent hosts.
"The *yakkhas* such as Āḷavaka, the Brahmās such as Baka,
the Nigaṇṭhas such as Saccaka, and the twice-born such as Kūṭadanta—
you have tamed them all by means of that Truth. Therefore, show a miracle!"
Having spoken thus, the lay devotees entreated him, saying, "Venerable Sir, out of compassion for us and in order to shatter the wrong views of the multitude,
please display a miracle. Then, by means of the Buddha’s power, the power of the Elders, and the power of the lay devotees’ declaration of truth (*saccakiriya*),
the sand mound split open and the relic of the footstool rose into the air.
Having emerged from the earth, she stood there radiating six-colored rays of light and displaying her splendor.
Then the great multitude raised thousands of hand-claps, celebrated with shouts of "Sādhu!", and let out a great roar as they performed a grand act of worship.
Even those of wrong view, upon seeing this marvel, were filled with wonder; their minds were transformed, they abandoned their wrong views, became devoted to the Triple Gem, and went for refuge.
Thus was Kaliṅgara of great power even when touched by the foot of the Conqueror,
the sole Lord of the world who is free from taints.
"Indeed, he is of great power and inconceivable.
This is the third story concerning the footstool.
24. In the story of the novice Uttara, this is the sequential narrative.
It is said that he, having performed his duties under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merit conducive to liberation through various births,
became a master of magical sciences (*vidyādhara*) during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha and resided in the Himālaya.
At that time, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Sumedha, cultivating solitude, went to the Himālaya.

He sat down, having folded his legs crosswise in a delightful place. At that time, a *vidyādhara* traveling through the air saw the Blessed One resplendent with six-colored rays of light and honored him with three *kaṇikāra* flowers.
By the power of the Buddha, the flowers remained above the Teacher in the shape of a parasol. Having become even more filled with serene confidence because of this, at a later time...
Having passed away and been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he experienced sublime celestial prosperity.

Remaining there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from that state and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha in the city of Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy brahmin. His name was Uttara, and he possessed a most excellent form.
Having reached maturity and attained perfection in the brahminical sciences, he became one worthy of honor by the world through his birth, appearance, learning, virtue, and conduct.

Seeing his attainment of such wisdom, Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, desiring to give him his own daughter, made his intention known. [The Prince], however, due to his inclination toward renunciation...
Having rejected that [view], he attended upon the Dhammasenāpati from time to time;
hearing the Dhamma in his presence, he gained faith, went forth, and, being perfect in his conduct, waited upon the Elder.
At that time, a certain illness arose in the Elder, and for the sake of medicine for it, the novice Uttara—
Early in the morning, having taken his bowl and robe and departed from the monastery, he placed his bowl on the bank of a pond along the path and went near the water to wash his face.
At that time, a certain highway robber who had committed a crime, being pursued by guards, fled from the city through the main gate; while fleeing, he [dropped] the bundle of jewels he had carried.
Having thrown [the bundle] into the novice’s bowl, he fled. That novice, too, had approached the vicinity of the bowl—which was also the vicinity of his enemy;
the king’s men, pursuing the thief, saw the bundle in the novice’s bowl and, thinking, "This is the thief;
this man committed the theft," they bound the novice with his hands behind his back and [delivered him] to Vassakāra.
They presented him to the brahmin. At that time, Vassakāra, being appointed to the king’s judicial office, was administering punishments and executions.

Thinking, "This man previously did not heed my word; he went forth among the pure heretics," and because of his deep-seated enmity, he issued an order without even investigating the matter, saying, "Impale this man alive upon a stake! The king’s men [placed him] upon a neem-wood stake.
They were terrified. Seated upon the tip of the stake, the novice monk thought, "Who will bring medicine for my preceptor?
and he called to mind the Elder Sāriputta. Then the Elder, having learned of that situation, informed the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Blessed One, surrounded by the Great Disciples, observed the ripening of his wisdom and went to that place. When the Blessed One had departed, throughout the entire city—

A great clamor arose, and a vast multitude of people gathered. Then the Blessed One, placing his hand—whose soft, tender fingers were enmeshed in a web and which, with its palm outstretched, emitted a yellow radiance from the rays of the jewels upon his nails like a flowing stream of molten, natural vermilion-gold—upon Uttara’s head, said:
"Uttara, this fruit of the evil kamma you committed in the past has now arisen; therein..."
He said that one should practice endurance by means of that power of reflection. For this very reason, he said:
"In the past, it is said, you were a boy in a certain village;
having come together with other boys, you were playing in a playground."
Then, taking a fine needle, you terrified the living flies there upon that thorn with neem-juice.
Listen to me as I tell you of another evil deed of yours.
In the past, you cursed your own mother with anger, saying,
"Sit upon a bed of living spikes," even though she was advising you for your own welfare.
Because of these two evils, you are now wandering in the ocean of saṃsāra.
"For five hundred births you dwelt upon the thorny Nimbaja tree, a stake for living beings.
This is your final birth; even here, it has reached its fruition.
In this manner, and according to his disposition, he taught him the Dhamma, which was like the sprinkling of the deathless nectar. Uttara—
Having attained sublime rapture and joy through the gladness and happiness born from the contact of the Teacher’s hand, he ascended the path of insight (vipassanā) as previously cultivated.

Because his knowledge had reached maturity, through the excellence of the Teacher’s teaching, he exhausted all defilements by following the sequence of the paths and became one possessing the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña). This was after he had heard the Dhamma there together with those assembled.
They say that there was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand beings among gods and humans.

But Uttara, having become one possessed of the six super-knowledges, rose up from the stake, stood in the air, and displayed a miracle. The great multitude became filled with a sense of wonder and amazement.
At that very moment his wound healed; yet even while experiencing such suffering, he addressed the monks, saying, "Friends..."
When asked, "How were you able to apply yourself to insight (vipassanā)? he replied:

"Friend, long ago I had already clearly seen the peril in saṃsāra and the true nature of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra). Therefore, even while experiencing such suffering, I was able to increase my insight and attain a distinguished state.
Then, at a later time, in the midst of the community of monks, he [related] his own former conduct...
Explaining the meaning of these words, he spoke these verses:
“The Perfectly Awakened One named Sumedha, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks,
desiring solitude, went to the Himalayas.”
Having entered deep into the Himalayas, the foremost, compassionate Sage,
the Supreme among Men, sat down after folding his legs in the cross-legged posture.
At that time, I was a Vidyadhara, a wanderer through the sky.
Taking my well-fashioned trident, I then went through the sky.
Like a fire upon a mountain peak, like the moon on the full-moon day,
the Buddha illuminated the forest like a blossoming king of sal trees.
Having emerged from the forest grove, the Buddha’s rays streamed forth;
resembling the color of a flame, they gladdened my mind upon seeing them.
Searching about, I saw a flower, a *kaṇikāra* with the fragrance of a deva.
Taking three flowers, I worshipped the Best of Buddhas.
By the power of the Buddha, those three flowers at that time had their stems upward and their petals downward, casting shade for the Teacher.
By that well-performed karma, and by my volition and aspiration,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
There, a well-constructed celestial mansion of mine is known as "Kaṇikārī."
Sixty yojanas in height and thirty yojanas in width,
divided into a thousand sections and a hundred parts, adorned with banners and made of gold—
hundreds of thousands of such celestial chariots appeared before me in the sky.
There were couches made of gold, of jewels, and of rubies;
there were also couches of crystal, each according to one's desire.
And there was a costly bed, with cotton mattresses and embroidered coverlets.
With my upper robe draped over one shoulder and using a pillow for support,
having emerged from my dwelling, I wander on a tour of the devas whenever I desire to go, preceded by a host of deities.
I stand beneath the flower; it is my canopy above.
For a hundred leagues all around, it is covered with *kaṇikāra* blossoms.
Sixty thousand musical instruments attend me morning and evening.
They constantly attend upon me, unwearied by day and night.
There, with dances, songs, cymbals, and instrumental music,
I delight in playful pleasures and rejoice, seeking my desires.
There, having eaten and drunk, I rejoiced among the Thirty-three gods;
accompanied by throngs of women, I rejoiced in that most excellent celestial mansion.
And five hundred times I exercised sovereignty over the gods.
Three times over, I was a universal monarch (cakkavattī);
my local sovereignty was vast and beyond counting.
Wandering through various states of existence, I obtained great wealth in each birth.
I lack no enjoyment whatsoever; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
I transmigrate through only two states of existence—among gods and among humans;
I know no other destination. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
I recognize two classes of people, the Khattiyas and the Brāhmaṇas;
I do not know of low-born families [enjoying this], for this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, palanquins, and chariots—
I obtain all of that indeed; this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
A multitude of female slaves, a multitude of male slaves, and women adorned with ornaments—I obtain all of that indeed; this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
Silk garments, woolen blankets, and those made of linen and cotton—I obtain all of this;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
New clothes, new fruits, and food of the finest flavors;
I obtain all of this; it is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Eat this, enjoy this, sleep upon this bed;
I obtain all of this; it is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
I am honored everywhere, my fame has risen on high;
I have become one of great influence, with an assembly that is never divided;
I am the foremost among my kinsmen—this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
I know neither cold nor heat, nor does fever exist;
furthermore, mental suffering does not exist within my heart.
Having become golden-hued, I transmigrate from existence to existence.
"I do not know the reason for this change in my appearance; it is the fruit of this worship of the Buddha.
Having passed away from the world of the gods, impelled by the root of merit [I performed], I was born in the city of Sāvatthī into a very wealthy family of great sāl-tree merchants."
Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, I went forth into the homeless life;
though I was only seven years old when born, I attained arahantship.
The Buddha, the Visionary One, ordained me after recognizing my virtues.
I am worthy of worship as if I were young; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
My divine eye is purified, and I am skilled in meditative concentration;
I have reached the perfection of the higher knowledges—this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Having attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), skilled in the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*),
and having reached perfection in the true Dhamma— this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
For thirty thousand eons, I worshipped the Buddha.
I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
My defilements have been incinerated, and all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a snake that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me, being in the presence of the Best of Buddhas;
I have attained the three knowledges and fulfilled the Buddha’s teaching.
The four analytical insights and these eight liberations as well.
"The six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Upon hearing this, many beings became devoted to wholesome deeds, as did even those beings of the future who possess the causal conditions.
Thus they are unable to abandon evil;
even by people who do not desire it, suffering arises.
Therefore, one should avoid evil with cries of distress.
The fourth story: The Case of the Novice Uttara.
25. In the Story of the Port of Kāvīrapaṭṭana, this is the sequential narrative:
It is said that in Jambudīpa, in the kingdom of Coḷa, there was a place called the Port of Kāvīrapaṭṭana. There, many Māhissarakas were followers of wrong views.
They lived there. While some artisans were performing mural paintings in one of the temples, they depicted an image of the Blessed One on a wooden panel, bowing down in an act of homage to the Lord.
At that time, many lay devotees (upāsakas) went to that temple and, while looking at the murals here and there, saw that painting on the panel.

Having seen him, they thought: "Alas, we have seen that which should not be seen! In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—in all the immeasurable world-systems—there is no one who is superior to the Blessed One, nor even anyone equal to him, setting aside the Blessed One himself.
The Blessed One is worthy of homage and worship by all classes of beings. What these people have done toward him is utterly unworthy."
Weeping and lamenting, they went to the king’s gate and raised a cry. Hearing this, the king had them summoned and asked, "Why do you raise such a cry? They replied as follows:
"O King, our Blessed One is the god beyond gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās;
he is immovable like Mount Meru, profound like the ocean, infinite like space, and vast like the earth."
They praised the virtues of the Blessed One with such words as "patthaṭo" (spread out). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Bearing the thirty-two marks, like the moon in a fine constellation, Endowed with the secondary characteristics, like a blossoming king of sal trees."
Enveloped in a net of rays, he was like the radiant mountain of gold;
surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, he was like the sun with its hundred rays.
The Supreme Victor was like a golden mountain, and the female ascetic was like a peak of rock.
With a heart full of compassion, like the ocean at its ebb;
with fame renowned throughout the world, like Sineru, the best of mountains;
the wise sage is spread wide with glory, resembling the sky.
With a mind unattached everywhere, like the wind,
the Leader is the support for all beings, like the earth, that supreme Sage.
Unstained by the world, he is like a lotus by water.
He shines like a mass of fire that consumes the forest of wrong views;
like a medicine that destroys the poison of the defilements everywhere;
and like Mount Gandhamādana, adorned with the fragrance of his virtues.
The wise one is a mine of virtues, like the ocean is of jewels;
he is a remover of the stains of defilement, like the Indus River is of forest thickets.
He is like a victorious great warrior, crushing the army of Māra.
Like a universal monarch, he is the possessor of the jewels that are the factors of enlightenment;
like a great physician, he is the healer of the disease of hatred;
like a surgeon, he is the one who lances the tumor of wrong views.
The Teacher, our Blessed One, O Lord, is worshipped by the Great Brahmas;
he is always to be revered by the lords of gods, asuras, and siddhas.
Among all those who are foremost and honored in every world-system, [he is the most supreme].
"O Great King, their path is the Blessed One; he shines with majesty for us," they said.

"O Lord, what has been done by the celestial hosts is improper," they declared. Having heard that, the king said, "Sirs, all people speak of the greatness of their own respective deities. But how do you speak of the greatness of your Teacher?"
"Let us inform you," [the monks said]. "Lay followers, it will not be difficult for you, O Great King.
Have a plank brought, wrap it in clean cloth, seal it with your own seal, and place it in a well-guarded and well-protected shrine.
After seven days have passed, have it brought out and examine it; then you shall know the great majesty of our Teacher."

They said: "Then the king, having had it constructed according to the specifications they stated, placed it within the temple, closed all the doors, sealed them, and appointed guards to protect it. Thereupon, all those lay followers gathered together;
for seven days they gave alms, observed the precepts, performed the Uposatha rites, and cultivated loving-kindness toward all beings for the sake of all beings.
Bestowing their merit upon the virtues they themselves had performed and making offerings to the Three Jewels, they proclaimed thus:
"By the outflow of the wholesome deeds we have done, may all the deities of great psychic power and great majesty in the world,
as well as the Four Great Kings who protect the world, attend upon our Teacher and demonstrate their state of being present everywhere."

They performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*). Then, by the power of their merit, at that very moment, the sandalwood-wool rug throne (*paṇḍukambala-silāsana*) of Sakka, the king of the gods, manifested signs of heat.
Thereupon, surveying the world of men, he saw that adverse effect brought about by those of wrong view;
deeply moved, he came and, having paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, the Lord, he lay down and related what had occurred.
Having spoken to the lay followers (*upāsakas*), he returned to his own place.

Then, on the seventh day, at the break of dawn, they all went into the presence of the king, paid homage, and spoke thus: "Your Majesty, our lord has prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the Blessed One.
Then the king, having heard their words, had a drum beaten throughout the city and addressed the great multitude:
Having gathered them together and being surrounded by them, he went to the temple, caused the lock to be broken, had the door opened, and had a plank brought;
then he had the wrapped garment removed. Then the king and the great multitude, having seen that great miracle, abandoned their wrong views and all went for refuge to the Teacher. Then the king...
Having had that temple demolished and having caused a great, beautiful monastery to be built, he performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived and was reborn in the world of the gods.
While the Teacher’s marvelous teaching was being maintained—
Seeing [the Buddha], those wise ones perform meritorious deeds and exercise spiritual power;
they perform great acts of merit toward that Lord of Sages who has attained final Nibbāna.
The fifth story: The Story of Kāvīrapaṭṭana.
26. In the Story of the Murderer of Thieves, this is the sequential narrative:
At one time, it is said, our Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in the Jeta Grove, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
Bestowing upon the great multitude the attainment of heaven and liberation. At that time, five hundred thieves came from the forest to the city;
having committed their thieving deeds during the night, they supported themselves with their wives and children.
Then one day, as those thieves were entering the city for the purpose of thievery, they saw a distressed countryman at the city gate and said, "O friend, where..."
They asked, "Where do you dwell? and he explained that he was a native of the country.
Then they said to him, "Sir, why will you live in this miserable dwelling? Come, join us in the work of banditry;
provided with clothes and ornaments, support your wife and children. Do not live in this wretched state. But he thought, "These people are speaking what is appropriate."
He accepted their words. Then, saying to him, "In that case, come with us," they took him and entered the city, where they committed acts of robbery, plundering here and there.
At that time, a man from the countryside who had acquired wealth thought, "This indeed is the better way," and so he made his living by committing robberies along with them.
Then one day, the king’s men, having finished their work, seized them all, bound them tightly with their hands behind their backs, and presented them to the King of Kosala.
When the King saw them, he said: "Listen! I grant a gift of life to whoever among you shall put these men to death and bring about the end of their lives.
Hearing this, all those thieves, out of a sense of mutual kinship, friendship, and connection, [consulted one another].
They did not wish for him. However, that man from the countryside said to the king, "I shall kill all of these," and being permitted by him, he killed them all.
Seeing this, the king was pleased and gave him the office of executioner.
While living there for twenty-five years, killing criminals and those condemned to death, he eventually became old.
Then, because of his feeble strength, he was unable to kill the thief even with just a few blows; the king, having learned of this, assigned the task of killing thieves to another.
Thereafter, having been deprived of the title "thief-killer" (coraghātaka), he lived in his own home.
At that time, a certain man, having mastered a mantra, [used] the breath from his nose...

He knows a spell for killing humans. For instance, desiring to cut or break off anything from the hands, feet, ears, nose, head, or other parts, he recites the spell and releases a nasal exhalation; that very spot is cut or broken.
Such is the great power of that spell. Then, having attended upon that man and received the spell, [he went] to the king.
He sent a message: "Previously, because I was old, I had to painfully cut and hack off the hands, feet, and other limbs of thieves;
even when they were to be executed, I would execute them with great pain. But now I shall not do so;
by the power of my mantras, I will perform the work of cutting and hacking. When the king heard this message, he said, "Very well," and [sent him].
Having summoned him, he restored his former position to that very man. From then on, while performing that work, he passed another five years.

Having become old, with his life-span exhausted, weak, and destined for the bed of death, he cried out with a loud and terrifying scream amidst the agony of the sensations of death, with his eyes closed...
As he lay there, he saw with his own eyes the terrifying hell-guardians, blazing with nets of fire and brandishing iron mallets and clubs;
consequently, upon hearing that terrifying sound, the people in the neighboring houses were so terrified that they fled, leaving their homes empty.
It is said that on that very day, the Elder Mahāsāriputta was surveying the world with his divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

Seeing that the executioner had died on that very day and was being reborn in hell, and knowing that upon my arrival there he would be reborn in heaven through his faith in me, [the Elder] thought, "Today it is fitting for me to show him favor.
Having dressed in the morning, he went to the door of the man's house. Then, seeing the Elder, the man became enraged.

With his body trembling and making a *taṭataṭa* sound from rage, thinking, "Today, having pierced and split him open, I shall kill him," he lay down and muttered incantations while releasing a breath from his nose.
At that moment, the Elder had entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*);
emerging from cessation, he stood radiant like the sun. Then, after the man had tried three times in that same manner, he was unable to do anything at all to the Elder.
Unable to do otherwise, his heart filled with extreme wonder, he pacified the Elder’s mind and had the Elder partake of the milk-rice he had prepared.
The Elder, having pronounced a blessing for prosperity, returned to the monastery.

As the executioner recollected the alms he had given to the Elder, he passed away at that very moment and was reborn in the heavenly realm. "Oh, how wonderful are the sons of the Buddha who are free from passion! he exclaimed.
This is the majesty [of giving]. Thus, even one reborn in hell is reborn in heaven by the power of that [giving].
For it is said: "Generosity is the refuge of humans; generosity is the warding off of miserable destinies;
generosity is the staircase to heaven; generosity is the supreme bringer of peace."
Through the giving of whatever is desired, generosity is like a wish-fulfilling gem;
for beings, generosity is like a kalpa-tree or a vessel of fortune.
Through the generosity of one who possesses virtue, even the glory of a wheel-turning monarch [is attained].
They obtain the prosperity of Sakka as well as supramundane happiness.
Yet this one, devoted to evil deeds, stands on the path to hell in the forest of hell—
this was said by the Elder Sāriputta regarding the alms-food he had received.
Having avoided the states of woe, which are crowded with manifold sufferings,
he went to the excellent city of the gods, surrounded by a host of deities.
Therefore, out of faith, give gifts in this fertile field that grant all desires.
"By those giving gifts, virtue too must be protected; thus protection is exceedingly beautiful"—this is how it is stated in some places.
Then, having assembled and sat down in the Dhamma Hall, the bhikkhus asked the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, in which of the four states of misery was that wicked man reborn? Thereupon the Teacher said: "Bhikkhus, yesterday [the matter of] Sāriputta..."
"By the power of the gift he gave, he was reborn in the world of the gods; as a result of that very merit, it was prophesied that in the future he will become a Paccekabuddha.
"O Sāriputta, one who has bestowed such a gift reaches the path to heaven in an instant."
Therefore, give gifts to those who are happy, if you desire heaven and liberation in the future life.
The sixth story: The Story of the Robber-Slayer.

27. The Discourse on the Sequence of Events Concerning the Faithful Lay Disciple (Saddhūpāsaka-vatthu) In the past, it is said, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, there lived a certain man who was faithful and devoted to the Triple Gem.
He made his living by working at a sugar-cane mill. Then, seeing a sick bhikkhu, he [offered him] a ladleful...
He gave ghee; likewise, he gave a single lump of sugar to one bhikkhu.
Then, on another day, seeing a hungry dog, he showed it kindness by giving it a morsel of food. Next, he gave a kahāpaṇa coin to a man burdened by debt.
Then, one day, while listening to the Dhamma, [he gave] a garment to the bhikkhu who was teaching the Dhamma.

Having performed such meritorious deeds, he made this aspiration: "As I wander through various existences, may whatever I desire—whether in the oceans, mountains, or elsewhere—all be fulfilled for me.
Later, having passed away, by virtue of those very roots of merit, he was reborn in the world of the devas like one awakening from sleep, and there he enjoyed great divine splendor.
Having experienced [the results of his deeds] and passed away from there, he was reborn during the time of our Blessed One in Sāvatthī into a wealthy family of great sāl-tree lineage.
When he reached the age of discretion, he heard the Dhamma from time to time;
having heard of the disadvantages of the household life and the benefits of going forth, he went forth and before long attained arahantship. Later on...
Having paid homage to the Teacher, he went to the city of Uggā accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus.
There, the wife of a merchant was faithful and possessed serene confidence.
Seeing the Elder walking for alms together with the five hundred bhikkhus, she went in great haste, took the Elder’s bowl, and fed him along with the five hundred bhikkhus.

Having requested the Elder to reside there permanently, he had five hundred gabled houses built, adorned them, and settled five hundred bhikkhus there; he then provided constant service with the four requisites.
Thereafter, the Elder established him in the five precepts, and after dwelling there as long as he desired, he wished to go elsewhere.
Gradually he arrived at the village of Paṭṭana; having stayed there, he boarded a ship from that place and traveled across the surface of the ocean surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus.
As he was crossing the ocean, a wind in his stomach arose and caused him pain.
Seeing this, the bhikkhus asked, "Venerable Sir, by what means will this be pacified in the future?"

The Elder said, "Friends, in the past my illness was cured by drinking even a single bowl-measure of ghee. The monks said, "Venerable sir, how shall we obtain ghee on the surface of the ocean? Please consent [to our seeking it for you].
Having heard this, the Elder said, "Venerable sirs, ghee is not difficult for us to obtain. Take my bowl, draw up some water from the ocean, and—"
When he said, "Bring it," the monks did so. As soon as that water was drawn out, it turned into ghee.
Then, seeing this, the monks were filled with a sense of wonder and amazement; they offered the ghee to the Elder.
