As soon as the Elder had drunk the ghee—so it is said everywhere—the affliction was pacified. Then, by the monks...

When they said, "Venerable sir, what is this marvel? We have never seen anything like this before," the Elder replied, "In that case, you shall see the ripening of the merit of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
He then looked toward the ocean, thinking, "Let this become ghee.
Thereupon, within the range of his vision, all the water in the ocean was transformed and became ghee. Then the monks...
Filled with wonder, they asked, "Venerable sir, is there any other such merit?
Thereupon, the Elder said, "In that case, Venerable ones, look at my merit," and he looked all around at the various solid rock mountains;
they all became balls of molasses. Then, within the range of their vision, he showed them food vessels on all sides, filled with rice and curries.
It was provided with all its appurtenances. Then he looked toward the Himālayas, and it became entirely made of gold.
Then he looked toward the place directly in front of him, and there was a great forest grove; the entire forest grove was covered with cloths of various colors.
Having seen each of those miracles, the monks were exceedingly amazed and asked: "Venerable sir, by what meritorious deed did you obtain such things as these?"
They asked, "Will there be miracles? The Elder revealed all that wholesome merit he had performed during the time of the Self-Born One Kassapa.
Thus it was here: "In this auspicious aeon, the Leader named Kassapa..."
For the benefit and welfare of the entire world, the One Possessed of Vision appeared in the world.
At that time, I was appointed as a sugar-maker at a sugarcane mill;
by that work I made my living, supporting my wife and children.
At that time, I saw a bhikkhu whose faculties were exhausted and who was afflicted by disease;
he had come for the sake of ghee, having approached only a small jar [of alms] according to the practice of wandering for alms.
To that bhikkhu, I gave a measure of ghee equal to a *uluṅka*.
Faithful in the fruit of giving, with a mind burning with compassion,
as I wander through the cycle of existence from birth to birth by means of that kamma,
wherever I desire a vessel, there it arises in no small measure.
"I desire even a mere pot of fruit from within the ocean;
all that becomes a full pot—this is the fruit of the gift of a pot.
Listen to me regarding another delightful meritorious deed as well."
Then, O bhikkhu, seeing him oppressed by illness,
I took a lump of sugar and poured it into his bowl;
by that he became comfortable, and his disease was then dispelled.
By that gift of sugar to me, throughout my wandering among gods and humans,
wherever I am, sugar is easily obtained by me there.
And vast mountains become compliant with my will.
O monks, this is the fruit of giving sugar-candy:
listen well, O bhikkhus, to the merit I performed.
At that time, having seen a dog that was trembling and tormented by hunger, I acted.
I welcomed him with a portion of alms-food, and even that gift brought forth its fruit;
from that time on, there was no lack of food or drink.
In birth after birth, I was happy, having food and drink easily obtained.
Even now, if I have a desire and need for food,
may many *ukkhalis* (mortars) spring up all around my path of vision;
furthermore, may that merit I performed bring me protection.
To a man in debt, I gave a single kahāpaṇa coin;
by that meritorious deed, I have obtained the excellence of a peerless existence.
In birth after birth, I obtain abundant gold.
"O you who desire wealth, listen today! Even a mountain as massive as a solid rock would become entirely made of gold; this is the fruit of being released from debt.
Furthermore, O sirs, hear of another merit of mine, beautiful to hear."
During the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa, I was one who had heard much of the Sage’s Dhamma.
Having heard him teach the Dhamma, my mind was filled with joy,
and I offered a cloak to the Master of Dhamma for the sake of the Dhamma.
"By that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans,
I obtain abundant clothing, whatever is the most excellent and supreme in the world.
If I so desired today— knowing this today, and being aware of this today— I could even [bring] the Himavat mountain here."
With garments of various colors, I shall cover [him] on all sides.
If I so desire, this very day, I can clothe the deceased beings throughout the four continents— this is the fruit of the gift of cloth.
By the power of those meritorious deeds,
having experienced prosperity in the realm of sensual pleasures, he was born into a family of great wealth in the supreme city of Sāvatthī.
Having reached maturity and being well-established in happiness,
he heard the Dhamma and went forth into the teaching.
Consuming the supreme flavor of the supramundane through the vehicle of the Sage,
I abandoned the defilements and attained arahantship.
One should never vomit up what is wholesome, even if it be considered "trifling."
It yields infinite fruit; it bestows even Nibbāna.
Then, having heard his teaching of the Dhamma, the bhikkhus and the great multitude performed wholesome deeds such as giving, and for the most part they became destined for the heavenly realms.
Even by means of mental serenity, one gains little merit—
Knowing that it becomes so great in this way,
O noble ones, do not neglect it thinking, "I have little merit.
Remember the goddess here who gave the parched grain.
The Seventh Story: The Faithful Lay Disciple (Saddhopāsaka-vatthu).
28. In the story of the pauper, this is the sequential narrative:
After our Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, a certain poor man living in the city of Bārāṇasī worked for wages in another's house.
At that time, the city dwellers, having had pavilions and such constructed in various places, gave great alms-offerings.
Seeing this, the poor man thought: "Because I have not performed merit in the past, I live by working for hire in others' houses, struggling with hardship and difficulty.
Even for my lower and upper garments, I have only as much space as is needed for my dwelling."
"I receive [this] as suffering. Now, the appearance of a Buddha has occurred and there is the Saṅgha of monks.
All these people, having given gifts, are clearing the path to heaven. It is fitting for me also to give a gift;
that will lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time. However, I do not have even a single measure of rice, and one who has not exerted effort..."
Thinking, "It is not possible to bring him to his goal; for this purpose I shall exert myself and give gifts," he set out from there seeking employment.

Having gone here and there and worked for wages, he gathered together the provisions he received as pay and the sesame, rice, and other grains obtained through alms-round, and having enlisted the help of others, he [proceeded].

Having had a pavilion constructed there and adorned it with wild flowers and other offerings, he invited the monks, seated them in the pavilion, prepared milk-rice for everyone—using the term *pāyasa* throughout—and fed them. Then, at the time of his death, he recollected that noble act of giving which he had performed.
By virtue of that wholesome karma, like one waking from sleep, he [was reborn] in the world of the devas.
He was reborn. In accordance with the merit he had performed, a vast golden celestial mansion (*vimāna*) appeared for him.
Within a radius of three *gāvutas* on all sides, deities took up various kinds of musical instruments and offered their worship.
Constantly, thousands of celestial nymphs (*devaccharā*) stood surrounding him; the phrase "thousands of celestial nymphs" is used everywhere in this manner. Thus, he possessed great prosperity.

He experienced [the result]. Then one day, the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita, a resident of the Suvaṇṇasela Monastery who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), while wandering on a tour of the celestial realms, saw that young god shining with incomparable divine splendor.
Approaching him, he stood there and asked about the deed he had performed. He explained it to him exactly as it was; thus it is.
The palace was made entirely of gold and composed of jewels;
it was adorned with hundreds of golden pinnacles, difficult to behold and radiant.
It was strewn with hundreds of gabled chambers and filled with golden garlands.
It was hung with clusters of pearls, delightful here and there;
filled with many hundreds of chambers, adorned with couches and seats,
divided into suitable sections, it was built by one who increases merit.
There, in the midst of the circular dance floor, women dance;
some sing, some play, and some strike upon stringed instruments.
Then, at a distance of three gavutas from there, all around the palace, [they continue their revelry].
Taking up bows, arrows, and other weapons, the Sahacchara sons of the gods rejoice as they constantly surround [him] with dance,
song, and the like; they leap, shake, and applaud him from all sides.
"Thus, you who now possess such great psychic power speak as if you were a mere child.
I ask you, son of the gods: what deed did you perform in the past?
The son of the gods replied:
In the past, in the supreme city of Bārāṇasī, I was a man of ill fortune.
There, people gave alms after having invited monks.
While I myself lived by wages, I saw the great multitude giving alms.
Joyful, delighted, and glad, I then thought thus:
"These people, having provided themselves with garments and ornaments, give gifts;
even in the afterlife, they experience prosperity, being truly joyful."
Now that a Buddha has arisen, the Dhamma prevails in the world;
now there are those of virtuous conduct, the sons of the Conqueror, worthy of offerings.
There is the unsettled and the settled, and likewise some who stand in blindness; indeed, the states of misery are filled.
Beings who turn their backs on what is wholesome surely go to an evil destination.
Now, having become miserable, I live with great difficulty;
poor, wretched, and dejected, with little wealth and no home.
"Now I shall sow the seed in this excellent field, esteemed as good;
perhaps by means of it I might be happy in the future.
Thinking thus, he begged for alms and performed various kinds of labor.
Having had a pavilion built there and invited the bhikkhus,
I gave them milk-rice with great effort for the sake of the Deathless.
By the ripening of that kamma, I [resided] in the delightful world of the devas.
"I was born among divine pleasures, rejoicing in manifold ways;
long-lived, beautiful, and full of splendor I became.
Thus the young god spoke at length concerning the meritorious deed he had performed, and the Elder, having returned to the human world, [related it as well].

He manifested to people the celestial attainments he had personally witnessed through his own divine eye. Having heard this, the great multitude performed wholesome deeds and for the most part was reborn in the heavens.
Thus, even those who were destitute and miserable found no place of refuge [in the lower realms].
One who gives gifts attains distinction;
if you desire heaven or even the state beyond, then,
having destroyed the stain of stinginess, give!
The eighth story is that of the Miser. 29.
Regarding the story of the Devaputta, this is the sequential account:
It is said that previously, in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Nārada, this island was known by another name.
At one time, however, there was a famine and a failure of crops; a great fear of drought oppressed living beings.
At that time, a certain disciple of the Blessed One Nārada, having walked for alms in a certain village, went out with his bowl as clean as when it had been washed.
Then, in a certain house, people [were preparing] a measure of rice in a small cloth bag.
Having bound [the rice] and thrown it into water, they cooked it; then, taking the water and drinking it, they lived on.
When they saw the Elder, they paid him homage, took his bowl, cooked a meal with that rice, placed it in the bowl, and gave it to the Elder.
Then, through the power of their faith, that pot became filled with food; they witnessed this marvel.
Seeing that the result of the gift given to the noble one was visible to them this very day, they were filled with joy.
Having assembled a great multitude and fed them with food, they afterwards ate themselves; yet the place from which the food was taken remained full.
From then on, giving alms to the great crowds who arrived, they were reborn in the world of the gods at the end of their lifespan.
Then that elder, taking his almsfood, went and sat at the foot of a certain tree, intending to eat.
It is said that a certain son of the gods who had been reborn in that tree, weary from hunger, saw the elder eating;
he cast off his celestial form and stood near him in the guise of an old man. The elder continued to eat without even looking up.
When the son of the gods had finished eating and left behind the final morsel of food, he cleared his throat and made himself known as being present.
Seeing him, the Elder felt remorse and placed that last morsel of alms-food into his hand.
Then, having taken the morsel of food and standing there, he thought: "Indeed, previously I have [given] to recluses and brahmins, or to the poor and the destitute..."
"Or at least, even for crows or dogs, such food has never been given before; it is because of that that I do not receive alms-food even though I am a deva.
Come now, I shall give this portion of alms-food to the Elder himself;
that will lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time. Having thought thus, and having abandoned all hope for the portion of alms-food, he [gave it] to the Elder.
Approaching him, he said, "Master, enough for your servant of this world; please grant me favor in the next world," and having spoken thus, he poured [the food] into his bowl.
As each morsel of food fell into the bowl, right there at a distance of three *gāvutas*, divine food vessels appeared.
The son of a deva [then prostrated] to the Elder with the fivefold salutation...
Having paid homage, he then took divine food and, having first given it as an offering, ate it himself afterwards.
From the second day onward, Deputta gave a great almsgiving to the Elder and the assembled multitude;
at the end of his life, he was reborn in the world of the gods, where he experienced successive divine splendors throughout the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure.
In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, having passed away from there, he was reborn in the household of a wealthy but wrong-viewed householder in Bārāṇasī.
They gave him the name Deva. Later, when he had reached the age of discretion, his parents passed away.
Looking upon the storehouses filled with gold, jewels, pearls, and other riches, [he thought]: "My..."
"Since my parents, being of wrong view, have gone to the next world without performing any act such as giving from this life and without taking even a single *kākaṇika* with them,
I shall take that [wealth] and go," he resolved. Having had a drum beaten and having assembled the poor,
the needy, and the destitute, within seven days he placed his entire fortune at the disposal of charity.
Having given [the gift], he entered the forest, went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isi*), performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*,

and having realized the five supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he became a traveler through the air. At that time, the Blessed One named Padumuttara,
residing in the city of Haṃsavatī, surrounded by gods, Brahmās, and others, was teaching the Dhamma connected with the Four Noble Truths.
While he was sitting there preaching, the ascetic, traveling through the air,
saw the great assembly of people and the six-colored rays of light emanating from the Blessed One’s body; wondering, "What is this?", he descended from the sky,
sat down with the great grace of a Buddha, and seeing the Blessed One preaching the Dharma amidst the assembly, his mind became filled with serene faith.
Having sat down and heard the Dhamma, he paid homage to the Blessed One and returned to his own hermitage.
Then, having remained there for as long as his lifespan lasted, at the end of his life he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Experiencing divine splendor for thirty aeons, he wandered from one to another among the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure. In fifty-one successive existences, he became Sakka, the king of the gods.
Having experienced human prosperity as a wheel-turning monarch throughout twenty-one successive existences,
and having been born into a certain noble family in Sāvatthī during this current dispensation of a Buddha after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna,
he reached the age of seven years and saw a certain bhikkhu teaching the Dhamma. Upon seeing him, he approached and listened to the Dhamma, whereby the perception of impermanence arose within him.
Having attained it, he reached Arahatship while still seated there.
Then, having acquired the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he surveyed the meritorious deeds he had performed himself and, proclaiming that former conduct in the midst of the monks, said:
"Nārada, it is said, was a perfectly enlightened Buddha in the past, the supreme among men."
While he was liberating the world from suffering and bestowing the state of immortality,
at that very time, his disciple— whose bonds were severed—
having begged for alms on the island, was about to consume the food he had obtained.
I went to the foot of a tree, where I was a tree deity;
hungry and looking out, I stood near him.
He, his heart filled with compassion, gave me a portion of food.
Standing there with alms-food in hand, enduring hunger at that time,
I thought: "Because I did not give even a small gift to the virtuous in the past,
I am oppressed by hunger, even though I have been born in a celestial realm."
"Today I have gained a good field, and there is indeed a gift to be given;
here I shall sow the seed for the sake of liberation from existence.
Having thought thus and paid homage, he said, "Master, enough of this slave of yours."
"Perform acts of gathering merit here in this world for the sake of the next world.
Having said this, he gave it to me; and being full of compassion, he himself ate as well.
By that meritorious deed, I obtained great wealth at that very moment.
Passing away from there, I was reborn among the Cātumahārājika devas, experiencing great glory;
for a long time I dwelt there, endowed with divine powers.
One hundred thousand aeons ago, there was one named Padumuttara.
The Leader of the World, the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma,
appeared. At that time, I was a powerful ascetic in the forest grove,
having attained the five super-knowledges, traveling through the air.
Then, while traveling by air, I saw the Victor in the delightful city of Haṃsavatī,
surrounded by the radiance of the Buddha, adorned with the splendor of his halo,
attended by hosts of devas, as he was teaching the Dhamma.
Having seen him, I stood in the midst of the assembly in the sky.
Having heard the Dhamma, I was uplifted; and after passing away from the Teacher’s presence, when I fell from there, I was reborn in the delightful Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
For thirty thousand eons, wandering among gods and humans, I did not know a miserable rebirth; I obtained abundant happiness.
Fifty-one times, I exercised sovereignty over the gods.
Then twenty-one times I was a wheel-turning monarch;
I held regional sovereignty many times in various places during this auspicious aeon, whenever the Tathāgatas attained final Nibbāna.
Impelled by a meritorious deed,
I was reborn in the most excellent city of Sāvatthī into a preeminent family, seven years old at birth.
Having heard the Dhamma being preached by a certain bhikkhu, I—
Having brought an end to existence, I attained arahantship.
That gift was well-bestowed by me then, and the supreme Dhamma was well-heard;
through the power of that deed, I have brought an end to suffering.
And having spoken thus, he urged many people toward wholesome deeds. "By such giving,
even with the very last morsel of alms,
and by listening to the Dhamma for even a moment,"
Beings obtain a threefold prosperity;
who, O sir, could describe the fruit for one who gives abundantly?
This is the ninth story, concerning the Son of the Devas.
30. This is the sequential narrative concerning the Elder Sīvali.
It is said that one hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world, leading beings to the great Nibbāna of the Deathless through his teaching of the Dhamma.
At that time, the Blessed One was at Haṃsavatī together with a retinue including the king.
He placed one bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who receive offerings.
Then, seeing him and desiring that position for himself, the king gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet.
At that time, the Blessed One said to him, "In the future, in the teaching of the Blessed Gotama, you shall obtain that position."
He explained it thus. Having heard this, the king was gladdened; having performed meritorious deeds, he was reborn in the world of the devas.
Later, having been born as the son of a merchant in Bārāṇasī, he attended upon a thousand paccekabuddhas for the rest of his life with gifts of the four requisites.
After being reborn in the world of the devas and enjoying great prosperity there, when he passed away from that state during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he...
He was reborn in a certain noble family in the city of Bandhumatī.
At that time, he served in the capacity of the king’s military commander and performed his duties for the monarch.

Meanwhile, the lay devotees (upāsakas) residing in the city approached the Fully Enlightened One, Vipassī, paid homage to him, and said: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One, together with his disciples, show us favor by accepting an invitation for tomorrow's meal."
Having invited [the Blessed One] and given a great almsgiving, they all, being of one mind, had a magnificent and costly great monastery built dedicated to the Blessed One.

While giving a great almsgiving during the monastery-consecration festival, they declared, "In this assembly of givers, it cannot be said that there is no such person as so-and-so," and having prepared the offerings, they looked over the assembly of givers; not seeing fresh curd and honeycomb, they [sent] men...
Having summoned him and given him a thousand [pieces of gold], they sent him forth with the command, "Quickly seek out curds and honey and bring them here.
Taking the thousand pieces of gold, they wandered here and there searching for curds and honey and stood at the gateway.
At that time, Senagutta, carrying the king's own portion of curds and honey, arrived at the great gate.
Then, seeing the curd and honey, they said, "Friend, take this coin and give us this.
When he replied, "I will give it to you later," some said, "We will not give it," and they increased their demand up to a thousand.
Then Senagutta asked, "This is of little value; why do you ask for a thousand? What will you do with it? When they replied, "For the sake of the Buddha," [he gave it].
Thinking, "I myself shall give," he prepared sugar, honey, molasses, and other items by mixing them with ginger, black pepper, and so forth, and presented them at the head of the almsgiving.
Through the power of the Teacher, that offering became sufficient for the sixty-eight thousand bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Then, having experienced prosperity in the worlds of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he...
In a later time, during our Blessed One’s era, he took rebirth in the city of the Koliyans, in the womb of Suppiyā, the chief queen of King Mahāli Licchavi.
Having dwelt in his mother’s womb for seven months and seven years, he experienced the suffering of a difficult birth for seven days. As he was emerging from his mother’s womb...
His parents named him Sīvalī. Thus, for so long a time, this man of great merit experienced suffering within his mother’s womb solely due to the power of evil committed by himself.
It is said that in the past, having been a king, while engaged in battle with a rival king, he consulted with his mother.
She [offered] a stratagem, saying, "If you besiege the city, you will be able to capture the enemies."
"Madāsī, having besieged the city at her word, seized it on the seventh day;

by the power of that evil deed, such great suffering befell both mother and son. Then, on the seventh day after the time of giving birth, she recollected the Blessed One and delivered the child easily.
Delighted, on that seventh day, she [offered] to the community headed by the Buddha...

She gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; then, when her son was seven years old, he went forth from home, and upon seeing the Teacher, requested ordination. The Teacher directed him to the Elder Sāriputta;
thereafter, with the Elder Sāriputta as his preceptor (upajjhāya) and Moggallāna as his teacher (ācariya), he went forth. Then, at the very moment of shaving his head, he attained Arahantship.
He graced the Buddha’s dispensation; by the power of merit performed in the past, he became one of great merit and the foremost among those who receive offerings.

Then, on one occasion, while the Blessed One was traveling to the Khadiravanavihāra to see the Elder Revata, he reached with thirty thousand bhikkhus a wilderness thirty yojanas in extent that was waterless and devoid of food. For the most part...

The deities were devoted to the Elder Sīvali. Therefore, having sent the Elder Sīvali ahead on his journey and dwelling in monasteries built by the deities, the Blessed One—partaking of almsfood prepared by the deities—reached the Elder Revata.
Having brought that task to completion, he returned to Jetavana and established him in the foremost position among those who receive gains. Thus it is stated in the Apadāna.
The Conqueror named Padumuttara, the eye-seer regarding all phenomena,
arose as a Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.
His virtue was incalculable, and his concentration was like a diamond— [the latter phrase] appearing in some versions as "vajirūpamā."
Inconceivable is his supreme knowledge, and his liberation is beyond compare.
In the assembly of humans, gods, nāgas, and brahmas—
crowded with recluses and brahmins— the Leader teaches the Dhamma.
Accompanied by his disciples, possessing great gains, meritorious, and bearing radiance,
the Confident One placed him at the head of those in assemblies.
At that time, I was a khattiya in the city named Haṃsavatī— [the term] "Haṃsāvatavhaye" applies everywhere [in the verses].
Having heard those words of the Victor concerning the many virtues of his disciple,
I invited him for seven days and, having fed him together with his disciples and given a great almsgiving, I aspired for that very state.
Then, seeing me bowed at his feet, that bull among men, the Great Hero,
spoke these words in a loud voice. Thereupon, the great multitude,
desiring to hear the words of the Conqueror, [listened].
The devas, dānavas, and gandhabbas, and Brahmās of great psychic power, as well as recluses and brahmins, paid homage with palms joined:
"Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!"
"A great gift was given by a khattiya, lasting for seven days—or perhaps even more than seven days (the reading *sattāhakampito* does not appear in all versions).
Desiring to hear its fruit, O Great Sage, please explain it.
Then the Blessed One said: "Listen to my words."
Well-established in the immeasurable virtues of the Buddha,
a gift, upon reaching the donor, brings immeasurable fruit—
even if that donor possesses great wealth and aspires for the highest state.
"May I too become one who attains vast gains, just like the monk Sudassana"—
this he shall obtain in the future. In a hundred thousand aeons, born into the Okkāka clan, [he will become a Buddha].
A teacher named Gotama will appear in the world.
His legitimate heir to the teachings, born from his very mouth and fashioned by the Dhamma,
shall be a disciple of the Teacher known by the name Sīvali.
By that well-performed karma, and through my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off this human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Then, at another time, in the supreme city of Bārāṇasī,
I was once the son of a merchant, wealthy and possessing great riches.
Having invited a thousand individual Buddhas as my leaders,
I diligently satisfied them with sweet food and drink.
Passing away from there, I experienced great glory in the realm of the five sensual pleasures, surrounded by celestial nymphs in a palace made of jewels.
Thus inconceivable are the Buddhas; inconceivable are the qualities of the Buddhas.
For those with faith in the inconceivable, the fruition is also inconceivable.
Ninety-one aeons ago, a Leader named Vipassī arose,
possessed of beautiful eyes and possessing insight into all phenomena.
At that time, in Bandhumatī,
I was the beloved and desired son of a certain family, occupied with my work.
Then, a certain guild [honored] the Great Sage Vipassī.
He had a large pariveṇa built, which became renowned as such.
When it was finished, he gave a great almsgiving consisting of various kinds of solid foods, fresh curd, and honey; yet he did not see any *vicīna* fruit there.
Then, taking fresh curd, honey, and ghee, I went to the house of Kamma-sāmi;
wherever I went, I saw that very same [food].
Even after giving a thousand [coins], they would not give those two things.
Then I reflected thus: "This will not be insignificant, since all these people honor the Tathāgata;
I too shall perform a service for the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha."
Then, having reflected thus, I mixed curds and honey together and offered them to the Lord of the World along with his Saṅgha.
By that well-performed deed and by my volition and aspiration,
Having cast off my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Then, having become a king of great renown in Bārāṇasī,
I was besieged by Sattuka and caused the city gates to be blocked.
Then, while my husband’s enemies were attacking him, I was protected for one day by those very enemies;
subsequently, as the result of that, I fell into a terrible hell.
And now, in this final existence, I am born in the city of Koliya.
Suppavāsā was my mother, and Mahāli the Licchavi was my father.
Due to the karmic merit of a kṣatriya and because of the obstruction of a city gate,
I dwelt in pain within the womb for seven months and seven years.
For seven days I remained at the gate, overwhelmed by great suffering;
because of my mother’s act of giving, she too was thus deeply afflicted.
Now, having been looked upon with compassion by the Buddha, I have emerged safe and sound.
On the very day I went forth, I entered the homeless life.
Sāriputta was my preceptor, and Moggallāna, of great psychic power;
as he shaved off my hair, the Great-Minded One gave me instruction.
While my hair was being cut and my beard was being shaved—so it is said in some places—I attained Arhatship;
gods, nāgas, and humans brought me the requisites.
And [I saw] the one named Padumuttara and the Guide Vipassī.
I worshipped them with joy, especially with the requisite offerings.
Then, as the result of those actions,
I obtained an exceedingly vast and supreme gain everywhere— in the forest and the village, in the water and on the land.
When the Leader, the Supreme Guide of the World, went with thirty thousand bhikkhus to see Revata,
then, O Great-Minded One, for my sake, the deity [offered] things most excellent— most excellent in every respect.
The Great Hero, the Leader of the World, together with his Saṅgha, was attended by me through various conditions.
Having gone, I saw the Buddha at Revata;
then, having gone to Jetavana, I established him as the foremost in this [list].
"Among my disciples who are gainers, O bhikkhus, Sīvalī is the foremost," so the Teacher, the benefactor of the whole world, proclaimed her in the midst of the assembly.
"The defilements have been burnt away by me; all states of existence have been uprooted."
Like a snake that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed was my arrival in the presence of the Best of Buddhas;
I have attained the three knowledges and fulfilled the Buddha’s teaching.
"The four analytical knowledges, and these eight liberations;
the six direct knowledges have been realized: the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed the Venerable Sīvali Thera spoke these verses.
Having heard of this great and wondrous conduct,
the power of merit, and the glory of the glorious one,
abandon indolence and perform what is wholesome.
Desire for sensual pleasures, desire for existence, and the cessation of enjoyment—
this is the tenth story concerning the Elder Sīvalī.
The third chapter, "Deceived by a Yakkha," is concluded.
The Chapter on Mahāsena.
31. This is the sequential narrative concerning King Mahāsena:
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, a king named Mahāsena reigned as a righteous ruler in the city of Pāṭaliputta.
The Dhamma King. Having observed the heaps of wealth belonging to his father, grandfather, and so forth, he thought:
"These people have abandoned this property and entered the jaws of Death. Oh, the ignorance of those caught in saṃsāra!

They do not realize that by keeping wealth they bring about their own destruction, and by keeping themselves they bring about the destruction of wealth; thus they fail to understand both the attainment and the loss of prosperity."
Having reflected on all this and having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith.
Day after day, satisfying ten thousand bhikkhus with sweet food and drink, he accumulated manifold merits. One day, while sitting in private seclusion, he thought thus:
"Rather than giving gifts by inflicting hardship upon the people through the king's command, it would be better to perform the work with my own hands."
Thinking, "The gift given by me, having been obtained after making [this resolve], will be of great fruit and great benefit;

thus it must be done by me," he, while his brother was still alive, had the kingdom handed over to him, took his younger brother, and without informing anyone, departed from the city in a certain disguise and went to the city named Uttaramadhura. There lived a certain merchant of great wealth.
Having lived there, they approached and stood near the merchant. When he asked, "For what purpose have you come?
the king said, "I shall perform labor for wages in your house. Having been granted permission by him, he performed the work for three years.
Then one day, the merchant saw them, summoned them, and said, "You are exceedingly delicate; nevertheless, in this..."
"You have lived in this house for a long time performing work; during all this time, not even a trace of laziness has been seen in any task, let alone misconduct.
Aside from the rice gruel and food, there is no other service required from me;
for what purpose do you perform this work? he asked. When the king heard his words, [he reflected that] in this district, rice is of such pleasing quality...
"It is often heard [that rice grows there]. Therefore, we have come here for the sake of rice," he said.
Hearing this, the merchant was pleased and gave them a thousand cartloads of rice. Having obtained the rice, the king said to the merchant, "Sir, bring this to our city.
Hearing that, the merchant said, "Very well," and [loaded] a thousand cartloads full of rice for the king.

He brought him to the city. Having arrived at the city, the king filled carts with various kinds of cloth, silver, gold, and other goods, sent them back to the merchant, and having established a firm bond of friendship, he stored the grain that had been brought in the royal palace.
Then, after a few days had passed, the king took up a pestle and began to pound the grain with his own hand; as he pounded it again and again—

The youngest sister winnowed [the grain]. Thus, both of them made a large heap of rice, brought firewood, water, and other necessities, cooked sour-soup rice (*ambilabhatta*), prepared five hundred seats at the royal palace, and announced the time, saying:
"May the noble ones come out of compassion and eat at my house. Hearing this, the five hundred bhikkhus [arrived] through the air.

They arrived, and the king served them as much as they desired. Then, from among them, a certain elder named Mahāsiva who resided on Piyaṅgudīpa took some food and, resolving with the thought, "Let these people see me," he went through the air to Piyaṅgudīpa.
There he gave the food to five hundred bhikkhus and partook of it himself. By the power of that act, there was enough for everyone as much as they desired.
Thus, even with a small gift, noble persons gladden the hearts of the donors and provide them with a firm foundation.
For it is said:
"Even with a small thing, the wise man gladdens the hearts of the donors."
They increase their faith like the moon with its rays increasing the ocean of milk.
Not employing [wealth] for improper purposes, nor making hoards,
they do not destroy their requisites without having made use of them.
"Neither those who do not fall into theft, nor those who likewise do not commit such acts, distribute [their gains] among those of virtuous conduct;
rather, having eaten it themselves, they remain virtuous.
Then the king, standing right there together with his younger sister, saw five hundred bhikkhus enjoying themselves on the Piyaṅgu Island.
Seeing this, he became joyful and elated. Later on, as they both recollected the excellent gift they had given, before long they both became stream-enterers.
Without counting their own suffering, having abandoned great glory;
Desiring future existence, those who delight in the virtuous and the auspicious—
realizing that merit performed with effort yields great fruit—
the wise person performs it with their own hands.
The first story, concerning King Mahāsena. 32.
In the story of Suvaṇṇatilakā, this is the sequential narrative:
it is said that in the city of Anurādhapura on the island of Laṅkā, a certain woman—whether she was a mother to one woman or a mother to another woman—somewhere...
Endowed with faith, she constantly performed flower offerings at the Abhayuttara Cetiya.
Then one day, having gone with her daughter to that cetiya for the purpose of making a flower offering, she did not see water in the hall where flowers were placed;
so, placing the flower basket in her daughter’s hand, she took up a water jar.

She went to the lotus pond. Then, while her mother had not yet returned—this applies everywhere as "before she had even returned"—that girl took a handful of flowers, made a mandala, and having worshipped it, made this aspiration:
"In the same way, [may I become] the Great Hero, the Wise One, the Self-Existent, the Great Seer."
By the power of that deed of offering a flower to the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Lord who is supreme in the three worlds,
I shall become preeminent among those possessing form, endowed with perfect height and proportions.
Upon seeing me, may all men who are intoxicated by sensual desires be freed from them;
may rays of light issue forth from my body like those of the sun garlanded with beams.
May my sweet speech, which touches the heart and is pleasant to the ear, be beautiful.
"May her voice proceed just like that of the Kinnaras.
Then her mother came and, seeing the flowers offered upon the unwashed seat, said, "Why has this Caṇḍālī offered flowers for the Blessed One on an unwashed seat?
This was improper of you. Upon hearing this, she became angry with her mother and said, "You are the one who is a Caṇḍālī!"
She reviled [him]; having performed such merit and demerit, when she passed away from there, she was reborn in Jambudīpa as the daughter of a Caṇḍāla-Gandhabba Brahmin in Uttaramadhura.
She possessed supreme beauty, and rays of light issued forth from her body like streaks of lightning from the mouth of a cloud. Within a space of four cubits all around her, [the darkness vanished].
The darkness was dispelled by the radiance of her body. From her mouth issued the fragrance of a blue lotus, and from her body the scent of sandalwood.
Between her two breasts there was a single golden-colored mole, from which a light shone forth like that of the rising sun.
Whomever she looked upon, for the most part, became as if mad, losing their senses through the intoxication of passion.
Ah, how great is the power of the wholesome and the unwholesome!
For it was because of that [deed] by which she was called "the mother of anger" and "the Caṇḍālī," that she became a Caṇḍālī— loathsome and of low birth.
Having observed the virtues of the Sambuddha, she then made offerings;
by the power of that merit, she became beautiful and charming.
In whatever manner one performs meritorious or evil deeds, [so shall it be for them].
According to each respective [deed], one obtains a fruit like that of a peacock.
Through evil one is born among animals, but through skillful [deeds] one becomes a peacock;
such is the karma for the beauty and the eye-patterns of peacocks.
Therefore, her parents gave her the name Suvaṇṇatilakā.
Indeed, although the people in that city were captivated by the sight of her beauty and her voice, they did not give her in marriage out of fear of contempt, thinking, "She is a Caṇḍāla girl.
Then, in that city, the son of the eldest Caṇḍāla Brāhmaṇa [approached] her parents for this purpose...
He sent clothing, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and so forth to her presence, saying, "Let them give us a golden tilaka.
They reported this matter to her. She, feeling loathing for him, made a joke of it.
Thereupon, the Brahmin’s son, feeling ashamed, went into the presence of the king, set aside his lute, and while singing, spoke thus.
Lalanā, with eyes moving like those of a doe,
youthful, ruddy, and with trembling lips—
the man who indeed makes her dear to his eyes, [is truly blessed].
But he did not abandon his low birth.
When asked by the king, "What is this?", he replied:
"O King, how can clay on the ground be equal [to gold]?"
"O Deva, sometimes even a low-born female dog of the breed of gold may equal a lion of noble lineage."
Having spoken thus, he said: "Your Majesty, in this city there is a daughter of the Caṇḍālas named Suvaṇṇatilakā.
She does not accept gifts sent by those of her own caste; she desires only those of noble family, thinking, 'When indeed shall the crow be united with the golden swan, O King?
When the king heard this, he summoned her father and informed him of the matter.
Having spoken thus, he asked, "Does she speak the truth? He replied, "She speaks the truth, Your Majesty; she desires only one who is endowed with noble birth.
The king said, "If that is so, tell me: in the city of Pañcamadhura there is a brahmin named Uddāḷa.
He is of noble birth, irreproachable on both his mother’s and father’s side, and because he finds women disgusting and repulsive, he does not live together with a woman."
As he went from his own house to the royal palace and back again, he had the road sprinkled with sixteen jars of milk and water.
Whenever he saw a woman, thinking, "I have seen a bringer of misfortune," he would wash his face with that milk and water.
He said, "Your daughter is capable; let her live together with him. Tell your daughter this matter. Having heard this, he also went home.
Having gone there, he summoned his daughter and spoke to her according to the very instructions given by the king.
When she heard this, she said, "If I am able, I shall live with the Uddāḷa Brahmin; do not worry about me, nor create any delay;
I will go early in the morning. Her father, saying "Very well," [gave her] a cloak made of fine woolen cloth (*cittakambala*) worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Having had his daughter’s body clothed and having had her take up musical instruments such as the lute, he set out on the road together with his daughter.
While traveling, in a certain city along the way, he performed music for the king, seating his daughter behind him;
then, while she was seated behind him, Suvaṇṇatilakā—
Bringing her gaze within the range of his eyes, he looked at her with longing; then, removing a portion of her wrapped cloak, she revealed the radiance of her body.
But the king, seeing both the radiance of her body and the perfection of her form, became overcome by lust, lost his mindfulness, and fell into a state of delusion;
after a moment, regaining his breath, he considered whether she was married or unmarried.
Having asked her name and heard that she was the daughter of a caṇḍāla, he was unable to bring her back out of fear of contempt. Grieving and lamenting,
"What use is life to me who does not obtain such a jewel of a woman, endowed with such beauty and grace?", he—
intoxicated by passion and not knowing what ought or ought not to be done— seized a sword, cut off his own head, and passed away.
In the same way, five kings along the road, intoxicated by the pride of her physical beauty, had their heads cut off with a sword and met their end.

For indeed, beings—whether through gold, silver, female and male slaves, children, wives, or any other such dear things—fall into ruin and calamity when they are infatuated by desire on account of what is beloved. Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
From the beloved arises sorrow,
from the beloved arises fear;
for one who is completely freed from the beloved—
There is no sorrow, so whence fear?
From affection arises sorrow;
from affection arises fear.
For one who is completely free from passion, there is no sorrow; whence could there be fear?
From attachment, sorrow is born.
From delight fear is born;
for one who is completely free from delight,
there is no sorrow— whence could there be fear?
From desire arises sorrow;
from desire arises fear. For one who is completely freed from desire, [there is no sorrow or fear].
There is no sorrow, whence could there be fear?
From craving arises sorrow,
from craving arises fear.
For one who is completely liberated from craving, there is no sorrow; whence could there be fear?
Then, proceeding by stages, he went to the city of Pañcamadhura and informed the king that he had arrived.
Having been permitted by him, he went and saw the king.
At that time, the brahmin Uddāḷa was seated on a fine woolen seat not far from the king, and the Gandhabba brahmin was also seated, performing music together with his daughter.
At that moment, Suvaṇṇatilakā, sitting behind her father’s back, asked, "Which one is the brahmin Uddāḷa? and [pointed] to him.
Hearing that "this is he, seated upon the auspicious throne," they gazed at him with eyes as pure as blue lotuses.
Smiling gently, her lips crimsoned by the radiance of her teeth, she looked at him; then, removing her outer garment, she released the splendor of her body.
Seeing this, the brahmin went mad with grief; his limbs scorched by sorrow, his mouth and nose filled with hot breath, and his face bathed in tears—
With his eyes parched, he lost consciousness. Then, after a moment, having regained his breath, he withdrew from the presence of the king like a sick man and went to his own home.
Having summoned his sons and daughters-in-law, he spoke to them thus:
"Sirs, when a calamity has arisen..."
He attends upon one when near;
he remains the same in pleasure and pain—
he is a friend and a kinsman.
He who proclaims another's virtues and conceals their faults—he is a friend, he is a kinsman.
Here, "paṭisedheti" (he restrains) must be supplied [as the verb] in all instances; "so mitto so ca ñātako" (he is a friend and he is a kinsman) [must also be supplied].
There is a woman named Suvaṇṇatilakā, a delight of the senses and an abode of desire.
My mind was shattered by her dark, fierce, and curved eyebrows;
those beings dwelling within her lotus-face, having become honey-bees for my eyes,
do not even remember me and take their delight right there.
My mind has gone forth, leaping over those very things—over the deep moat of shame and the lofty rampart of fortitude.
I am bewildered, I am utterly deluded; all the directions are lost to me.
"Be my refuge; show me your favor.
Having heard this, they said to him:
"O Teacher, that Caṇḍālī whom you desire is free from passion."
How indeed could there ever be a union of sandalwood with filth?
Fortune departs from men who go where they should not go;
fame, longevity, strength, wisdom, and reputation likewise depart from them.
Then the Brahmin said to them:
"This world does not give up its supreme jewel in the midst of impurity;
even those from low-born families seize the young woman, the treasure of women."
Having spoken thus, and having ascertained whether she had a husband or not, he said, "Bring her here," and they did so.
From the moment the Brahmin arrived at her house, he did not go to attend upon the king for four months.
Now, five hundred princes were learning various crafts in the presence of that Brahmin.
Having understood that reason— that as long as Suvaṇṇatilakā remained, there would be an obstacle to their learning the craft—
they thought, "By whatever means possible, it is right to kill her.
Having summoned a rogue elephant and given him a bribe, they said to him, "Intoxicate the elephant with liquor and kill Suvaṇṇatilakā."
Then they all assembled in the royal courtyard and sent a messenger, saying, "We wish to see the teacher.
When the brahmin had arrived and sat down, they exchanged greetings with him and said, "Teacher, we wish to see the teacher and the teacher’s wife.
Then he took the golden mark and sent men, saying, "Come! They did accordingly.
Then, when she reached the middle of the street, they released the elephant.
Striking the ground with its trunk as it charged forward, and pursuing her wherever she went, it seized her with its trunk and forced her to sit upon its forehead.
Thereupon, the kings, being unable to kill her in that manner, employed men on the following day.

They had her killed during the night. The brahmin too, having sought out such a woman, lamented and wailed, "Death is indeed better for me than life," and thinking that death was preferable in some respects, he had a wooden pyre constructed in the royal courtyard, entered the fire, and died.
Thus, those who have fallen under the power of women encounter great misfortune and even death. For this was said by the Blessed One:
This is a deceptive disguise, a deceptive dress— like a mirage;
it is sorrow, disease, and calamity,
and these bonds are indeed harsh.
The snare of Death lies in wait within those caves;
the person who places his trust in them is the lowest of men among men.
Having performed merit in a previous birth through wise reflection, she attained such a destination as this; thus,
in some cases, those performing wholesome deeds endowed with wisdom and endowed with fortitude [attain such a state].
"Make Nibbāna alone your goal.
This is the second story concerning Suvaṇṇatilakā.
33. In the story of Kapaṇā, this is the sequential narrative.
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen throughout Jambudīpa went,
for the most part, to pay homage to the Great Bodhi Tree, saying, "We shall worship the Jayamahābodhi. Later on,
many monks gathered and were traveling to pay homage to the Great Bodhi Tree when, having gone for alms in a certain village, they...
Having gone to the refectory and finished their meal, they rested for a short while.

At that time, a certain poor and destitute woman, seeing the monks seated there, approached them, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and standing to one side, asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going?
When the monks heard her, [they spoke of] the majesty of the Great Bodhi Tree and...
Speaking thus as they set out themselves to go for the purpose of paying homage, they said:
"Wherever the Jina sat and, having destroyed the army of defilements along with the army of Māra—
the one whose banner is the sea-monster— became the unsurpassed Buddha."
The Great Hero, standing firm and not disturbing the state [of the world],
honored his own eye for seven days and nights with the radiance of the blue lotus.
By casting away the thorns from the eyes of gods, asuras, humans, and others, he cleared the path for their vision.
He who shines like a peacock with his emerald-green leaves,
who stands upon the surface of the earth like a celestial tree,
bestowing whatever is desired both in this world and in the next.
To that person who worships even a fallen old leaf here in this world,
that tree bestows the enjoyments of existence. To whomsoever a person constantly pays homage with perfumes, garlands, and water, [that tree grants his wishes].
Whether internal or external, he destroys his evil deeds.
He who gives for the sake of this world,
and he who gives for the sake of the world beyond—
"Let us go to pay homage to the Bodhi tree of victory, which has attained perfection.
Having heard this, the bhikkhus were uplifted and filled with joy, and they said to him: "Venerable sir, I am working for wages in another's household."
"I am making my living with great difficulty and hardship. Even for tomorrow, I have no rice-paste, no husked rice, nor indeed anything else;
let alone other wealth, I have not even this single garment. Why? Because of merit not performed in the past.
Therefore, Venerable Sir, out of favor toward me, please tie this garment as a banner upon the Bodhi tree."
Having asked for it and washed the cloth, she gave it to them. The monks also took it out of compassion for her and departed.

Having given the cloth, her mind filled with joy and gladness, she went home; that very night, during the middle watch, struck by a wind from a weapon, she passed away and became a terrestrial deity in a delightful grove on the path by which those monks were traveling.

Having made the offering, she was reborn; then, by the power of her merit, divine *kappa*-trees appeared in an area of three *yojanas*, from which various multi-colored banners and streamers hung down.

Sons of the gods and daughters of the gods, adorned with all manner of ornaments, took hold of those very banners and streamers and played about. They performed many wonders, such as dancing and singing.
Then, on the second day, those monks, while proceeding toward the Bodhimanda, reached that place in the evening and, thinking,
"Today we shall stay in this forest grove and depart tomorrow," took up residence there. Then, during the night, at a distance of three yojanas,
various colored banners were displayed by the deities, along with songs, instrumental music, and so forth, as well as *kappa* trees.
And seeing that all this divine sovereignty had arisen through her power, they were struck with wonder in their minds;
addressing the goddess, they asked: "By what kamma were you reborn here? Standing there with palms joined in reverence after bowing to the monks, she said:
"Venerable sirs, you did not recognize me. The monks replied: "Sister, we do not recognize you."
When this was said, she spoke thus, describing her own nature:
"Yesterday, having gathered together in the assembly hall, you sat there;
I, that wretched woman, went into your presence and paid my respects."
I, who yesterday offered a cloth for the purpose of worshipping the Bodhi tree,
have passed away during the night, oppressed by illness.
Endowed with manifold prosperity and adorned with various ornaments, I was thus.
I was born here in this grove within a celestial mansion strewn with jewels.
Yesterday you saw my body covered in dust and grime;
today behold my body, radiant and luminous.
"Yesterday, venerable sir, you saw me wearing soiled garments;
today, venerable sir, see my supreme celestial robe.
My hair, once sparse and with its tips scattered and fallen out, [is now restored]."
Yesterday my head was repulsive with its mass of excrement and covered in lice;
today, by the power of my merit, it has been transformed into something beautifully dark-blue,
with hair neatly braided and adorned with flowers.
Formerly, with my own head, I carried timber, water, and other supplies;
by that merit, today I bear this garland upon my head as a burden.
Furthermore, yesterday I gave a thick cloth for the sake of a banner.
"Today, O venerable ones, I have been reborn with great divine success.
Knowing what must be done, one should perform deeds such as giving which yield great fruit;
for among gods and humans, the supreme gift is that which bestows happiness."

Having heard this, all the bhikkhus were filled with a sense of wonder and amazement. At the end of that night, the deity invited the bhikkhus, personally satisfied them with divine foods to be chewed and eaten, and then set out with them.
Giving gifts along the way, she proceeded toward the Great Bodhi tree, accompanied by all manner of banners, flags, and flowers endowed with various colors and fragrances.
Having worshipped the Bodhi tree with lamps and incense, and having given divine garments for the sake of robes for the monks, she returned and dwelt in that very grove.
Performing various meritorious deeds, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
The monks, proclaiming that marvel here and there, encouraged many people toward meritorious actions.
Knowing that even such a wretched person,
having developed faith in the teaching of the Jina by means of a coarse rag and having made an offering, obtained celestial splendor—
"Be intent on worship in the three bases"—the third base is for the poor. 34.
This is the sequential narrative concerning the story of the Elder Indagutta.
It is said that after the final passing away (parinibbāna) of our Blessed One, there was a city named Pāṭaliputta in Jambudīpa.
There, a king named Dhammāsoka—possessed of great psychic power (mahiddhika) and great majesty (mahānubhāva), a wheel-turning monarch by his command—reigned.
His authority prevailed throughout the entire Jambudīpa, for a distance of one yojana above the sky and below the earth.
At that time, all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa and eighty-four thousand kings, having taken their respective armies and vehicles, came and waited upon the great king Dhammāsoka.
On that occasion, the great king named Devaputta, from the city of Devaputtanagara, took his own army and vehicles and went to wait upon the king. Dhammāsoka...

Having seen the Great Kings, the sons of the gods, he exchanged sweet greetings with them and asked: "In your kingdom, are there noble ones who are deeply learned, well-versed in the scriptures, and possessed of great virtues? Hearing this, the royal son of the gods replied:
"Yes, Your Majesty, in that city there is a great monastery named Sīhakumbhaka. Therein dwell many thousands of monks who are virtuous and of few desires."
They were contented and seekers of solitude. Among them, the Elder named Indagutta, who was a master of the Three Piṭakas along with their commentaries, became their leader.
In many ways, he praised the Dhamma to the monks, including both humans and devas.
Being virtuous, he became renowned in the world on account of his own virtues. Hearing of this, the king was delighted in heart and desired to see the Elder.
"Having made the offering, you yourself must go, request the Elder, and bring him here," he said.

Upon hearing this, the king of the devaputtas, surrounded by a great fourfold army including his own elephant, hand-strength, and mounts, went into the presence of the Elder Indagutta, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, the Great King Dhammāsoka desires to see the Venerable One. When the Elder consented, saying, "Very well," [the king departed].
The king sent word to King Dhammāsoka informing him that the Elder had accepted [the invitation].

Thereupon, King Dhammāsoka, filled with joy, dispatched a message to the kings in the regions over which his own authority extended, saying: "Let all of you adorn the road by which the Elder will come.
Then those kings, delighted and overjoyed, caused the proclamation of drums to be made in their respective cities.
From the city of Devaputta to the city of Pāṭaliputta, they leveled the fifty-five-league road between them, adorning it like a divine path for the deities,
and sent this message to the great king Dhammāsoka: "Your Majesty, here."
"Let them adorn the path for our lord’s journey"—
thus was it sent by the Great King. Then, having removed stones, thorns, and the like from it, they prepared the way.
Having leveled the uneven ground and having thoroughly swept it,
and having scattered sand as bright as washed pearls,
rows of cloth festoons were raised here and there.
There were archways made of black iron, gold, and emeralds, as well as many rows of various archways made of flowers; above those archways, there were further archways.
In various places, bouquets of flowers were fashioned.
Likewise, rows of lamps were lit with fragrant oils;
they were adorned with lotuses, water-lilies, flowers, and sprouts,
and garlands of jars filled with scented water were set out.
The forest on both sides of the road was thickly crowded with blue and yellow banners and flags intermingled; there,
the flags stood high, stirred by a very gentle breeze.
The Brahmās, Nāgas, Suras, and others shine forth as if calling out, with Nāga-campaka, Punnāga, Ketakī, and Vakula trees;
with lotuses and water-lilies born in the ponds; and with the splendor of Mālatī flowers.
The road was made variegated with many garlands and wreaths;
having spread out foot-cloths upon the ground that had been sprinkled and swept,
they scattered parched grain and the five kinds of flowers, making it delightful.
Having adorned her hands with flowers, ornaments, and the like,
she proceeded from here and there to decorate the road; and in various places along that path, she came upon circles of drums.
The fourfold host of women dance, uninterrupted by their passionate emotions,
grasping at cymbals, flutes, and other instruments as they strike many strings.
They sing sweet songs, singing there in perfect harmony with the rhythm.
Resounding with shouts of "Sādhu!", with the booming of kettledrums,
with the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses,
and crowded with many groups of monkeys on the treetops, it was filled with that tumult.
On both sides of the path, beautiful celestial maidens resembling goddesses stand with joyful minds, holding bouquets of flowers.
Likewise, they carry full jars filled with clusters of lotuses and water-lilies.
There, the women stand having grasped eight auspicious items.
There, lotus ponds were dug here and there for the purpose of bathing, provided with cool water and adorned with steep banks.
In various places there were delightful gift-halls,
and many articles for giving were gathered therein.
Thus have we performed manifold kinds of worship.
"Setting aside the Great Gaṅgā, let the lord of the earth know that.
Having heard this, King Aśoka sent sixteen yakkhas with the command, "Adorn the Gaṅgā!
They went there with their retinues and, by their own power, established mortar-stones within the Gaṅgā at a spot three *gāvutas* in extent. Having established them...
Having erected pillars and fitted together the crossbeams, they brought heartwood from red sandalwood from the Himalayas and spread it over the floor.
Having adorned it with numerous modes of worship, they sent this message to the king:
"O Great King, for what purpose we have all been sent by you here—"
Now listen to all that we have done:
having erected pillars of priceless red sandalwood, we built [a bridge] over the Ganges, which is three *gāvutas* deep and one *yojana* wide.
Having brought [materials] from the Himalayas, he had a bridge beautifully constructed there,
with ornamental arches on both sides well-fashioned with jewels.
There were full water-jars, half-flags, and likewise rows of lamps.
On both sides, having fashioned jewels as supports—
adorned with strings of gold, gems, pearls, and the like,
strewn with sand and bright, washed pearls.
In various places along the perimeter of the bridge,
great jewels were set, beautified by canopies of many colors.
Right there, divine flowers and other such things were suspended.
"What remains here to be done is finished;
let the gods themselves acknowledge the appropriate ritual for our worship. Having said this, they sent word back.
Upon hearing that too, the great King Aśoka sent them a message saying, "You yourselves must bring the Elder here."
Saying, "Very well," they went into the presence of the Elder Indagutta, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, it is time to depart for the city of Pāṭaliputta.
Thereupon, the Elder set out on the road measuring fifty-five *yojanas*, surrounded by a Saṅgha of sixty thousand monks.
Furthermore, the inhabitants of the city of Devaputta [honored him] with various kinds of garlands, perfumes, scented powders, banners, flags, and so forth.
Having honored him with many dancers, singers, and musicians, they departed.
Then the Elder, being honored by the inhabitants of Jambudīpa with a grand ceremony of worship, gradually reached the bridge over the Candabhāgā River.
Beholding the great ceremony of worship there, he thought: "Such a magnificent ceremony of worship as this is now not for anyone else in Jambudīpa."
"It is so; this was done by me alone. I alone am supreme and peerless"—having thus given rise to the conceit "I am superior to one who is superior," he stood there.

At that moment, a certain elder whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsavatthera), seeing with his divine eye (dibbacakkhu) that he stood with a mind stiffened by such conceit, approached him, paid homage, and, exhorting the elder, spoke as follows. Therefore:
Do not be under the sway of conceit; for conceit, O Venerable One, brings one under its control, and conceit, O Venerable One, has been made master of one—this applies everywhere.
It always brings about harm, having cast one down from existence as if from a tree.
A being whose conceit has flourished is bound by craving and aversion.
Having become a monkey, a snake, a dog, and so forth, one is born among various states of existence.
O Master, do not indulge in pride; purify yourself.
A monk who is himself impure does not satisfy the donor.
"If you desire great fruit and great prosperity for those who give, those who offer, and those who worship, then be free from conceit, thinking: 'May they attain Nibbāna.
Hearing this, the Elder, having become disenchanted with *saṃsāra*, remained right there and, establishing the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*), [abandoned] the physical body born of karma.
While reflecting upon them, he attained *arahatta* together with his companions through the analytical knowledges (*sambhidā*) and then went forth.
Thereafter, the great King Dhammāsoka, surrounded by a powerful army and accompanied by a grand display of offerings, came out to meet him on the road;
having paid homage, he performed twice as much honor and hospitality as before, and together with the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, led the Elder to his own city. Then, for him—
Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, with a mind full of faith, he established himself in the five precepts and had a great monastery constructed.
He provided the sixty thousand monks who had come together with the elder with the four requisites.
Then the elder, dwelling there for a long time while elucidating the Three Piṭakas along with their commentaries, attained final Nibbāna right there. Thereafter...
The king, together with his retinue, having performed the disposal of his body and taken the relics, caused a great stūpa to be built.
Thus do those who have performed meritorious deeds on earth in former times honor them by the power of their virtues.
"Even including the gods, let them attend to this:
always perform meritorious deeds with diligence.
This is the fourth story, concerning the Elder Indagutta.
35. The Narrative of Sākhamālapūjikā: This is the sequential account.
Our Blessed One, having fulfilled the ten perfections, was successively reborn in the Tusita heaven;
being entreated by the devas, he took conception in the Sakka royal family, emerged from his mother’s womb, and in due course attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
Having reached that state, he remained for forty-five years from then on,
taught eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma, delivered countless beings across the wilderness of existence, and having fulfilled all the duties of a Buddha,
he passed away between the twin Sāla trees in the Upavattana of the Mallas at Kusinārā, upon a prepared couch with his head toward the north.
On the full-moon day of Vesākha, lying on his right side on a couch, mindful and clearly comprehending,
having passed into the final watch of the night after exhorting the bhikkhus, he attained final nibbāna through the element of nibbāna without residue at the time of the powerful dawn,
causing the great earth to tremble. When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, had thus attained nibbāna, the Elder Ānanda [addressed] the Malla kings...

He reported this occurrence. Then the people of Kusinārā, together with the gods, Brahmās, and others, having assembled, honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped the Blessed One’s body with dance, song, music, garlands, perfumes, and so forth;

and having constructed canopies of cloth and other decorations, they led it to the center of the city, to the shrine of the Mallas known as Makutabandhana, [where they treated it] as one would that of a wheel-turning monarch.
Having wrapped the body with a new cloth like a shroud, and then having wrapped it with carded cotton— thus having wrapped it with five hundred pairs of garments—
they placed the Blessed One’s body in an iron oil-vat, covered it with another iron vat,
prepared a funeral pyre of all kinds of perfumes, and set the body upon the pyre. Then, by the Elder Mahākassapa, [the Blessed One’s]...
When his foot was saluted with the head, through the supernatural power of the deities, the funeral pyre burst into flames all at once.

When the Blessed One’s body had been consumed, relics resembling jasmine buds remained. At that time, it is said, a certain woman living in a village in the kingdom of the King of Kosala was returning from a festival.
On the way, afflicted by a wind-disease that had arisen in her own body, she was unable to reach Sādhukīḷha;
however, having gone to the Teacher’s cremation ground, she offered three branch-flowers at the Blessed One’s physical relics.
With a mind full of faith, she prostrated herself with the fivefold greeting and departed. That very night, during the middle watch, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
She was reborn in a golden celestial mansion thirty *yojanas* in extent. To manifest her past karma, branch-like flowers the size of wheels hung here and there;
by means of these alone, the entire mansion became a single radiance, and from that point on, it remained so everywhere.
Furthermore, it was like a fragrant casket, and she herself possessed a physical form that had attained the pinnacle of beauty.

Having seen the excellence of the celestial mansion and the perfection of her retinue, her mind was filled with wonder. Thinking, "By what meritorious deed performed in the past—by what deed done in a former life have I obtained this? she looked about.
Seeing the three branch-flowers that had been offered to the Blessed One’s relic-body, her heart became serene. [She saw] a [stupa] the size of a great wheel...
Carrying a large branch of flowers in her hand, she went there for the purpose of worshipping the relics.
At that time, the people gathered there, seeing both her exquisite beauty and the great branch of flowers in her hand, were filled with wonder and asked, "Mother, where do you dwell?
And where did you obtain these flowers? Having heard this, the daughter of the gods [replied] herself...
Having shown them all— the prosperity they had obtained through the power of worshipping the branches and garlands of the Blessed One’s relic-body,
the celestial mansion, and their former dead corpse— he spoke at the conclusion of his Dhamma teaching:
"O sirs, you who have assembled here, behold my success!"
By what means? By means of three branches and garlands from the relics of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having worshipped the Sage’s relics with these, I returned satisfied at the end of that very night.
I was carried away by a harsh wind; I remember that well-performed deed.
By virtue of that meritorious action, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
There I had a palace, rising thirty yojanas high.
It is renowned as being strewn with excellent gabled pavilions, and in some places as having rows of trees and garlands.
Just as a casket is perfumed by all kinds of fragrant scents,
so is my abode scented with divine fragrances.
The branch-flowers are the size of a wheel; they are found here and there, appearing like shimmering cloth.
A divine fragrance wafts forth, frequented by bees and honey.
From a single flower, indeed, pollen as much as a water-jar is shed.
Adorned with those golden nets, the gods play and sport.
Having donned garlands and divine ornaments, the sons of the gods, together with the celestial nymphs, are occupied with dancing, singing, and other such delights.
"Behold this, O serpents! Beings are shrouded in delusion;
yesterday my corpse was cast away, now it has become putrid.
It is strewn with maggots and swarmed by a play of flies."
In former times, men sought with many means that food of the crows,
vultures, and other creatures dwelling in the cemetery; yet now they even long to see it— oh, the ignorance born of craving!
Yesterday, I properly placed the relic of the Lamp of the World, the stainless and illustrious one, upon the earth; today, I am established in heaven.
Having abandoned such a body, I have now obtained this one.
Behold me, resplendent with beauty, as I speak in my divine form.
Listen now to my words, you who have gathered here:
for one who has not performed meritorious deeds, there is not even the slightest happiness to be found.
"Whoever plants even a single drop of merit as a seed in the Sasana shall not fail to obtain its fruit"—
in some versions this reads "na hānatthaphalam," meaning "not without fruit"— until the attainment of Nibbāna.
Thus, that deity, having displayed the divine splendor she had obtained and having exhorted the multitude of people with divine branch-flowers...
Having worshipped the relic of the Victor while people were looking on, she went to the world of the devas together with her celestial mansion.
Seeing this, the great multitude performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and thus filled the world of the devas.
For in this way, by means of a mere flower, she [honored] the relic...
Having worshipped among the gods, he obtained prosperity;
may you too, O worthy ones, find happiness in the three heavens if you desire pleasure—
where, then, is it better to perform meritorious deeds?
The fifth story: Concerning Sākhamālapūjikā. 36.
In the story of the brahmin Moriya, this is the sequential narrative:
After our Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, there was a great village named Macala in the kingdom of Magadha. There...
There lived a brahmin named Moriya, who was faithful and possessed serene confidence; he had a wife named Senā, who was likewise faithful and possessed serene confidence in the Three Jewels.

Both of them, living in harmony and mutual affection, invited the Saṅgha of monks and constantly offered alms, serving them with the four requisites such as robes, while guarding their virtue and performing the Uposatha rites.
They spent their days performing these acts. Consequently, the wealth in his house was for the most part exhausted through such acts as giving.
Then the brahmin lady informed the brahmin, saying, "Master, the wealth in our house is completely spent. How can we continue to practice giving?
Thereupon the brahmin said, "Do not worry, dear lady. We shall establish the practice of giving by whatever means possible."
Having said this, he spoke again to demonstrate his own enthusiasm for that very thing:
"For who in this world, knowing that 'this is the fruit of giving,' would not give even a little, day after day, to those of virtuous conduct?"
"O Bhaddā, what wise man in this world, delighting in what is beneficial, would not give gifts that lead to rebirth in the heavenly realms?
Having spoken thus, he entered the forest and filled his basket with various kinds of leaves and fruits.
Having said, "Even by gathering and selling [the produce], we shall not discontinue our giving," from that time forth he went into the forest,
gathered leaves and fruits, and having sold them, remained there constantly bestowing gifts.
Then one day, the brahmin entered the forest, filled his basket with leaves and fruits, and was returning home from the grove carrying it on his head.
Having seen a beautiful cave— bending under the weight of flowers, fruits, and shoots, filled with many kinds of trees,
frequented by flocks of cātakas and various quadrupeds, its sandy floor covered with scattered flowers, leaves, and filaments, and possessing a flowing stream of cool,
stainless water that was free of mud and perfectly level— he set his basket on the bank, descended, and bathed.
At that moment, a son of the gods dwelling in a certain tree there, seeing him bathing, wondered, "Is this being of virtuous disposition or of evil disposition?
Examining him with his divine eye, he perceived: "This is a wonderful man;
though he has fallen into misfortune, out of fear that his own tradition of giving might be interrupted, he has come to the forest."
Thinking, "Having gone and brought back leaves and fruits, he maintains his livelihood with hardship and toil,
yet he does not interrupt the practice of giving," she resolved that all the leaves and fruits placed in her basket would turn into gold by virtue of his qualities.
Then, through the power of that resolve, everything became gold.
Then, having placed the great wish-fulfilling jewel (*maṇiratana*) upon a heap of gold atop a golden full basket, he vanished and withdrew to stand aside.
Thereupon, the brahmin, having bathed and emerged, saw the jewel shining with a brilliance that surpassed the color of the gold filling the basket; suspecting and fearing, he approached the basket.
Unable to go forward and stretch out his hand, he stood still. Seeing him, the son of the gods stood there with his body visible and said, "Do not fear, brahmin.
These were created by me; take them and go. Then the brahmin, having heard the words of the son of the gods, thought, "This son of the gods says, 'These were created by me; take them and go.'"
He speaks. "Does he give by his own power, or rather by the merit performed by me?"—thinking thus, "I shall ask him," he spoke to the son of the gods while still with palms joined:
"Now I ask you with palms joined, O son of the gods of great psychic power."
"You give me gold and the supreme wish-fulfilling gem,
yet no one knows who you are to us— not a relative, nor a friend, nor a benefactor."
Seeing what purpose would you give me this wealth?
By what austerity, by what virtue, and by what conduct and quality [would you do so]?
