"By what means, O Lord, would you give to me? What good deed have I accumulated?
What indeed is my past karma, and by what karma will you give?
Or do you give through your own power? Tell me that when I ask."
Then the son of the gods said, "O Brahmin, it is not that I am a god, nor can I give anything to others; rather, this is produced through the power of the good conduct you performed in the past.
Having spoken thus, he beheld his former karma with the divine eye and, explaining it to him, said:
"When the Sambuddha Kassapa, the lamp of the world, had attained final Nibbāna..."
The teaching of that Buddha was spread everywhere.
At that time, in a frontier village, you were the son of a noble family;
you were faithful and confident, a donor who delighted in wholesome deeds.
At that time, having gone forth as a solitary wanderer, while traveling along a path,
you were pursued by bandits who stripped you of your bowl and robes.
Having fashioned a garment from broken branches and likewise donned it, you went on.
You entered the village searching for a piece of cloth.
Then, seeing him wandering there, your mind was filled with trembling;
you gave him a pair of garments, having faith in the fruit of giving.
Having served that bhikkhu with a dish of rice according to his strength, he sent him away after paying homage, his mind purified by faith.
"You have performed this merit; this is your own deed."
"Such is the principal fruit of that meritorious deed of yours.
Having spoken thus, he said: "O Brahmin, this wealth of yours has been made by me immune from seizure by kings and others;
take it without suspicion and do with it as you intend. Furthermore, this jewel-treasure grants whatever is desired."
"He procreated; by that very power, instruct him: 'Support your wife, children, and others without interrupting your giving.

Having heard this, the brahmin, giving a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and guarding his virtue according to the very method prescribed by him, lived for a long time and, passing away from there at a later stage, was reborn in the world of the devas.
Thus, even those who are destitute of wealth do not abandon the practice of giving;
therefore, sirs, when there is something to be given, [one should give].
"Do not be negligent regarding acts of giving.
This is the sixth story, concerning the brahmin of the Moriya clan.
37. In the story concerning the son, this is the sequential narrative.
It is said that once, about sixty monks dwelling on the island of Laṅkā, desiring to pay homage to the Great Bodhi Tree at Jayamahābodhi, consulted together and boarded a ship at Mahātittha.

Having reached Jambudīpa, they disembarked at the port of Tāmalitti (Tamalittapaṭṭana)—the spelling *tamalittapaṭṭane* being found in some places—and in due course arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputta. Then, in that city...
As those bhikkhus were wandering for alms, a certain poor man saw them and, after a long time, said:
"At last I have seen them; everywhere I have seen the sons of the Buddha. Overjoyed, he called his wife and said: "My dear, I wish to give a gift to these noble ones.
Because we did not perform merit in the past, we have now been born into poverty; let us sow seed in these fields of merit."
"If we do not plant it, we shall become just like this again," he said, and then asked, "What gift do I have in my house?
Upon hearing this, she replied, "My lord, I see nothing in the house that can be given to the noble ladies.
However, I am able to give a gift by killing my own son. Having heard her words, he said, "Bhadde, what is the use of killing your son?"
"I shall give a gift," he said. Upon hearing this, she replied, "Master, do you not know? Our sons have died;
our kinsmen, friends, and companions who were seen together and shared our joys and sorrows are coming to us, and they bring some kind of gift with them.
We thought we would give a gift using that very gift. When she had said this, the lay follower said to his mother, "Very well, do so."
Thus she made her resolve, but being unable to bring herself to kill her son, she said:
"Who would wish to depart from a beloved son, obtained with such difficulty, who calls out 'Mother, Mother!
so dearly, with his beautiful dark eyes and handsome face?"
"Even when about to kill his mother, he weeps for his mother alone:
'I cannot bring myself to kill her; my heart trembles.
Having spoken thus, he sent the son to his father, saying, "Master, I am unable to kill the son; you must kill him. Then the father also, being unable to kill him, spoke as follows. For it is said:
Sons, celebrated as "sons," alleviate the suffering of their father;
sons bring happiness to their father's suffering and are always his heirs.
Therefore, [I have] a son like myself, a young child who speaks so sweetly.
"I am not able, O lady, to separate you from life.
One who kills his own son incurs infamy and ill repute;
indeed, such a man experiences the kamma of taking life."
Having spoken thus, he sent word: "Kill your own son yourself.
When he had said this, those seeking a means to take Māra's life spoke as follows: "We are not able to kill him;
however, behind our house there is a great anthill where a certain Nāga king resides. We shall send the prince there."

"Having bitten him, he will kill him. Thinking, "This indeed is the means," they summoned the prince, adorned him with necklaces, bracelets, and other ornaments, placed a ball in his hand, and sent him off, saying, "Dear boy, go to the vicinity of the anthill in the backyard and play.
Then the boy went there and began playing with the ball.
He dropped a ball into the hole of an anthill. Then, thinking, "I shall catch the ball," he thrust his hand into the hollow of the anthill.

Thereupon, the snake, becoming enraged, raised its head from the hole and stood watching with its great hood expanded, making a hissing sound like the noise of a whistling reed, as if the noose had slipped from the boy's hand. Then, for him—
The prince, knowing nothing at all, grasped the serpent’s neck firmly.
Then, through the power of his parents’ faith, the Naga king caused a wish-fulfilling eight-faceted throat-jewel (*kaṇṭhamaṇiratana*) to fall into the prince’s palm.
Standing by the door and watching his son’s actions, the prince’s parents saw that jewel and quickly—

Having gone there and lifted their son, they took the jewel-treasure from his hand. Then, having placed that jewel-treasure upon a pure seat and performed the preliminary rites, they made this request:
"Give us this and that. Thereupon, by the power of the jewel-treasure, they had a great pavilion constructed at the door of their house;
having adorned the pavilion with canopies and other ornaments, they prepared seats for the bhikkhus.
Having prepared the ground and seated those sixty monks, they gave a great almsgiving.
Then, having heard of the power of the jewel-treasure, the city-dwellers gathered together.

Thereupon, in their midst, he proclaimed the acquisition of the jewel-treasure through the power of his own faith, saying, "I shall relinquish this for the sake of the gift alone," and having established it in one place, by its power—
"Those who give gifts and guard their virtue for as long as they live are reborn in the world of the devas at the end of their lifespan.
Having severed affection even for one's own kinsmen,
they give gifts here among human beings.
"What man, indeed, who is prosperous, would not give,
when he remembers that giving is the fruit of giving?
This is the seventh story, concerning a son.
38. This is the sequential narrative concerning the story of the three brothers, the honey-merchants.
In the past, it is said, those three brothers lived together in Benares, supporting their wives and children by selling honey.
Then, one of them went to the borderlands and [obtained] honey from the hands of the Malaya-dwellers (or, according to some readings, the Mala-dwellers).
"Kiṇitvā" (having bought) and "vakkiṇitvā" (having sold)—these terms apply everywhere: one person would buy honey wherever it was found and bring it to the city;
another, having sat down in Bārāṇasī, would sell the honey brought by the former. At that time, a certain Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana was afflicted with a disease of the wounds.
Then, another Paccekabuddha [provided] him with honey...
Knowing that it would be comfortable there, he remained on Mount Gandhamādana itself;

having put on his robe and traveled through the air, he descended at the city gate and stood there looking about, wondering, "Where can I obtain honey? and observing everywhere where it might be found.
At that time, a certain maidservant who was living by working for hire in another family had taken a water-jar for the purpose of fetching water.
As she was going to the bathing place, having stepped off the path, set down her water-pot, and paid homage, she stood to one side.
Then the Paccekabuddha asked, "Sister, among those who are wandering for alms here, at which place can honey be obtained?
Having heard his words, she stood at the spot where the honey-shop was located and extended her hand.
"Venerable sir, this is a honey-shop," she said, pointing it out.
Thinking, "If this Paccekabuddha does not obtain honey from the shop, I will give him honey even by giving him the cloth I am wearing," she stood right there looking on.
Then, as the Paccekabuddha wandered on gradually from place to place, he eventually arrived at that very honey-shop.
Then a householder, seeing him, took the bowl from his hand, placed it on a stand, and taking a jar of honey, as he was offering it toward the bowl, he accidentally turned it upside down.
Then, as the honey filled the bowl and overflowed, it flowed back onto the ground. Seeing this, the merchant Somanassa made this aspiration:
For it is said in the Mahāvaṃsa:
"There, toward the Buddha who had received the bowl, that merchant, filled with faith,
gave honey from his own mouth, pouring it until the bowl was full."
Seeing the honey that was full, overflowing, and fallen upon the ground, he was filled with faith and then made this aspiration:
"By means of this gift, may I possess sole sovereignty over Jambudīpa."
"Your command shall extend for a league in the sky and for a league upon the earth.
Having spoken thus, he gave him the bowl. The Paccekabuddha accepted the bowl and remained standing right there:
"May whatever you have desired and prayed for be fulfilled for you very quickly!"
May your heart’s aspirations be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
May everything you desire and pray for be entirely accomplished;
may your heart’s aspirations be fulfilled, like the radiance of a wish-fulfilling gem.

Having spoken thus and increased their merit, he departed. Then, as they were on the way, a water-carrier girl standing by the road approached the Paccekabuddha and asked, "Venerable sir, did you receive any honey? He replied, "I received it, sister.
She asked, "What did he say before giving it to you? The Paccekabuddha told her everything. Having heard this, she said, "Venerable sir, please stay right here for a short while."

"For the sake of favoring the maidservant": having gone quickly home, she put on her old ragged garment (*piḷotika*), washed her own sarong, brought it back, made it into a cushion, and gave it to the Paccekabuddha.
Then, making an aspiration while saying, "O Venerable One, when that giver of honey rules over the entire Jambudīpa as a sole monarch, may I become his chief queen," she spoke thus.
"Venerable sir, when you become a king upon this earth, O giver of honey, I shall then be his beloved chief queen—
beautiful in form, sweet-voiced, of noble lineage, virtuous in conduct, and radiant."
"May she be dear to you, pleasant, and grant your every wish"—thus he spoke at one time.
Then, having uttered this blessing, "May it be so for her as well," the Paccekabuddha departed through the air back to Mount Gandhamādana.
Later on, those three of them, having come together, were preparing a honey-mixture when they saw that jar of honey.
They asked, "Where? He told them of the deed he had done himself and said, "If you would approve of my merit in that matter, it would be well;

if not, take from my hand honey worth its weight. When they replied, "We have no need for that," and when they added everywhere, "It is not from our own hand," and further asked, "What kind of honey did he give you? the other, having heard this—
"There are those called Paccekabuddhas who dwell on Mount Gandhamādana; having donned saffron robes, they wander for alms from house to house.
These are peaceful and virtuous," he said. Then, among them, the eldest, Brāhmaṇacaṇḍāla, was also wandering about wearing saffron robes.
"Surely this one is a Caṇḍāla," he thought, and said so. The middle one became angry and [replied], "Your Paccekabuddha..."

"Throw him into the great ocean," he said. Then, having heard their words, the giver of honey restrained them in many ways, saying, "Sirs, do not speak harshly to the Paccekabuddhas, who are noble, of great authority, and of great power;
do you not fear the sufferings of hell? and so forth. Having thus proclaimed their virtues, both of them, upon hearing this—
With hearts full of serene confidence, they rejoiced, saying, "Excellent!

Later on, having passed away and wandered through the realms of gods and humans, experiencing great prosperity in various places, they were reborn in their respective destinations two hundred years after the final passing (parinibbāṇa) of our Teacher. Thus it was said.
Asoka was Madhudosandhi, Mittādevī was a maidservant,
Nigrodha was a speaker of insults, and Tissa was a proponent of the other side.
Among them, Nigrodha, the speaker of insults, was the son of Sumanarājakumāra, the eldest son of King Bindusāra, who was himself the eldest merchant.
Having offered [the sacrifice], he was reborn. This is the account of his lineage:

it is said that while King Bindusāra was still weak, Prince Aśoka abandoned the kingdom of Ujjenī which he had obtained, came here, brought the entire city under his own control, and seized Prince Sumanas. On that very same day, Prince Sumanas had a queen named Sumanā.

Her pregnancy reached full term. She went out in disguise and, while traveling toward a certain village of Caṇḍālas not far away, she heard the voice of a deity dwelling in a banyan tree near the house of the chief Caṇḍāla, who was saying, "Come here, Sumanā! Upon hearing this, she approached that tree.
The deity, by her own supernatural power, fashioned a single *sāla* tree and gave it to her, saying, "Dwell here.
She entered that *sāla* tree, and on the very day she arrived, she gave birth to a son.
Because he was protected by the deity of the *nigrodha* tree, she gave him the name Nigrodha. From the day he was seen, the eldest outcaste [treated] him as his own sister's son.
Thinking as if it were so, he established a regular routine of service. The princess lived there for seven years, and Prince Nigrodha also reached the age of seven.
At that time, a certain Arahant named Mahāvaruṇa Thera, while staying in residence, saw the boy’s perfection of causal conditions and thought, "The boy is now seven years old;
it is time to ordain him. Having thus reflected, he had the matter announced to the princess.
He ordained Prince Nigrodha, and the prince attained *arahantship* at the very edge of the razor-sharp blade. Thus it is said in the Mahāvaṃsa:
"Then the Elder Mahāvaruṇa, seeing that boy endowed with the necessary conditions for liberation (*upanissaya*), asked his mother: 'Is he an *arahant*?'"
"He ordained him at the edge of the razor; he attained arahantship.

It is said that one day, having attended to his body early in the morning and performed the duties toward his teacher and preceptor, he took his bowl and robes and set out, thinking, "I shall go to the door of my mother’s house. And her dwelling place was by the southern gate.
Having entered the city and gone through its center, he was to depart by the eastern gate.
At that time, King Asoka, the Dhamma-king, was walking back and forth in the eastern direction within the lion-window.
At that very moment, Nigrodha reached the royal courtyard with his faculties and mind composed, looking only a yoke’s length ahead. By means of that—

It is said that one day, while standing at the lion-window, he saw the novice Nigrodha walking through the royal courtyard—tamed, guarded, with senses calmed, and perfected in his deportment. Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him:
"All these people have distracted minds, resembling wild animals wandering about; yet this youth is undistracted and exceedingly [serene]."
His looking forward and looking around, as well as his contracting and extending [the limbs], were graceful. "Surely there must be supramundane Dhamma within him," thought the king;
at the mere sight of the novice, his mind became serene and affection was established. Why?
It is said that in the past, when he was performing meritorious deeds, this novice had been the king’s elder brother, a merchant.
"Either through former co-residence in a previous life, or through benefit received in the present, such affection arises for him, just as a lotus [grows] from water.
Then the king, having conceived affection and great respect, sent his ministers with the command, "Summon the novice! But they delayed for too long.
Again, he sent two or three messengers, saying, "Let him come quickly. The novice went by his own natural pace.

The king, recognizing that a suitable seat had been prepared, said, "Be seated. He looked here and there and, seeing that there were no other monks present, approached the royal throne under the raised white parasol; he observed the king’s gesture for him to take the bowl.
He showed it [to him]. As soon as the king saw the novice approaching the couch, he thought, "Today this novice shall indeed become the master of this house.
The novice placed his bowl in the king's hand, ascended the couch, and sat down.
The king [presented] all the varieties of rice-gruel, hard food, and cooked meals prepared for his own use.
He offered it to him. The novice accepted only as much as was necessary for his own sustenance.
At the conclusion of the meal, the king said, "Do you know the instruction given to you by the Teacher? "I know it, Great King, though only in part. "Dear son, tell it to me as well.
"Very well, Great King," he replied, and for the sake of offering thanks, he recited a verse from the *Appamādavagga* (Chapter on Heedfulness) that was appropriate for the king.
He spoke thus. But the king, having heard that "heedfulness is the path to the Deathless, while heedlessness is the path of death," said, "I have understood, dear one;

please finish [the recitation]. At the conclusion of the thanksgiving, the novice received thirty-two regular meals and thirty-two meal-shifts—thus obtaining them everywhere—and on the following day, taking thirty-two bhikkhus with him, he entered the royal palace.

He performed his meal duties. By this very means, the king increased the number day after day, saying, "Let thirty-two other monks also receive almsfood with you," until he had cut off the food supply for sixty thousand brahmins and wanderers,
and established a permanent meal within his own residence for sixty thousand monks.

[The King was established] through the very faith inspired by the Elder Nigrodha. The Elder Nigrodha, in turn, having established the King and his retinue in the three refuges and the five precepts, caused them to establish an unshakable faith within the Buddha’s teaching, based on a faith that transcends the level of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The King, moreover, having had the great monastery named Asokārāma constructed, [provided for] sixty thousand monks...
He established a regular provision of food. Throughout the entire Jambudīpa, in eighty-four thousand cities, he had eighty-four thousand monasteries constructed.
Therefore it was said:
"By the fault of speaking like a caṇḍāla..."
Born in a village of Caṇḍālas,
he attained the joy of realization;
he was free from all taints— thus it is said in some places that he was one without outflows (anāsava).
This is the narrative method regarding the Elder Nigrodha.

As for the merchant Madhudāyaka, having passed away from the deva-world and been reborn in a royal family in Pupphapura, he became the prince named Piya-dāsa; and having had the royal parasol raised over him, he exercised sole sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa.
How so? King Bindusāra had one hundred sons. All of them, except for Tissa-kumāra, who was of the same mother as himself, were [deprived by] Asoka...

Having set them aside, he had them executed. While exercising rule for four years without being formally consecrated, at the end of those four years—in the eighteenth year after the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata—he attained the consecration of sole sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa.
Then, throughout the eighty-four thousand cities of the whole Jambudīpa...
Kings would come and wait upon him. He had three palaces suitable for the three seasons:
one called Mahāsappika, one Moragīva, and one named Maṅgala; in these he resided, surrounded by many thousands of dancers.
She who showed him the honey shop was the king’s daughter named Asandhimittā, who was like a celestial nymph.
She was the eldest of sixty thousand women and became the chief queen of King Dhammāsoka. Immediately after his consecration, these royal powers came to him:
his command prevailed throughout the earth for a depth of one *yojana*, and likewise in the sky above.
From Lake Anotatta, deities daily brought sixteen water-jars by means of eight baskets.
They brought [the tooth-sticks]. Having conceived faith in the Teaching, he gave eight jars to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
two jars to about sixty bhikkhus who were masters of the Tipiṭaka; two jars to the chief queen Asandhimittā; and four jars he used himself.
"Devatā, devatā" [was said] thus everywhere. Thus, from the Himālayas, the Nāga-creeper tooth-stick...
Every day they brought him oil, soft [food], and delicious [food];
by means of this, the daily requirement for tooth-sticks was fulfilled for the king, the chief queen, the sixteen thousand dancers, and the sixty thousand monks.
Day after day, deities also brought him *agada*-myrobalan, *agada*-pumpkin, and gold-colored [fruits] endowed with fragrance and flavor.
They brought mangoes cooked in honey. From the Chaddanta Lake, they brought five-colored robes for wearing, a yellow-colored hand-towel and a hand-wiping cloth—in all such cases—and celestial drink.
Day by day, from the Nāga realm, they brought fragrant ointments, a non-woven cloth made of jasmine flowers for his clothing, and highly precious collyrium.
The dragon kings bring [the grain]. From the very waters of the Chaddanta Lake, they bring nine thousand new cartloads of rice every day.
The mice make it free of husks; not even a single broken grain remains.
In all the king’s quarters, only this rice is used for consumption. Honey-bees produce honey.
In the smithies, hammers struck the anvils with a clear sound. Karavīka birds came and performed an offering for the king, warbling with sweet voices.

Endowed with these supernatural powers, one day the king sent a golden chain as a gift and summoned Mahākāla, the Nāga King, who had beheld the forms of the four Buddhas and possessed a lifespan of an eon.
Having seated him upon a magnificent couch beneath a white parasol,

having performed worship with hundreds of varieties of water-born and land-born flowers as well as golden flowers, and having surrounded him on all sides by sixteen thousand dancers adorned with every ornament—
[I pay homage] to that Perfectly Enlightened One, the Wheel-Turner of the Excellent True Dhamma, possessed of infinite knowledge.
Having said, "Bring the form of the Perfectly Enlightened One within the range of these eyes," he manifested [the Buddha],
who was adorned with the eighty minor marks produced by the radiance of merit scattered throughout his entire body,
and who, through the splendor of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, appeared like a blossoming *kamala*, *uppala*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotus.
The surface of the water was like the vault of heaven, resplendent with a shimmering beauty from the spreading mass of rays from the clusters of stars;
it was as if the summit of the Golden Mountain were encircled by rainbows, lightning, and the radiance of the sun, all gathered together;
its beautiful crest was made radiant by a garland of victory banners of various pure colors, appearing like a veritable elixir for the eyes.
And for seven days, beholding the form of the Buddha, he performed what is known as the "eye-worship" (akkhipūjā) for the hosts of Brahmas, gods, humans, nāgas, and yakkhas.
It is said that after receiving his consecration, the king adhered to non-Buddhist sects for exactly three years;
in the fourth year, he gained faith in the Buddha’s teaching. His father, however, Bindusāra, was devoted to the Brāhmaṇas.
He established a regular meal for sixty thousand brahmins, brahmin sectarians, and white-robed wanderers. Asoka, too,
giving away the same alms as his father throughout his inner apartments and all his palaces,
one day stood at the lion-window and, with a mind devoid of tranquility—
Seeing them eating with improper conduct, their senses unrestrained, and their deportment undisciplined, he thought: "Having examined such an offering, it is right to give it to those who are worthy.

Having thought thus, he said to his ministers: "Go, sirs, and bring into the inner apartments those ascetics and brahmins whom each of you considers most virtuous; I shall give alms. The ministers replied: "Very well, Your Majesty."
Having assented to the king, those various white-robed wanderers, Jīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, and others, brought them forward and said, "Great King, these are our Arahants.

Then the king, having had high and low seats prepared within the inner palace, said, "Let them come," and as they arrived one after another, he said, "Sit on seats suitable for yourselves. Some sat on fine chairs, some...
They sat upon wooden benches; seeing this, the king realized, "There is no solid core within them," and having given them food and drink appropriate for their status, he dismissed them.
As time passed in this manner, one day, while standing at the lion-window, he saw the novice Nigrodha.
Through the faith that arose toward him, he became devoted to the Buddha’s teaching, and [he gave] sixty thousand [pieces of gold].
Having removed the heretics and fed sixty thousand bhikkhus, having gained faith in the Buddha’s teaching,
and having constructed the Asokārāma and settled them there, he one day gave a gift to the sixty thousand bhikkhus in the Asokārāma.
Sitting in their midst and entertaining the Saṅgha with the four requisites, he asked this question, "Venerable sirs..."

"How much, sire, is that which is called the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One? "Great King, there are nine divisions (aṅga), and according to the aggregates (khandha), there are eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma.
Having gained confidence in the Dhamma, the king thought, "I shall honor each single aggregate of Dhamma with a single monastery.
On that very same day, he disbursed ninety-six crores of gold and commanded his ministers: "In each city, [build] one monastery."

He commanded, "Have eighty-four thousand monasteries built in eighty-four thousand cities," and he himself began the work for the sake of the Asoka Mahāvihāra at the Asoka Monastery, saying, "For the sake of the Asoka Monastery.
The Saṅgha appointed the Elder Indagutta— possessed of great psychic power, great majesty, and whose taints were exhausted— as the overseer of the new construction.
The Elder completed whatever was not finished by means of his own supernatural power;
thus, within seven years, he brought the construction of the monastery to completion. On a single day, letters arrived from all the cities.
The ministers reported to the king: "Your Majesty, eighty-four thousand great monasteries are finished. Then the king—
Having approached the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he asked, "Venerable sirs, eighty-four thousand monasteries have been built by me; from where shall I obtain relics? [The bhikkhus replied:
"Great King, we have heard that there is indeed a relic-treasury, but it is not known to be in such-and-such a place.
The king had the Cetiya at Rājagaha demolished; not seeing the relic, he had it restored to its original state.
Taking with him the four assemblies—the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—he went to Vesālī.
Not obtaining [permission] there either, he went to Kapilavatthu; not obtaining it there either, he went to Rāmagāma. At Rāmagāma, the Nāgas did not allow the stupa to be broken.
The spade that fell upon the stupa was shattered into pieces; thus, not obtaining it there either—
Having demolished all the shrines from Allakappa, Pāvā, and Kusinārā, and having failed to find the relics, he restored them to their original state.
Then, returning to Rājagaha, he convened the four assemblies and asked: "Has anyone ever heard of a relic deposit being made in such-and-such a place?
Thereupon, an elder of one hundred and twenty years said: "In such-and-such a place there was a relic deposit."
"I do not know. However, when I was seven years old, my grandfather Thera had me take a flower-basket and said, 'Come, novice, there is a stone stupa in such-and-such a grove. Let us go there.
Having gone and made offerings, he said, 'It is fitting for you, novice, to investigate this site. Great King, I know only this."
The king, saying "This is the very spot," went there and had it excavated; having removed the stone stupa and the earth, he saw the plastered floor beneath.

Then, having had the plaster and the bricks removed, he gradually descended into the courtyard and saw sand made of the seven precious gems and wooden figures with swords in their hands rolling about; he [saw] the yakṣa-slaves...

Having summoned them and even having had an offering of oblations performed, he said: "Since I do not see an end [to this], I shall pay homage to the deities, take these relics, and enshrine them within eighty-four thousand monasteries, performing honor for them. May the deities not create obstacles for me!
While wandering on his tour, Sakka, the King of Devas, saw him and addressed Vissakamma, saying: "Dear son..."
King Aśoka Dhammarāja, thinking, "I shall have the relics brought out," entered the monastery enclosure. Having gone there, he commanded, "Have the wooden figures removed.
He went in the guise of a village boy from Pañcacūlaka, stood before the king with a bow in his hand, and said, "Shall I carry them away, Great King?
"Carry them away, my dear," [the king replied]. Taking an arrow, he pierced the very joint [of the structure], and everything was scattered about. Then—
The king took the key and seal from the casket; seeing the mass of jewels and reading the inscription on the leaf which said,
"In the future, may poor kings take this gem and pay honor to the relics," he became angry and said,
"But for kings like me— [the word] 'king' occurs everywhere [in the inscription]— to call them 'poor kings'!"
Thinking, "This is improper," he repeatedly tried to open the door until finally it opened, and he entered the interior of the house.
There, lamps that had been burning for more than two hundred and eighteen years continued to blaze exactly as before;
flower carpets appeared at that very moment as if blue lotus flowers had just been brought and arranged, and fragrances wafted at that instant.
They became as if they had been ground and set aside. The King took a golden plate and, having read:
"In the future, a prince named Piya-dāsa shall raise the royal parasol and become the Dhamma-king named Aśoka;
he will cause these relics to be distributed," he said, "I have been seen by the noble Elder Mahākassapa," and folding his left hand, with his right hand—

He clapped his hands. At that spot, having left behind only the relics for veneration and taking all the remaining relics, he closed the relic chamber in the same manner as it had been previously sealed.
Having restored everything to its original state and enshrined [the relics] in the stone stūpa above, he established the relics in the eighty-four thousand monasteries.
Then one day, having gone to the monastery and paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the king sat to one side and said:
"Venerable sir, even if I were to spend ninety-six billion pieces of wealth and have eighty-four thousand monasteries and cetiyas built, I would not be an heir.
Who else would be an heir? [The Buddha replied: "O Great King, you are indeed called a donor of requisites; however, he who..."
"When it is said that one who ordains both a son and a daughter is called an heir to the Teaching," King Asoka,
aspiring to the status of an heir to the Teaching, saw Prince Mahinda standing nearby and asked, "My dear son, will you be able to go forth?
Having heard the king's words, the prince— who already desired to go forth by his own nature— was filled with exceeding joy.
"I go forth, I go forth," he said thus at every instance, O King. "Having ordained me, become an heir to the Teaching," he said.
At that time, the king’s daughter Saṅghamittā was also standing in that place. Seeing her, [the prince] said, "Mother, will you also be able to go forth?
"Very well, dear brother," she replied, consenting. Having obtained the consent of his children, the king—
With a joyful heart, he approached the community of monks and said, "Venerable sirs, please ordain these boys and make them heirs to my teaching.

The Saṅgha, having accepted the king’s request, had the prince ordained with the Elder Moggaliputtatissa as preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and the Elder Mahādeva as teacher (*ācariya*). [The word] "had ordained" (*pabbajjāpesi*) applies in all instances. By the Elder Majjhantika...
The teacher ordained him, and at the very moment of his ordination, he attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
For the royal princess Saṅghamittā as well, her preceptor was the nun named Therī Āyupālā—this name, "Therī Āyupālā," applies everywhere [in the relevant texts].
Her preceptress was the nun named Therī Dhammapālā. As for the King, however, he [supported] the Buddha’s Dispensation in manifold ways.

Having purified [the Saṅgha] with the assistance, help, and aid of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, he expelled sixty thousand immoral heretics from the Buddha’s dispensation and brought the Third Council to completion.
Regarding that assembly, it is asked: "How many monks and how many nuns were there?"—thus it is stated in all such cases; for it has been said:
At that assembly, there were eighty crores of bhikkhus;
among them, there were one hundred thousand ascetics whose taints were exhausted.
There were nine million bhikkhunīs present there.
"And among them, there were one thousand bhikkhunīs whose taints were destroyed.

Thus, that King Asoka, having become the preeminent king over the whole of Jambudīpa, dwelt adorning the Buddha’s dispensation. This is the summary here; the detailed account, however, is told in the Mahāvaṃsa. For it is said:
"Because of its completeness, this Tisso is like a honey-footed bee; its intentions are full of sweetness."
"He attained success everywhere, at all times, and in every way.
As for the merchant Majjhima, however, due to his fault of speaking ill of others, he was reborn on Laṅkā in the great ocean.
His sequence of events should be understood as follows: it is said that in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, a king named Muṭasīva reigned for sixty years.
He had ten sons, endowed with the virtues of merit and wisdom, who were mutually devoted to one another’s welfare, as well as two daughters;
all of them lived together in harmony and mutual affection. Then, at a later time, when King Muṭasīva had passed away, the ministers anointed Prince Devānaṃpiyatissa as king.
At the very moment of his consecration, many wonders occurred for him.
The teachers of the Mahāvaṃsa narrative, explaining these matters, have said:

"Among those [sons], the second son, renowned as Devānaṃpiyatissa, was the most meritorious and possessed of the greatest wisdom among all ten brothers. (In some places, the name is given as Muṭasīva).
Upon the passing of his father, he became King Devānampiyatissa.
Simultaneously with his consecration, many wonders occurred throughout the entire island of Laṅkā, including hidden treasures and precious gems.
Having risen up from within, they ascended the surface of the earth.
Having reached the vicinity of the island of Laṅkā on their broken ship,
those jewels born there ascended onto dry land.
At the foot of Mount Chāta, three bamboo poles grew there,
equal in measure to a chariot goad. Among them,
one was a creeper-staff, and there the creeper had the luster of silver.
Golden-hued and radiant, these delightful trees are seen.
Upon one tree there is a cluster of flowers;
various flowers of diverse colors are seen there, blooming in full splendor.
There was a single bird-bone, yet there were many birds and deer there;
various and of diverse colors, they appeared as if they were still alive.
There were horses, elephants, and chariots, all soiled with dust, along with bracelets and finger-rings.
The kakudha fruits were naturally ripe; such were the eight kinds [of offerings].
Pearls rose up from the ocean and settled in rows upon the shore;
all this was the manifestation of the merit of Devānampiyatissa.
Sapphire, beryl, and ruby gems— these jewels, as well as pearls and those staffs,
were brought into the presence of the king within seven days itself.
At that time, the Great King Devānampiyatissa and the Dharma-king Aśoka were friends who had never met.
Therefore, he sent these jewels and many other gifts as an offering for the great lord of men, Dharmāśoka, with the message: "Give these to my friend.
Upon seeing them, the latter was filled with faith and [sent] the five insignia of royalty and other [gifts].
And he sent many kinds of gifts for the purpose of his consecration, saying, "Let them perform the consecration for my friend.
Not only did he send these material gifts, it is said, but he also sent this gift of the Dhamma:
"I have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha."
I declared myself a lay follower in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans.
O Supreme among Men, having inspired confidence in my heart regarding these three most excellent matters, I go for refuge out of faith.
The ministers, having returned to Laṅkā, consecrated the king.
At that time, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, while investigating where in the future the Teaching would become well-established, perceived that it would be well-established in the border regions;
he then dispatched various elders to those respective places and [sent] the Elder Mahāmahinda—
"Go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and inspire confidence there," he instructed. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Elder Mahāmahinda and said:
"Venerable sir, King Muṭasīva has passed away. Now the Great King Devānampiyatissa rules the kingdom.
And you were prophesied by the Perfectly Enlightened One as a monk named Mahinda who would [go] to the island of Tambapaṇṇi in the future."
"May he inspire faith. Therefore, venerable sir, it is now the time to go to Dīpavara; I too shall be your companion.

Having accepted his words, the Elder rose into the air from the Cetiyapabbata monastery, accompanied by himself as the seventh, and alighted on Mount Missaka to the east of Anurādhapura. This is what is known today as Cetiyapabbata.
They perceived it. At that time, it was a festival day in Tambapaṇṇi;
the king, having commanded his ministers, "Celebrate a festival," set out from the city surrounded by forty-four thousand men and proceeded to Mount Missaka, desiring to sport in the hunt.
Then, a certain deity dwelling on that mountain thought, "I shall show the Elder to the king."
A deer with the color of a rohita fish was grazing on grass and leaves nearby; thinking it was improper now to shoot at one who was heedless, the king pressed his bowstring.
The deer began to flee by way of the Ambatthala road, and the king, pursuing him, ascended to Ambatthala itself.
The deer vanished not far from the elders, and the Elder Mahinda—
Having resolved, "Let the king see me alone as I approach from nearby; let him not see the others," he said, "Tissa, Tissa, come here!
When the king heard this, he thought: "In this island of Tambapaṇṇi, there is no one born who is capable of addressing me by the name 'Tissa.
Yet this man, wearing torn and ragged garments and a coarse saffron robe..."
"Vasana addresses me by name; who indeed might this be—is he a human or a non-human? The Elder said:
"We are recluses, O Great King, disciples of the Dhamma-King;
out of compassion for you alone, we have come here from Jambudīpa."
Recalling the message sent by King Dhammāsoka, the lord of men, he thought, "Have the noble ones arrived?
and immediately laid aside his weapons and sat to one side, engaging in friendly and courteous conversation—engaging in all manner of polite and welcoming discourse.
As he did so, those forty thousand men also arrived and surrounded him.
Then the Elder showed the others as well; having seen them, the king asked, "When did these people arrive? [The Elder replied,] "Great King, they arrived together with me.
"But now, Great King, there are other such ascetics in Jambudīpa as well.
"Great King, at present Jambudīpa is ablaze with the saffron robes and fanned by the wind of the seers."
“Possessors of the threefold knowledge, attained to psychic powers, skilled in the full understanding of the minds of others, Arhats with taints destroyed—many such were the disciples of the Buddha.

Upon hearing this, the king was filled with faith. Then the Elder, having discerned the clarity of his wisdom through the simile of the tree and other means, taught the Dhamma while the humans and devas raised shouts of “Excellent! Thus it was spoken.
Knowing him to be wise, the Elder taught the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta, O high-minded Mahīpāla.
At the conclusion of the teaching, he, together with those forty thousand men, was established in the refuges.
Then the king, having requested, "Venerable sir, please accept almsfood at my home tomorrow," departed.
He had the city and the royal palace decorated, seated the Elders, and served them with exquisite food.
Then, together with five hundred women headed by Queen Anulā, he sat down to one side. Thereupon, the Elder caused the rain of the jewel of the Dhamma to fall. Then those five hundred women—

They attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*). Then, one thousand in the elephant stable and one thousand in the Nandana Grove—thus on the second day, he established two thousand five hundred living beings in the fruit of stream-entry.
On the third day, eight thousand five hundred living beings; thus, for many hundreds, many thousands, and many hundreds of thousands.
He caused the Dhamma to drink the nectar of the dead.
For it is said: "The great sun Mahinda, situated in the midst of the sky that is Laṅkā, caused the lotuses of those to be enlightened to bloom with the rays of the Dhamma."
That Mahāmahindacanda, situated in the midst of Laṅkā’s atmosphere,
awakened the beds of night-lotuses of those ready for training with the rays of the Dhamma.
That Mahāmahindamegha rained down a shower of the waters of the Dhamma.
"He has caused the sprouts of merit to arise within the mental seeds of the virtuous.
Then the King, having had the relics filling the alms-bowl used by the Perfectly Enlightened One brought from the hand of the novice Sumana,
and having had the relic of the right collar-bone brought from Sakka— thus, in every respect at Cetiyapabbata—
Beginning with the [Mahā] Thūpa, he had stūpas constructed at every yojana throughout the entire island of Laṅkā;

having enshrined the Southern Relic there, he established the Thūpārāma Stūpa. Then, having installed the great southern branch of the Jayamahābodhi brought by the Therī Saṅghamittā, he performed worship.
The full detail of this account, however, is to be understood from the Mahāvaṃsa.
Thus, through the fault of his opponent, he was born in the ocean of enemies;
having thus attained approval, he became the lord of Laṅkā.
Thinking, "Even evil bears fruit in this way," [he reflected].
"Knowing that this is the fruit of merit,
O sirs, perform meritorious deeds with wise reflection,
so that having gone there, you shall not grieve."
The eighth story: The Story of the Three Honey-Merchants.
39. Regarding the daughter of King Bodhi—this being the sequence of the narrative throughout the story:
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna and the Dispensation was well-established in Laṅkā, there was a village there called Hakureḷi.
There, a certain young girl was staying, playing here and there together with other village girls.
At that time, there was a large pond near the village. There stood a *marutthara* tree which remained perpetually covered in blossoms.
People, gathering flowers for the purpose of worshipping the Buddha, would descend into the water, climb the tree, and pluck the flowers.

Seeing her, the people thought, "Let them go with ease and gather flowers," so they brought a single dry *pālibhadda* staff, made it into a bridge, and set it up. From then on, people went by that way and gathered flowers.
Then, having passed away from there, by virtue of that same wholesome kamma, she was reborn in the city of Pāṭaliputta in Jambudīpa, in the household of King Somadatta.
Having been offered as a sacrifice, she was reborn, possessing a supreme form and resembling a celestial nymph (*devaccharā*). Her parents, however, addressed her as "Princess Bodhirājakumārī.
By the power of merit performed in the past, a single colt named Suvīraka, capable of traveling through the air, was born for her.
Furthermore, the father of the princess was one who held the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha as his mother.

Having performed offerings and generating great merit, he saw a young Sindhava horse and, his mind filled with joy at the thought, "I have found a companion for the performance of meritorious deeds," he mounted the horse and went three times a day to pay homage to the Great Bodhi tree.
When the princess saw him, she went to her father and asked repeatedly, "Father, where do you go so often? The king said nothing.
He spoke, and then she, persisting again and again, questioned her father. Thereupon the king, complying with her, said this:
"In former times, while fulfilling the ten perfections, our Blessed One gave away his head, his blood, his eyes, his flesh, and even his life."
Having attained and then relinquished both his wife and sovereignty, and having reached the ultimate pinnacle of perfection—
having spent no small number of millions of years in Kapilavatthu—
he was born into the Sakya royal family as one who has no equal in the world.
Having renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch, the Lord of Men,
seeing the four omens, went forth from his home and departed;
having approached the foot of the Bodhi tree, he sat upon the diamond throne.
Having manifested himself with a thousand arms, crowded with various weapons— [the phrase] "crowded with various weapons" applies everywhere—
he assumed a terrifying appearance resembling a black mountain.
Having manifested this form, he mounted the elephant Girimekhala.
Having summoned the army of Māra, the one who bears the dolphin-banner arrived.
By the power of the perfections, having put that army of Māra to flight,
the Victor sat where he was and destroyed the thousand-fold host of the enemy of defilements.

I go constantly to pay homage to that Victorious Bodhi tree, which for seven days was served by the Jina with abundant showers of water, and which is honored by gods, brahmas, siddhas, uragas, humans, and others.
That person who, having gone there, always reveres the Bodhi tree with various offerings such as perfumed water,
lamps, and incense, doing so thoroughly—
such a person becomes free from disease both for themselves and for others.
He becomes honored and respected, long-lived, powerful, and happy.
Therefore, by a person who desires their own welfare and seeks that goal,
the row of Bodhi trees should always be venerated with faith.
Having heard this, the young woman, her body suffused with joy, paid homage to her father and said, "Father, I too shall go.
However, the king did not wish for her departure due to fear of misfortune. Then, having entreated her father up to three times, she was permitted by the king.
From that time on, she constantly mounted a thoroughbred horse with her father to pay homage to the Bodhi tree.
He went. Then, at a later time, the king, lying upon his deathbed, thought: "My daughter goes constantly to attend upon Bodhi;
whatever fear may arise for her in the future will arise from that [tree]. What should I do about this?
Thereupon, having summoned his horse-keeper and whispering into his ear, he said: "Dear son, my daughter goes frequently..."
"Having made you her companion, she is going to pay homage to the Bodhi tree. Whatever danger might befall her there would be improper;
therefore, protect my daughter during her journeying to and fro. Having thus entrusted his daughter to him, he passed away.
Then the princess, having performed the funeral rites for her father's body, [went] three times a day...
Having ascended her horse, she went to attend upon the Bodhi tree. When people saw the perfection of her beauty, their minds were filled with wonder, and they thought:
"Ah, we have seen a gift worthy of a king! Let us go and inform the king;
perhaps the king might give us something. Having gone into the presence of the king, they paid homage and stood before him, saying this:
Having arrived at the seat of enlightenment, with a mind constantly delighted,
one maiden goes forth worshipping, like lightning flashing with splendor amidst the clouds.
She, bearing a mass of dark-blue lotuses, possessed of large and long eyes;
With a complexion like the sound of a golden lute, her breasts were beautiful and auspicious;
her lower lip was like a rain-cloud mingled with the rays of the sun;
she had a prominent nose and dark eyebrows, and the radiance of her smile was enchanting.
"O Great King, such a thing as this has never been seen by us before, nor has it ever been seen at any time.
Come, O Siri Deva, and you shall see her at the seat of enlightenment.
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart became bound to her by the mere contact of that sound, and he took his fourfold army...
When the princess arrived to pay homage at the Bodhi tree, he had his army surround the outer wall and commanded his men, "Seize her! Thereupon, the army stood ready to capture her.
Seeing them, the princess quickly approached a horse and, sitting upon its back, gave it a signal with her heel. Taking her, he—
She leaped into the air with great speed. However, because she was seated poorly, she was unable to withstand the horse's momentum and slipped from the horse's back.

Seeing the princess falling, the Sindhava horse, remembering the King’s instructions, came galloping forward, bit her by the hair, lifted her up, and having set her down upon his back as she was about to fall, carried her through the air.
Having led him, he established him right there in the city of Pāṭaliputta; [the reading] "he caused him to enter right there in the city of Pāṭaliputta" occurs in some places.
Thinking, "Even animals, when they remember a benefactor, do not abandon him," let all living beings be grateful; [the reading] "let living beings be" occurs in some places.
From that time forth, having performed meritorious deeds,
she became one whose destination was heaven. Whoever honors this tree-king honored by the ascetic Nandana is wise.
He becomes possessed of wealth and free from calamity;
everywhere he is one whose form is praised.
This is the ninth story concerning the daughter of King Bodhi.
40. This is the sequential narrative concerning the story of Kuṇḍaliya.
In the island of Laṅkā, in the district of Rohaṇa, there was a great village named Mahāgāma.
Therein was a monastery called Tissavihāra, crowded with many hundreds of bhikkhus and adorned with numerous monastic cells. There lived a novice named Tissa.
He was dwelling there. On one occasion, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, he entered the village of Pāsāṇavāpi for alms.
Having obtained a meal sufficient for his sustenance along with some ghee, he departed;

and having reached the village gate, as he was walking toward the great village, he asked the people for a place where water was convenient. They replied, "Venerable sir, in a place not far from here, facing you..."
When it was said, "Go there to the place called Kakubandakandara, where the water of the Sandamāna river flows cool;

having bathed on its white-sand banks and sat in the cool shade upon that sandy ground, perform your meal and then depart," the novice replied, "Very well," and having gone there, he sat in a comfortable spot and began to eat his meal. At that time, by one [person]...
A certain female dog, having gone to the forest with a woodcutter, gave birth to her pups in that cave on a certain slope;
being hungry and with her limbs trembling, she lay down near the children.
Having smelled the fragrance of food from the novice’s bowl, she rose from her place, trembling as she approached him.

She stood there wagging her tail; seeing this, the novice, his heart trembling with emotion, placed the first morsel of food he had prepared for himself before her. Then, out of joy, she ate it. Seeing this, he was delighted;
making more and more morsels, he gave her the meal, washed the bowl, and put it away in its bag.

She departed from there. Then, through the faith directed toward the novice monk, that female dog, having passed away from that state, took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the king in Devaputtanagara in Jambudīpa. After ten months had elapsed, she emerged from her mother’s womb;
then, when the day of the hair-cutting ceremony arrived, her parents—because of her hair being curled like earrings (kuṇḍalāvaṭṭaka)—[named her accordingly].
They named her Kuṇḍalā. In due course, she reached the age of sixteen.
At that time, it is said, the novice Tissa, intending to pay homage to the Great Bodhi tree, boarded a ship and traveled to Jambudīpa;
eventually reaching Devaputtanagara, he proceeded through the great street, well-robed and well-clad, looking about the distance of a yoke for alms.
She arrived. The princess opened the lion-window and, looking down the street, saw the novice monk begging for alms;
she felt a resurgence of her former affection, and at that moment, she gained the knowledge of recollecting past births (*jātissara-ñāṇa*).
It is said that in the past, having been a bhikkhunī, she had given a book along with a leaf-pen and oil for a lamp, making the aspiration: "May I possess the knowledge of recollecting past births."
She made an aspiration; then, recollecting her past birth and seeing the service rendered to her by the novice, she was filled with joy.
She had him summoned, prepared a seat in the royal palace, and when he was seated there, she served him various kinds of exquisite food.
When the novice had finished eating and withdrawn his hand from the bowl, she approached him, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Then, by him—
Conversing with him, she spoke thus:
"O wise one, you do not recognize me; formerly I was your slave.
Because of that, I was happy, and therefore you were my master."
Having heard that, the novice said:
"I have no such slave-girl; I do not even know her.
Who are you, or whose daughter are you? Tell me that when asked."
Then, as she was urging him on, she said:
"I urge you today, O Seer, according to how I know this:
awaken now from your awakening, for I remember my former birth."
When you, O Venerable One, having begged for alms in the village of Pāsāṇavāpi, in Tambapaṇṇi, and in Rohaṇa,
sit down at Kakubandakandara and reflect upon the time when you have finished eating your meal.
At that time, I was a female dog, recently whelped and having found food.
Oppressed by hunger and eager to devour the children,
with all my limbs trembling, I stood near you.
Seeing me then, O Bhante, trembling and hungry, you,
having yourself been deprived of food, satisfied me with food.
At that time, with a gentle heart, I brought my mind to faith in you.
By that meritorious deed, in my second existence,
I was born here in a royal family, with all my desires fulfilled,
through the mere clarity of mind I felt toward the teaching of the Lord of the World.
Even for one who has gone forth, such accomplishments as these may exist;
oh, what kind of fruit indeed results from faith in the Perfectly Enlightened One!
Abandoning other duties, he delights in his own welfare.
"Unwearied by day and night, remember the Triple Gem.
Having thus reminded [the monk] of the service performed by the novice, and having invited him, saying, "Venerable sir, out of favor toward your former slave,
please dwell right here," and being accepted by him, he had a great monastery built and placed the novice at its head.
Having prepared [the offerings], he invited many hundreds of bhikkhus, had them dwell in the monastery, and served them with the four requisites so that they were well-supplied.
The novice, too, remembering the gift given by the female dog, was filled with joy; attending to the recollection of the Buddha, he attained Arahantship before long.
Dwelling in that very monastery, he passed away into Parinibbāna right there at the end of his life.
In the three planes, throughout the triple world, there is no giver of the Three Refuges to beings—save for the wish-fulfilling tree of the gods.
The tenth story: Kuṇḍalī.
The fourth chapter, the Mahāsenavagga.
With this, the narrative of the origin of Jambudīpa is completed.
